about: Inferview curriculum v2, synthesised from research/gaps/*.md (harness, workflows, security, training, frontier, ops, loops, formats, level-audit), research/brief.json and SPEC.md section 4. Every lesson, problem, teardown, lab and format carries source URLs; "checked" is the date the source was read by the research pass or during this synthesis. Problem briefs that contain numbers without a source are scenario inputs. Track slugs from SPEC section 4 are kept; six tracks are new and need a SPEC section 4 change before they can ship.

problemTypes.definition: An explanation or decision in prose; the reader types a short answer before the worked answer and follow-ups appear.
problemTypes.grading: Self-rated against the Depth block and follow-ups.

problemTypes.definition: Napkin arithmetic with at least one reader-chosen assumption.
problemTypes.grading: Graded against an accepted band wide enough for reasonable assumptions; the answer names the dominant term.

problemTypes.definition: A trace, log or snippet with a symptom and incomplete evidence; at least two real defects, one of which explains the symptom.
problemTypes.grading: Graded by the hypothesis pick (choices of equal length), then a self-rated ranking of secondary defects.

problemTypes.definition: Python 3 in Pyodide, standard library only, with visible examples and hidden property or invariant tests.
A system to design under an operating constraint, with a "what you give up" statement and a written artefact.
A story prompt at senior or staff scope with pushback follow-ups.
problemTypes.grading: Self-rated from a checklist of signals (ownership, alternatives, measured result, influence).

problemTypes.definition: Three to five options of equal length, every wrong option a belief a senior engineer has held.
problemTypes.grading: Graded; each option has a one-sentence reason shown after answering.

problemTypes.definition: A flawed artefact (design, trace, prompt, config, code or diff) with planted flaws; the reader lists flaws before opening a 6 to 12 item checklist.
problemTypes.grading: Self-rated from the tick ratio; not counted for the streak.

problemTypes.definition: A business process with constraints; the reader designs steps, state, retries, idempotency, approvals, budgets and rollout.
problemTypes.grading: Self-rated against a checklist; optionally partly graded by a fault-injecting workflow simulator.

problemTypes.definition: A progressive coding problem of three or four stages, each adding requirements and hidden tests, with a visible clock (the CodeSignal-style format reported at Anthropic, OpenAI, Ramp and Perplexity).
problemTypes.grading: Graded per stage by hidden tests; the stage reached is recorded.

problemTypes.definition: A multi-file package in the in-memory filesystem with seeded bugs to fix or a feature to add in an existing codebase (bug squash, AI-enabled round phases).
problemTypes.grading: Graded by hidden behaviour tests per bug or feature.

problemTypes.definition: An incident replay: a sourced timeline with checkpoints where the reader commits to a hypothesis before the next event; the reveal is the published postmortem.
problemTypes.grading: Graded by the checkpoint picks; the closing "which control would have caught it" answer is self-rated.

problemTypes.definition: A timed build-and-defend task: a planning window, a build in the reader's own environment, then review questions on data model, abstractions, path to production and AI use.
problemTypes.grading: Self-rated from a rubric checklist; never counted for the streak.

problemTypes.definition: A prepared talk, project deep dive or paper presentation followed by a probe list.

tracks.title: LLM foundations for software engineers
tracks.brief: The internals that set cost, latency and failure modes, taught at the level of a design review rather than an introduction. Tokenizers as a billing and security surface, embeddings as trained artefacts, attention layouts as serving decisions, decoding and determinism, the training pipeline as a map into the training and llmops tracks, and model selection from evidence. Every lesson assumes the reader can already define a token, an embedding and attention, and spends its words on mechanisms, published numbers and the decision each one drives.

modules.title: Tokenizers as cost, capacity and security surface
modules.brief: The tokenizer fixes the unit of billing, rate limiting and context capacity, so tokenizer changes are pricing events and special tokens are an injection channel.

lessons.title: The tokenizer as a cost, capacity and security surface
lessons.brief: A tokenizer fixes the unit of billing, rate limiting and context capacity, so changing models can change the bill for identical text. The lesson works from measured counts across encodings, pre-tokenizer regex differences, the language skew Petrov et al. measured, and Anthropic's note that Claude 4.7 and later produce more tokens for the same text. The decision it teaches is how to price a tokenizer change and when caching or per-language pricing absorbs it.

existing.note: Keep the measured counts, the pre-tokenizer regex difference and the special-token note as a reference table; drop the lexer preamble and the phone-screen question (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: BPE training versus encoding, and the edge cases that follow
lessons.brief: BPE training is a greedy loop over pair frequencies while encoding replays merges in rank order, so the two have different costs and different failure modes. The lesson covers byte fallback, digit and whitespace pre-splitting, vocabulary size against embedding and softmax cost, and why letter counting and long-number arithmetic suffer. The reader leaves able to implement both and to predict how an unseen word is split.

lessons.title: Chat templates and special tokens as an interface contract
lessons.brief: The chat template is the serialisation format between your messages and the model's training distribution, and a mismatch at serving degrades quality without raising an error. The lesson covers role tokens, the generation markers that assistant-only loss depends on, end-of-sequence alignment, and why special-token strings in user text are a security bug. The decision is who owns the template across a fine-tune and serve pipeline and which test proves it matches.

problems.brief: A vendor's new model emits more tokens for the same text: estimate the monthly bill, the rate-limit headroom and the cache hit rate at which the change pays for itself.
Train and apply BPE on a toy corpus; hidden property tests check the encode and decode round trip and merge-rank order on unseen words.
The same invoice costs more per message in Hindi and Japanese: quantify the skew from measured counts and choose between translation, model choice and per-language pricing.

A fine-tuned model rambles past its answer only in production: the serving template omits the end-of-turn token the training template emitted; the evidence is incomplete and the reader names what to collect.
Critique an input sanitiser that strips special-token strings from user text before templating, then name the encoding-level control it should have used.
Which change alters the token count of an unchanged prompt: a model switch inside one family, a tokenizer encoding change, whitespace normalisation, or reordering the system prompt?

modules.title: Embeddings: operation and training
modules.brief: Embeddings are trained artefacts whose geometry, storage format and training objective decide recall per byte and what a domain fine-tune can fix.

lessons.title: Choosing and operating an embedding model
lessons.brief: Metric choice, normalisation, Matryoshka truncation and int8 or binary storage are one decision about recall per byte stored. The lesson costs an index from published dimension and quantisation results and shows why two models cannot share one index. It ends with the migration choice between re-embedding everything and dual-writing behind a cut-over.

existing.note: Drop the personality-vector hook and metric definitions; keep the Matryoshka, quantisation and model table; training mechanics move to contrastive-training.

lessons.title: How embedders are trained: InfoNCE, negatives and false negatives
lessons.brief: Embedders learn from a contrastive loss whose negatives come from the batch, so batch size, duplicates and mined negatives change what the model learns. The lesson covers InfoNCE with temperature, GradCache for large batches, BM25 negatives in DPR, refreshed negatives in ANCE, and NV-Retriever's positive-aware mining against false negatives. The reader can implement a symmetric CLIP loss and a negative miner and say when a domain fine-tune is worth it.

lessons.title: Playbook: fine-tune the embedder, add a reranker, or change the chunks
lessons.brief: When retrieval fails on a domain, three levers compete for the same budget and each fixes a different failure. The inputs are labelled pairs, query distribution, latency budget and how often the corpus changes; the Sentence Transformers write-up shows a small fine-tuned reranker beating a larger general one on its own domain only. The playbook ends with what to measure after deciding: recall@k on held-out queries and the false-negative rate of mined pairs.

problems.brief: Implement the symmetric CLIP contrastive loss from paired embeddings with a temperature; hidden tests check symmetry, label alignment and numerical stability.
Recall fell after adding mined hard negatives: rank the causes when many mined negatives are unlabelled positives, and say what you would sample to be sure.
Search broke after an embedding model upgrade wrote new vectors into the old index; find the cause and plan a cut-over that keeps recall during migration.
Choose a Matryoshka dimension and storage format for 80 million vectors under a RAM budget, stating the recall you expect to lose and how you would measure it.
Two sentences with opposite meaning score high cosine: explain it from the training objective, then propose a mitigation and its cost in latency and labels.
Design training for a model that maps text, images and audio into one embedding space: architecture, supervision, losses, evaluation and deployment.

modules.title: Attention layouts as serving decisions
modules.brief: Attention mechanics stated once, then the layout choices (GQA, MLA, windows, hybrids) that set KV bytes per token and therefore what a GPU can serve.

lessons.title: Attention, causal masks and the online softmax
lessons.brief: Self-attention is a weighted gather whose cost is quadratic in sequence length at prefill and linear per token at decode once keys and values are cached. The lesson states the scaling factor in one line with its source and spends its words on the causal mask at training versus inference and the online softmax normaliser that FlashAttention and decode kernels depend on. The reader can write a decode step whose output equals a full recompute.

existing.note: Drop the hash-map section and the walk-me-through question; merge with the KV material from inference-anatomy into attention-layouts (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: MHA, GQA, MLA, windows and hybrids: picking a layout for a context target
lessons.brief: The attention layout fixes KV bytes per token, which sets batch size and cost at long context. The lesson computes bytes per token from published configs for Llama 3.1 (GQA), DeepSeek-V3 (MLA), Gemma 3 (local and global layers) and gpt-oss (banded windows) in front of the reader. The decision is which layout, or which open model, to serve for a 128K target and what quality evidence would reverse the choice.

lessons.title: FlashAttention 1 to 3: exact attention bounded by memory traffic
lessons.brief: FlashAttention is exact and does more arithmetic than the naive kernel, and wins by tiling in on-chip memory and recomputing in the backward pass to cut HBM reads. FlashAttention-2 reports 50 to 73% of A100 peak and FlashAttention-3 adds Hopper warp specialisation and FP8 with block quantisation. What changed in practice is that attention cost discussions must be about IO, and the walkthrough ends with what to say when asked whether it is an approximation.

problems.brief: Pick the attention layout, or the open model, for a 128K-context serving target on a fixed GPU budget, defending the KV bytes per token and the quality evidence you would require.
Causal attention with a KV cache and grouped-query heads; a hidden test compares every decode step with a full recompute.
How much KV cache does this batch need at mixed sequence lengths, and what changes with GQA-8 versus full multi-head?
Explain FlashAttention, the KV cache and RoPE, then state what each changes in a serving cost model and which one a profiler would show.
Decode diverges from the full recompute only for batched requests with left padding: locate the position-offset bug among several real defects in the cache code.
Which statement about FlashAttention is false, given options of equal length about exactness, recomputation, FLOPs and HBM traffic?

modules.title: Decoding, determinism and constrained output
modules.brief: Samplers as tail policies, why temperature 0 still varies, what grammar masks guarantee, and logprobs as an instrument.

lessons.title: Samplers as tail policies: temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p
lessons.brief: Each sampler is a rule for truncating the tail of the next-token distribution, and they differ in how they behave when the distribution is flat versus peaked. Min-p scales its cutoff with the top probability, which is why it holds up at high temperature where top-p admits low-probability tokens. The reader can implement and test the samplers and pick defaults for extraction versus open-ended generation.

existing.note: Sampler content stays here; determinism and constrained decoding become their own lessons.

lessons.title: Why temperature 0 is not deterministic, and when it matters
lessons.brief: Thinking Machines measured 80 distinct outputs from 1,000 temperature-0 completions of one prompt and traced the variation mainly to kernels that are not batch-invariant under changing load. The lesson covers what batch-invariant kernels cost, why seeds do not help, and why the effect breaks the on-policy assumption in RL. The decision is when to pay for deterministic serving (evals, RL) and when to design the product around variance.

lessons.title: Constrained decoding: what a grammar mask guarantees and what it costs
lessons.brief: A grammar mask guarantees syntax by zeroing invalid tokens at each step; it guarantees nothing about whether the content is right. The lesson covers token-boundary problems, mask compilation cost (XGrammar), and the disputed quality effect of strict formats (Let Me Speak Freely and the dottxt reply). The reader chooses per task between strict schema decoding, tool calls and validate-and-repair.

lessons.title: Logprobs as a debugging and confidence instrument
lessons.brief: Token log-probabilities expose near-ties that explain flips between runs and give a cheap confidence signal for classification and extraction. Instacart uses the probability of yes on the first token of a self-verification call to send low-confidence values to human auditors. The limits are that providers restrict logprob exposure, partly as an abuse control, and that calibration has to be measured on your own labels.

problems.brief: Write top-p and min-p samplers; hidden property tests check that the kept mass and the cutoff behave correctly on flat and peaked distributions.
Temperature 0 gives different answers across calls in production; the reader must ask for the evidence (logprobs, batch sizes, kernels) rather than be handed it.
What does constrained decoding guarantee about a JSON response, given options of equal length on syntax, schema, content and refusals?
An RL team wants bitwise-identical sampler and trainer; state what batch-invariant kernels cost in serving throughput, who pays it, and what you would accept instead.
Classify a million support tickets a day with calibrated confidence: logprob thresholds, a self-verification call, or a small classifier; defend the cost and the review rate.
Critique an extraction service that uses strict schema decoding and reports 100% schema validity as its quality metric.

modules.title: The training pipeline, mapped for application engineers
modules.brief: The on-ramp to the training and llmops tracks: what each stage fixes, what reasoning models cost, and where fine-tuning memory goes.

lessons.title: From pretraining to RL: the pipeline as a build system
lessons.brief: Pretraining, mid-training, SFT, preference tuning and RL with verifiable rewards each consume different data and fix different defects, and later stages can undo earlier ones. The lesson uses public reports (Llama 3's rounds of SFT then DPO, DeepSeek-R1's cold start then RL) to show what each stage changed and what it cost. It points into the training track for mechanisms and into llmops for applied fine-tuning.

existing.note: Post-training, LoRA and distillation depth move to the training track; applied fine-tuning moves to llmops/fine-tuning; the classic ML refresher is cut as below the bar.

lessons.title: Reasoning models and test-time compute inside a latency budget
lessons.brief: Reasoning models trade output tokens for accuracy, so effort settings are a latency and cost knob per route, not a quality switch. The lesson covers parallel sampling versus longer chains, compute-optimal test-time scaling results, and Anthropic's finding that visible reasoning is not a faithful trace. The decision is which requests get a reasoning model and how thinking budgets are capped.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning memory: where 16 bytes per parameter come from
lessons.brief: Mixed-precision Adam costs 16 bytes per parameter before activations (20 with FP32 gradient accumulation), which is why full fine-tuning needs sharding and why LoRA and QLoRA change the arithmetic. The lesson covers what LoRA freezes, QLoRA's NF4 base with higher-precision adapters, and where activations stop QLoRA's saving. The reader estimates memory for a stated model and picks the method before reading a vendor table.

problems.brief: Fine-tuning memory for a stated model: full, LoRA and QLoRA, with activations and ZeRO sharding as part of the question rather than a follow-up.
RLHF, DPO and GRPO in one diagram, with the failure mode and published hyperparameter choice for each stage.
Debug a GRPO step whose importance ratio should start at 1; a length-bias defect is a real secondary bug the reader must rank.
Critique a LoRA fine-tuning plan: targets only attention projections, uses the full fine-tuning learning rate and library default rank, and trains with a large batch.
Prompt, RAG or fine-tune for a product team, now that OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning is closed to new organisations; state the data volume and capacity conditions for each branch.
Put a reasoning model inside a stated latency budget: which requests get it, what effort, and what you measure to keep the decision honest.

modules.title: Model selection from evidence
modules.brief: Reading model cards for serving and legal consequences, running bake-offs that survive review, and deciding migrations against retirement deadlines.

lessons.title: Reading a model card for serving and legal consequences
lessons.brief: Each line of a model card (architecture, context, cut-off, licence) maps to a serving or legal consequence. For mixture-of-experts models total parameters set memory while active parameters set FLOPs, and an advertised window is not an effective one. The reader turns a card into a short list of risks to test before any bake-off.

existing.note: Effective context moves to multimodal/long-context; licence clauses move to llmops/economics-selection; the card-reading core stays.

lessons.title: Bake-offs that survive review: your tasks, paired comparisons, cost per success
lessons.brief: Leaderboards make a shortlist, not a decision, because contamination and task mismatch move rankings. The lesson builds a paired bake-off on your own traffic with clustered errors and reports cost per successful task next to accuracy; Anthropic reports clustered standard errors on popular evals more than three times the naive ones. The reader can defend a model choice to a reviewer who distrusts benchmarks.

lessons.title: Playbook: migrate to a new model version or hold
lessons.brief: A new model version arrives with a retirement deadline for the old one (Anthropic gives at least 60 days of notice), so holding is also a decision with a date. The inputs are regressions per prompt, cost and latency change, behaviour evals and the deadline; the options are migrate all, migrate per route, or hold until retirement. The playbook ends with what to measure for the first two weeks after the switch.

problems.brief: A 1M-token window still misses the answer in a long contract: explain why, then decide between the full document and retrieval with a cost for each.
Pick a model for a million classifications a day under a cost cap and a quality floor, with the bake-off design that justifies it.
From a bake-off's accuracy, tokens and retry rates for three models, compute cost per successful task, name the winner and the assumption that flips it.
Critique a model-selection memo that cites leaderboard ranks and a needle-in-a-haystack score as its evidence for a long-document product.
A consumer app with 900M monthly active users (scenario) plans to ship on Llama 4: which licence clause changes the decision?
A new model version arrives with the old one retiring in 60 days: plan the per-route migration, the behaviour evals, the hold criteria and who decides.

tracks.title: Building with model APIs
tracks.brief: Client engineering against model APIs as a reliability discipline: stream contracts, the two kinds of 429, failover that does not change behaviour, prompts that survive upgrades, structured output guarantees, prompt caching mechanics, and what a framework or agent SDK buys. The reader already ships HTTP clients; the track teaches what changes when the server is metered, non-deterministic and versioned with retirement dates.

modules.title: Client reliability against model APIs
modules.brief: Stream event contracts, stop reasons, the two kinds of 429, retry placement and cross-provider failover.

lessons.title: Stop reasons and the stream event contract
lessons.brief: A streamed response is a sequence of typed events whose order and partial states the client must handle, and the stop reason decides whether to continue, retry or surface an error. The lesson covers the event order and its traps (partial tool-input JSON, pings, mid-stream errors), max-tokens versus refusal versus tool-use stops, and what the 2026-10-21 API version changed. The reader can write a stream assembler that survives disconnects and resumes correctly.

existing.note: Keep the stop-reason list, stream event order with its traps, the two 429s and the provider table; drop the RPC preamble and the streaming explanation (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: Retries, rate limits and the two kinds of 429
lessons.brief: A rate-limit 429 with retry-after is transient, while a spend-cap 429 without it keeps failing until access resumes, and retrying it turns an outage into a storm. The lesson covers token-bucket limits on input and output tokens, cached reads excluded from input limits on most Claude models, jittered backoff, and keeping retries at one layer with a budget. The decision is where retries live in a stack and what every other layer does instead.

lessons.title: Failing over between providers without changing behaviour
lessons.brief: Cross-provider failover changes tokenisation, tool-call formats, safety behaviour and output distribution at once, so it is a product change rather than a networking one. The lesson covers which errors should trigger failover, circuit breakers in gateways such as LiteLLM, per-route eligibility, and the eval gate a fallback model must pass. The reader writes the failover policy and the test that proves it does what it says.

problems.brief: Review a retry and failover layer that retries every 429 and 5xx three times at the client, the gateway and the job runner, and fails over on the first timeout.
Retry a model call without making the outage worse: classify errors, honour retry-after, cap attempts with a shared retry budget; hidden tests inject spend-cap 429s.
A wall of 429s every morning at 9: separate the token-bucket cause from a red herring in the logs and propose the smallest fix.
Size per-tenant token buckets from input and output token limits and a measured cache hit rate, and say which tenant mix breaks the plan.
Design a model client library many teams will share: timeouts, retries, failover, idempotency and telemetry defaults, and which of them teams may override.
A request returns 429 with no retry-after header and an organisation spend-limit message: what should the client do?
Time to first token is unchanged but p99 completion time doubled for long answers after an SDK upgrade; rank the hypotheses and state the measurement for each.

modules.title: Prompts that survive model upgrades
modules.brief: Prompt structure that separates durable intent from model-specific workarounds, which techniques still pay on current models, and debugging prompt failures by slice.

lessons.title: Prompt structure that survives a model upgrade
lessons.brief: Prompts encode assumptions about one model's habits, so they should separate durable instructions from model-specific workarounds that must be re-tested on every upgrade. The lesson covers system versus user placement, delimiting untrusted data, examples as specification, and what current provider guides say changed between model generations. The reader can diff a prompt across two models and list the lines that need re-testing.

existing.note: The five workflow patterns move to workflows/patterns; prompts-as-code and rollouts move to llmops/prompt-lifecycle; structure stays here.

lessons.title: Few-shot, chain of thought and self-consistency: when each pays
lessons.brief: Each technique buys accuracy with tokens and latency, and reasoning models changed which ones still pay. The lesson covers chain-of-thought gains on non-reasoning models, the cost of each self-consistency vote, few-shot calibration effects, and tasks where explicit reasoning only adds latency. The reader prices a technique per request before adopting it.

lessons.title: Debugging a prompt that fails in production
lessons.brief: Production prompt failures cluster by input slice, so the method is trace sampling and error analysis rather than rewording. The lesson covers slicing by input features, reading near-tie logprobs, provider changes behind a model alias, and turning each confirmed failure into an eval case. The reader runs the loop from symptom to a gated fix.

problems.brief: Forty prompts, sixty days to a model retirement, twelve regressions on the new model: decide which ship degraded, which are rewritten and who signs off.
The same ticket gets different labels across runs: separate prompt ambiguity from sampling variance with the evidence you would request.
Prompts as production code: versioning, review, tests and rollout, with the conflict between fast iteration and a regression gate.
Critique a support-bot system prompt that mixes policy, persona, few-shot examples and three workarounds for an older model.
Self-consistency with five votes versus a reasoning model at medium effort: cost and latency per request for a stated workload, and which assumption flips the choice.
Prompt chaining or one large prompt for contract review under a fixed latency budget: decide, and specify the gate between steps.

modules.title: Structured outputs and tool calling
modules.brief: Which output guarantee each field needs, the tool-call protocol as a request your code may refuse, and evaluating tool use.

lessons.title: Strict schema, JSON mode, tool call or validate-and-repair
lessons.brief: Strict schema decoding guarantees a parse, JSON mode guarantees only syntax, and validate-and-repair works on any provider at the cost of retries. The lesson covers provider schema-feature limits, refusal handling inside structured responses, and bounded repair loops. The decision is made per field: which guarantee you need and what you log when it fails.

existing.note: Keep the provider comparison and repair loop; cut the vocabulary sections; add per-field guarantees.

lessons.title: The tool-call protocol: the model proposes, your code disposes
lessons.brief: A tool call is a request your code may refuse, so validation, authorisation and idempotency belong in the executor rather than the prompt. The lesson covers parallel calls and ordering hazards, streamed tool inputs, error results returned to the model, and iteration caps. The reader writes an executor that is safe under retries and duplicate calls.

lessons.title: Evaluating tool calls: right tool, right arguments, right order
lessons.brief: Tool-use accuracy decomposes into selection, argument correctness and sequencing, and each needs its own check. The lesson covers BFCL-style AST matching, executable checks, and end-state checks over multi-turn conversations as in tau-bench. The reader builds a tool-call eval for one internal API.

problems.brief: Guarantee valid structured output across two providers, one of which lacks strict schema support, and state the failure you still have to handle.
Write the tool-use loop with an iteration cap, error results returned to the model and duplicate-call protection; hidden tests inject failures.
Assemble a streamed reply with interleaved text and tool-input deltas; the event rules are enforced by hidden tests, not listed in the question.
Right tool, wrong arguments: diagnose from traces whether the cause is the description, the schema or the context, and fix the one that matters.
Rewrite a refund tool definition: naming, argument types, approval thresholds and error messages that tell the model what to do next.
Design the tool interface for a calendar agent used by three products, including how tools are versioned without breaking cached prompts.

modules.title: Context and prompt caching
modules.brief: Provider prefix caching mechanics and what invalidates them, strategies for exceeding the window, and when a semantic cache is a correctness bug.

lessons.title: Prompt caching: prefix rules, breakpoints and what invalidates them
lessons.brief: Provider caches match exact prefixes in a fixed order (tools, system, messages), so any change early in the prompt recomputes everything after it. The lesson covers breakpoints, minimum cacheable lengths, TTL refresh on use, cache-write premiums and current price tables for Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini. The reader predicts a hit rate from a prompt layout and then measures it from usage fields.

existing.note: Cut "context is a budget" and the four-moves list; keep cache mechanics, prices, cache breakers and the arithmetic; harness-specific caching moves to harness/cache-cost-latency.

lessons.title: Long conversations: truncation, summaries, context editing and compaction
lessons.brief: Every strategy for exceeding the window drops information, and the choice is which loss the task tolerates. The lesson covers clearing old tool results with context editing, server-side compaction, structured notes, and context rot as the reason a focused context answers better. The decision, per product, is what is pinned, summarised or dropped, and how recall of pinned facts is tested.

lessons.title: Semantic caching and when it is a correctness bug
lessons.brief: A semantic cache returns an answer written for a different question, so its similarity threshold is a precision decision with a cost per wrong hit. The lesson covers where it is safe (static FAQs), where it leaks (personalised or permissioned answers), and how cache entries are scoped. The reader sets a threshold from labelled near-duplicate pairs and states the leak it must never allow.

problems.brief: Model a provider's prefix cache from its documentation (prefix order, breakpoints, lookback, TTL refresh, minimum length) and predict hits for a request trace.
Token-budget allocator across system prompt, history and retrieved documents with priorities and pinned items; hidden tests check invariants, not one output.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported phone-screen task via a commercial blog)

problems.brief: What prompt caching saves per day for a stated assistant, including cache-write premiums and the TTL's effect on idle tenants.
Which change keeps the prompt cache warm: reordering tools, adding a timestamp to the system prompt, appending a message, or editing an early example?
The assistant forgets after ten turns; redesign context handling when a user deletion request and the cache cost pull in opposite directions.
How many agent steps fit under a $2 cap with and without a warm cache, given stated token growth per step.
Cache hit rate fell to near zero after a release; the diff added a request id to the system prompt and reordered tools, and only one of them explains the drop.

modules.title: Frameworks, SDKs and what to own
modules.brief: Which abstractions you are willing to debug in production, building or renting the agent harness, and what frameworks hide.

lessons.title: Playbook: framework, agent SDK or plain code
lessons.brief: The decision is which abstractions you are willing to debug at 2 a.m. The inputs are the need for checkpoints and interrupts (LangGraph), the provider coupling of agent SDKs, team familiarity and the cost of leaving. The playbook works a stated case and ends with what to measure after deciding: time to debug a failed run and the amount of glue code.

existing.note: Build-versus-rent harness becomes its own lesson; low-code tools move to workflows/operating-workflows.

lessons.title: Build or rent the agent harness
lessons.brief: Agent SDKs, hosted agent platforms and a hand-written loop differ in who owns the session log, sandbox, credentials and upgrades. The lesson compares the Claude Agent SDK, Claude Managed Agents, the OpenAI Agents SDK and your own loop on what each makes hard to change later. The reader writes the build-versus-rent memo for a regulated enterprise.

lessons.title: What frameworks hide: a chain, router and retriever in plain code
lessons.brief: Rebuilding a framework's core in a few hundred lines shows which parts are glue and which are hard (state, retries, streaming). The lesson compares LangChain agents, LangGraph state graphs and DSPy modules with plain code doing the same work. The reader can debug an opaque chain by knowing what it must be doing underneath.

problems.brief: Add a second provider without surprising users, with a 60-day retirement deadline on the first provider's model.
Would you use LangChain for this production service? Defend either answer against a reviewer who has been paged by it.
A regulated enterprise wants to stop running its own agent loop: make the build-versus-rent call on hosted agent platforms with the controls it must keep.
After a framework upgrade long agent runs end early with no error; find the changed default (recursion limit) among several plausible causes.
Rebuild a minimal router plus retriever without a framework; hidden tests check routing decisions and retrieval results.
Critique a proposal to adopt three frameworks in one product (an orchestration library, a RAG library and an agent SDK).

tracks.title: Evals and observability
tracks.brief: Evaluation as an operating discipline: error analysis and the labelling operation, golden sets that expose known failures, judges validated like classifiers, agent evaluation over repeated trials, and merge gates with statistics that survive review. Evals stays third because it is the most rewarded skill and the one the other tracks depend on. Release experiments and drift live in the llmops track; harness attribution lives in the harness track.

modules.title: Error analysis and the labelling operation
modules.brief: Failure modes come from traces; labels are a production process with throughput and drift; instrumentation decides what can be analysed later.

lessons.title: Error analysis: open coding, axial coding and saturation
lessons.brief: Evals start from failure modes found in traces, not from metrics chosen in advance. The lesson covers reading at least 100 traces, open then axial coding, binary labels per failure mode, and the rule of labelling the first upstream failure. The reader turns 100 traces into a ranked failure taxonomy with counts.

existing.note: Keep the OpenTelemetry section and the first-upstream-failure rule; replace the rest with the labelling-operation material (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: Running the labelling operation: who labels, how often, and how you know they agree
lessons.brief: Labels are a production process with throughput, agreement and drift, and Shankar et al. show reviewers' criteria shift as they see more outputs. The lesson covers dev and test splits per label, inter-rater agreement, expert time budgets and rotating what gets labelled. The reader designs a six-week labelling programme for a few expert hours a week and states what it refuses to gate.

lessons.title: Instrumentation: GenAI spans, what to log and what never to log
lessons.brief: The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions define model, agent and tool spans with token and cache attributes, and mark message content opt-in because it is personal data. The lesson covers what every call must log (resolved model id, prompt version, tokens, cost, latency, tool calls), sampling, and redaction. The decision is the content-capture policy per environment, written down before an incident forces it.

problems.brief: Build the labelling operation for a support assistant: label set, splits, agreement checks and a six-week plan for four expert hours a week.
A 95% eval pass rate and angry users: list what you would pull to explain the gap before looking at any provided evidence.
What 82 passes out of 100 does and does not tell you: the interval, and the sample size for a decision you can defend.
Show me an eval you built, then defend it against a reviewer who says it measured the wrong thing.
Reconstruct a hierarchical trace from a stream of span events that arrive out of order, with missing parents.
Critique a failure taxonomy with dozens of overlapping categories, Likert scores and no counts.

modules.title: Golden sets and metrics
modules.brief: Golden sets as designed samples, metric choice by question, and why public benchmarks stop meaning anything.

lessons.title: Building a golden set: sourcing, stratification and coverage
lessons.brief: A golden set is a sample designed to expose known failure modes, so it is stratified by intent and outcome rather than drawn uniformly. The lesson covers sampling from production, synthetic cases with a filter, code assertions as level-one checks, and versioning the set with its scores. The reader builds a 20-question set for a contract assistant and defends each slice.

existing.note: Curation from production logs moves to llmops/data-curation; contamination becomes its own lesson.

lessons.title: Retrieval and answer metrics: which one answers which question
lessons.brief: Recall@k, MRR and NDCG measure retrieval, faithfulness and answer relevance measure generation, and judge-based metrics inherit the judge's noise. The lesson covers RAGAS definitions and their assumptions, binary pass criteria, and the cases where a metric hides the failure. The decision is the minimum metric set for a RAG release.

lessons.title: Contamination and benchmarks that stop meaning anything
lessons.brief: Public benchmarks leak into training data and get optimised against, so scores rise without capability rising. The lesson covers Lee et al.'s finding that over 4% of standard validation sets overlapped training data, OpenAI's reasons for no longer reporting SWE-bench Verified, and how to keep a private set private. The reader can say what a vendor's benchmark gain does and does not prove.

problems.brief: Turn 100,000 conversations into a 500-case eval set: strata, dedup, labels and what you leave out.
Better on every benchmark, worse for users: rank the explanations and the one measurement that separates them.
Faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and recall: which one would have caught each of four described failures.
Size the suite to detect a three-point regression with a paired test, choosing the power and the flip rate you assume.
Critique a golden set of 500 synthetic questions generated by the model under test and graded by the same model.
Keep a golden set fresh while the product changes monthly: refresh cadence, retirement rules and comparable scores across versions.

modules.title: LLM-as-judge, calibrated
modules.brief: Judges validated like classifiers, their measurable biases, and when a human or a code check is cheaper.

lessons.title: Validating a judge: TPR, TNR and the corrected pass rate
lessons.brief: A judge is a classifier, so it is trusted by its true positive and true negative rates on human labels, not by raw agreement. The lesson covers the correction formula from judgy and its precondition, validation-set sizes, and re-validation when the judge prompt or model changes. The reader corrects an observed pass rate and gives its interval.

existing.note: Cut the predict block and TPR/TNR definitions; keep bias tests, the correction with its precondition, pairwise versus pointwise and when not to use a judge.

lessons.title: Judge biases and the tests that expose them
lessons.brief: Position, length and self-preference biases are measurable with swapped and controlled pairs. The lesson covers Zheng et al.'s bias tests, the self-preference evidence, and Tripathi et al.'s comparison of pairwise and pointwise judging. The decision is pairwise or pointwise for a given release question.

lessons.title: Playbook: human, code check or judge
lessons.brief: Each check type has a cost per item and an error profile, and the cheapest check that catches the failure wins. The inputs are how deterministic the failure is, label cost, volume and required precision. The playbook works a support bot with three failure modes and ends with what to measure after deciding.

problems.brief: Can you trust your LLM judge? Answer, then respond to pushback that the vendor reports 92% agreement with humans.
The pairwise judge prefers prompt A; which control experiment rules out position bias?
Score the judge against human labels, then correct the observed pass rate with an interval; hidden tests vary base rates.
Critique a judge validation report that quotes raw agreement on a set where failures are rare, with no TNR.
The judge agrees with humans 92% of the time yet failures slip through to production; explain from base rates and decide what to change first.
How many labelled examples to estimate a judge's TNR within a stated interval when failures are a small share of traffic.

modules.title: Evaluating agents
modules.brief: Outcome, trajectory and state grading, reliability over repeated trials, and what public agent benchmarks can and cannot tell you.

lessons.title: Grading agents: outcome, trajectory and state
lessons.brief: Agent evals grade the end state where possible and the path only where the path is itself the requirement. The lesson covers tau-bench's database-state checks, tau2's dual-control setting, trajectory checks for forbidden actions, and cost as part of the score. The reader designs an eval for a customer-service agent that can refund money.

existing.note: Harness-versus-model attribution moves to harness/evaluating-harnesses; grading and benchmarks stay.

lessons.title: pass@k versus pass^k: reliability over repeated trials
lessons.brief: pass@k rewards one success in k tries while pass^k demands success on all k, and production agents live on pass^k. The lesson covers tau-bench's published drop (pass^8 under 25% in retail for the strongest model at publication), how many trials to run, and confidence on small task sets. The reader computes both and decides which one a release gate uses.

lessons.title: Public agent benchmarks: what each measures and how it fails
lessons.brief: SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.0, GAIA, WebArena, OSWorld and BrowseComp each measure a narrow slice under a particular harness and infrastructure. The lesson covers OpenAI's audit (59.4% of 138 audited hard problems with material issues) and its decision to stop reporting Verified, plus contamination. The reader can explain why an agent that wins on SWE-bench fails on their own repository.

problems.brief: pass^4 from three flaky tasks with stated per-trial success rates, and the number of trials needed to trust it.
Zero out of a hundred after a harness change: separate an infrastructure fault from a capability drop.
Evaluating a coding agent for your repositories, with pushback on why SWE-bench numbers do not transfer.
Find where agent runs break: a trajectory grader over recorded runs that flags forbidden actions and first failing steps.
Evaluate a customer-service agent that can issue refunds: state checks, policy violations, pass^k and cost per resolved task.
A vendor shows a three-point SWE-bench Verified gain for its new harness: what does it tell you, and what would you ask for?

modules.title: Gates, online evals and success metrics
modules.brief: Merge gates with the right statistics, what runs inline versus sampled, and success metrics that do not reward agreeable answers.

lessons.title: Eval gates in CI: hard, statistical and report-only
lessons.brief: A merge gate must separate must-pass cases from statistical checks, because a paired flip test is the right tool for the second and the wrong one for the first. The lesson covers exact sign tests on flipped cases, gate tiers, eval cost control, and the tooling landscape after OpenAI's acquisition of Promptfoo. The reader writes the gate policy for a prompt repository.

existing.note: A/B design, release ladders and drift move to llmops; gates, online evals and metrics stay.

lessons.title: Online evals: sampled judges, guardrails and evaluators
lessons.brief: Online evaluation samples live traffic for judges that run after the fact, while guardrails act inline and pay latency on every request. The lesson covers sampling rates, judge drift, privacy limits on reading traffic, and the quality probes Anthropic added after its 2025 three-bug postmortem. The decision is what runs inline, what runs sampled and what runs nightly.

lessons.title: Success metrics for a probabilistic feature
lessons.brief: An AI feature needs one outcome metric, guardrail metrics and a cost metric, because engagement metrics reward agreeable answers. The lesson uses the GPT-4o sycophancy rollback and METR's finding that developers felt faster while measured slower as counter-examples to satisfaction-only metrics. The reader defines the metric set for a support assistant and names its owner.

problems.brief: Design an eval pipeline that gates prompt and model changes, then defend it when the gate blocks a release the CEO wants.
Is the regression real? Decide from paired flip counts with the hints removed, and say what you would do at the boundary.
Success metrics for an AI feature when resolution and re-contact rates move in opposite directions.
Eval cost control under a fixed monthly budget: which suites run per PR, nightly and pre-release, and what you stop running.
Offline quality improved and production quality fell after a release: rank the causes and the first measurement for each.
Critique a launch plan that ships on positive offline evals and a positive A/B test while expert testers say the model feels off.

tracks.title: AI workflows and durable execution
tracks.brief: How to design and run AI workflows in production, for engineers who already ship distributed systems: the workflow-or-agent decision, the five patterns as code, durable execution engines and how each one replays, changing code while runs are in flight, retries and idempotency when a step is a metered non-deterministic model call, approvals as a security boundary, batch stages, queues and per-step budgets, workflow tracing, replay testing, low-code tools and their licences, and back-office case studies from Uber, Instacart, Grab, Airbnb and Duolingo. It answers the owner's question "how do I create an AI workflow" directly and sits before agents because most production systems are workflows with model steps.

modules.title: Workflow or agent, and which pattern
modules.brief: Who owns control flow for each step, the five patterns written as code with their failure modes, and explicit state machines for model pipelines.

lessons.title: Playbook: workflow or agent
lessons.brief: The decision is who owns control flow for each step: code, or the model. Anthropic defines workflows as orchestrated through predefined code paths and agents as directing their own process, and OpenAI's guide gives three conditions under which an agent earns its place; the inputs are whether steps can be drawn in advance, reversibility, unstructured judgement, wait time and cost per run. The worked case is vendor-invoice intake with a refund branch, followed by what to measure: share of inputs that leave the happy path, cost per item and human-review rate.

existing.note: The prompting lesson's "one big prompt or a chain" section and five-pattern paragraph move here and into five-patterns.

lessons.title: The five patterns as code, with their failure modes
lessons.brief: Prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimiser each fit in a few dozen lines against a mock model, and each has its own failure mode and cost arithmetic. Chains add latency and are only better than one prompt when a gate sits between steps; a router's confusion matrix becomes the system's error floor; orchestrator plans are model output that needs the same validation as a tool call, at roughly 15 times chat tokens in Anthropic's research system. The reader picks a pattern for a stated system and computes its end-to-end success, latency and cost.

lessons.title: State machines and DAGs for model pipelines
lessons.brief: Explicit states, transitions guarded by deterministic validation, per-state retry limits and a terminal needs-human state turn a model pipeline into something you can operate. Airbnb's test migration moved each file through refactor, fix tests, fix lint and types, advancing only when validation passed, reaching 75% in four hours and 97% after four days of tuning with the rest done by hand. The lesson contrasts state machines with DAG schedulers (topological order, fan-in, partial branch failure) and teaches Airbnb's sample, tune and sweep loop.

problems.brief: Vendor-invoice intake with a refund branch and a two-day approval: steps, which steps are model calls, gates, idempotency keys, timeout behaviour, budgets and review routing.
Pick chain, router, parallel, orchestrator-workers or evaluator-optimiser for three stated systems and give the failure mode of each choice.
End-to-end success, latency and cost of a six-step chain versus a router with two parallel branches, from stated per-step error rates and latencies.
Scheduler for tasks with deadlines and prerequisites: earliest deadline first, never lease a task to two workers, survive a worker crash.
An agentic workflow that generates a one-hour movie: orchestration, state for continuity, quality gates and failure handling.
Your migration pipeline succeeds on 75% of files in the first sweep; how do you get the long tail, and when do you stop automating?
Critique an evaluator-optimiser loop with no iteration cap in which the critic is the generator grading its own output.

modules.title: Durable execution engines
modules.brief: How engines resume after a crash, the three meanings of replay, determinism and versioning while runs are in flight, and sagas for steps that cannot be undone.

lessons.title: How durable execution engines actually resume
lessons.brief: Temporal re-runs workflow code against recorded results, Inngest re-runs the handler and returns memoised step results, DBOS checkpoints each step into Postgres, and Lambda durable functions, Restate, Cloudflare Workflows and the Workflow SDK each keep a log; LangGraph instead checkpoints per super-step and re-executes nodes after a checkpoint on time travel, including model calls, and Inngest's bulk Replay creates new executions. The common contract is that a step can run more than once, its saved result wins once it exists, and anything external needs a key. The reader can say where each engine stores state, what it costs per step and what replay means on each.

existing.note: The durable-execution section (engines, Temporal determinism, Inngest memoised steps, the AgentsResume simulator) moves here; memory stays in agents; memory files move to harness.

lessons.title: Determinism and changing code while runs are in flight
lessons.brief: Reordering activities, reading the clock or random outside replay-safe APIs, or swapping a timer for an activity makes running workflows fail on replay, which is why model calls must be activities and deploys need a versioning plan. The lesson covers Temporal patching, Worker Versioning, new workflow type names, continue-as-new before the event-history limit, and Anthropic's rainbow deployments for long-running agents. The reader can ship a prompt and tool change while thousands of runs are mid-flight.

lessons.title: Sagas and compensation for steps that cannot be undone
lessons.brief: Garcia-Molina and Salem split a long-lived transaction into steps with compensating actions so partial progress can be undone without holding locks. Model-driven workflows call external systems that share no transaction, and some actions (an email, a payout) can only be compensated or gated before they happen. The walkthrough covers forward and backward recovery, compensation order, and what to say when a step has no compensation: put the approval before it.

problems.brief: After a deploy a share of running workflows fail with a non-determinism error; the diff swapped a timer and an activity among other harmless changes. Find it and ship the change safely.
You replay a LangGraph run from a checkpoint and the model answers differently: bug or expected, and how do you get a reproducible replay?
After a fix you bulk-replay 3,000 failed runs; what can repeat, and what do you check before pressing the button?
A long-lived agent workflow approaches its event-history limit: what do you carry over with continue-as-new and what do you drop?
Thousands of agent runs are mid-flight when you must ship a new prompt and a new tool: design the deploy.
A timeout refund workflow that is deterministic and safe to retry against an external payment API; hidden tests crash it at every boundary.
A step must send an email that cannot be undone; structure the workflow so a later failure leaves the system consistent.

modules.title: Retries, queues and per-step budgets
modules.brief: Where retries live when a step is a model call, admission control in front of a shared provider quota, and budgets per step rather than per run.

lessons.title: Idempotency and retries when a step is a model call
lessons.brief: At-least-once steps plus idempotent effects give exactly-once outcomes, but a retried model call returns a different output, and five layers of three retries put 243 times the load on a failing dependency. The lesson covers retry placement and retry budgets, non-retryable errors (a Claude spend-cap 429 has no retry-after), Temporal's default policy of unlimited attempts, start-to-close timeouts, and idempotency keys derived from run and step rather than per attempt. The reader records a model output once, treats it as the step result, and knows when a Stripe key outlives its window.

lessons.title: Queues, backpressure and flow control for model work
lessons.brief: The provider's token bucket is the shared bottleneck, so a workflow needs admission control in front of it. The lesson covers alarming on the age of the oldest message rather than depth, per-tenant isolation with separate queues or shuffle sharding, dead-letter queues that page someone, heartbeats for long steps, Inngest's flow-control vocabulary, and n8n queue mode. Grab's classification pipeline is the worked case: mini-batches through a queue with a workflow-level rate limiter because every deployment shared one tokens-per-minute quota.

lessons.title: Playbook: cost and latency budgets per step
lessons.brief: Per-run caps exist on most platforms; per-step budgets are what keep one slow or expensive step from eating the run. Each step gets a token budget, a timeout read from a latency percentile at a chosen false-timeout rate, a retry budget and a model tier, and a cascade pays only where Instacart found it did (a cheaper model matched quality on simpler attributes and lost accuracy on difficult ones). The worked case costs a three-step extraction pipeline with a review queue per document, every assumption labelled, including prompt growth in retry loops as Airbnb saw.

problems.brief: Five service layers each retry three times while the model provider is down: what load reaches the provider, and where should retries live?
Your activity uses the default Temporal retry policy and a step sends a malformed prompt the provider rejects with a 400: what happens?
Fifty tenants share one provider quota; design admission control so one tenant's backfill does not starve the others.
Critique a workflow that generates a fresh UUID idempotency key inside the retried step for a payment call.
Cap a customer's spend mid-trace and bill a trace whose cost is unknown until it finishes.
A feature calling a hosted model: separate transient from deterministic failures, validate in ordered checks, define the failure path, then handle a 3x cost overrun.
Set per-step timeouts for a three-step extraction from latency percentiles at a chosen false-timeout rate, and show what the retries do to the end-to-end p99.

modules.title: Approvals and handoffs between steps
modules.brief: Interrupt and resume mechanics across stacks, approvals as an authorisation and replay problem, and typed handoffs under engine payload limits.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-loop mechanics across stacks
lessons.brief: LangGraph interrupts restart the node from its first line on resume and match resume values by index, so side effects before the interrupt must be idempotent. The lesson covers LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK's approvals and serialisable run state, Temporal Signals versus Updates, Dify's Human Input node with its three-day default timeout, and Flowise checkpoints. The reader can implement a pause and resume correctly on two of these stacks.

lessons.title: Approval security: who may approve, what they see, and what a replay does
lessons.brief: An approval is an authorisation decision, so the design must say who may approve, show the reviewer the exact arguments rather than a model summary, and keep resume state on the server. The OpenAI Agents SDK warns that deserialising run state does not authenticate the snapshot or the reviewer and that approval does not give exactly-once execution. The lesson covers timeout policy (escalate or reject, never auto-approve money), replayed approvals, and OpenAI's two triggers for human intervention.

lessons.title: Structured handoffs between steps
lessons.brief: A step's output is the next step's input, so it gets a schema, a version and a size budget. Engines cap payloads (Temporal 2 MB per payload, Inngest 4 MiB per step output, Cloudflare 1 MiB per step return), which is why large artefacts move by reference using the claim-check pattern, as Anthropic's research subagents do. The lesson also covers OpenAI handoffs and input filters, and the security point that a handoff forwarding full history forwards any injected text with it.

problems.brief: An approval node inserts a record and then calls interrupt(); after approval there are two records. Explain and fix without losing the audit trail.
For a reviewer's approve or reject on a running workflow, do you use a Signal, a Query or an Update?
Critique a design that stores approval run state in a browser cookie and lets any logged-in user approve.
Approval design for a payments workflow: what the reviewer sees, timeouts, escalation, four-eyes rules and replay protection.
A handoff forwards the full conversation history to the next agent: what does injected text do, and what does an input filter change?
Invoice-to-ERP handoffs with typed contracts and the claim-check pattern under engine payload limits.
Design LangGraph's persistence layer for stateful agents with human-in-the-loop interruption.

modules.title: Batch stages and document pipelines
modules.brief: Batch APIs as a workflow stage with reconciliation, document pipelines from intake to system of record, and confidence routing to human review.

lessons.title: Batch APIs as a workflow stage
lessons.brief: A batch stage is submit, poll, collect, reconcile and re-submit, with results out of order (join on custom_id), per-request errors and expiries, and a 24-hour window (48 hours on Gemini). The lesson covers result retention per provider, batch queue limits as backpressure, best-effort caching inside batches, and OpenAI flex as a middle lane at batch prices that can return 429s. The reader designs a nightly batch stage that never silently drops an expired item.

lessons.title: Document pipelines from intake to system of record
lessons.brief: A document pipeline is intake, preprocessing, OCR or native PDF input, extraction to a schema, business-rule validation, confidence scoring, review routing and write-back, and each stage has a contract and a failure mode. Claude accepts PDFs as text plus page images with documented per-page token ranges, Uber's TextSense runs OCR, extraction, rules and a side-by-side review UI under Cadence, and Grab writes predictions to Kafka for owners to verify weekly. The reader works out throughput and cost per document for a stated volume.

lessons.title: Confidence and review routing for model extraction
lessons.brief: Review queues are sized by the confidence threshold, so the threshold is a staffing decision as much as a quality one. Instacart scores confidence from the probability of yes on a self-verification call and sends low-confidence values to auditors; the threshold is chosen on a labelled sample. The lesson covers calibration checks, the review-rate versus error-rate curve, and what Uber's reported accuracy figures do and do not mean per invoice.

problems.brief: A nightly 300,000-document enrichment against a 100,000-request batch cap and a processing-queue limit: how many batches, how long, and what you promise downstream.
Batch results are joined back to inputs by line number; what breaks, and how do you reconcile errored and expired items?
An invoice-processing pipeline that writes to the ERP and routes uncertain fields to people.
Score confidence on an extraction without labels and choose the review threshold, stating what the threshold costs in reviewer hours.
An inference job API: clients POST a job and poll; statuses, idempotency keys, retries, rate limits, partial batch failure and a model version change mid-flight.
A document processing pipeline that ingests and indexes large volumes of heterogeneous documents for model use.
Cost per 200-page contract sent as PDF pages at the documented per-page token range versus text extraction plus a page-image fallback for tables.

modules.title: Observing, testing and choosing workflow tools
modules.brief: Per-step tracing with the OpenTelemetry GenAI spans, replay and crash-injection tests, and when low-code tools are the right answer.

lessons.title: Observability per step
lessons.brief: A workflow trace is a tree of workflow, agent, model and tool spans, and the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (Development status) define invoke_workflow as an internal span that should not be emitted when the workflow is a detail inside an agent or tool. The lesson covers per-step metrics (latency, tokens, cost, retries, validation failures, review rate), linking engine run ids to trace ids, and Anthropic's practice of monitoring decision patterns without reading conversation content. The reader instruments a five-step workflow and writes the alerts.

lessons.title: Testing workflows: replay, golden traces and crash injection
lessons.brief: Workflow tests come in four layers: unit tests with recorded model responses, replaying recent histories against new code in CI, time-skipping so a three-day timeout runs in milliseconds, and killing the worker at every boundary while asserting one external effect each. The lesson warns about the three meanings of replay and shows Duolingo running its evals as Temporal workflows with deterministic graders first. The reader writes the test plan and CI gate for a refund workflow.

lessons.title: Playbook: low-code tools versus code
lessons.brief: n8n, Dify, Flowise and Zapier Agents are chosen on durability, testing, versioning, review, tenancy and licence, not on taste. n8n's Sustainable Use License limits use to internal business or non-commercial purposes and its queue mode needs Postgres and Redis, while Dify's modified Apache 2.0 forbids running a multi-tenant service from source without permission. Low-code wins for internal automations owned by operations with few steps and a human downstream; code wins when the workflow is the product, needs tests in CI, is multi-tenant or moves money.

existing.note: Low-code coverage is new; the frameworks lesson links here.

problems.brief: Which span do you emit for a graph run, an agent invocation and a tool call, and when should a framework not emit a workflow span?
Write the test plan and CI gate for a five-step refund workflow: replay tests, time skipping, crash injection and golden traces.
Operations wants the approval workflow in n8n or Dify: when do you agree, and what would move it to code?
An evaluation platform running async runs across thousands of datasets with LLM graders.
Clone a repository, run a coding agent, open a PR: one durable step or three, given workers may not share disks?
The workflow dashboard shows healthy p95 latency while customers report stuck runs: the alert watches queue depth, not the age of the oldest message.
A research-assistant agent platform where traces run for 30 minutes or more: resume, replay for debugging, spend caps and alerting.

tracks.title: Retrieval and RAG
tracks.brief: Retrieval as a systems problem: lexical and dense retrieval and what each misses, permissions and freshness against an ANN index, chunking chosen by eval, fusion and trained rerankers, late interaction and GraphRAG with their costs, locating failures by stage, vector index internals (HNSW by hand, filtered search, quantisation, object storage), and search evaluation with judgment pools and LLM assessors. Definitions of recall and inverted indexes are assumed; the track spends its words on decisions and published limits.

modules.title: Retrieval with permissions and freshness
modules.brief: What BM25 and dense retrieval each miss, permission and freshness constraints against ANN indexes, and when Postgres is enough.

lessons.title: BM25 and dense retrieval: what each misses
lessons.brief: BM25's IDF saturation and length normalisation are the tunable parts, and dense bi-encoders miss identifiers and rare terms that BM25 keeps. The lesson covers BEIR's finding that BM25 is a robust zero-shot baseline, bi-encoder versus cross-encoder cost, and Postgres full-text configuration traps. The reader predicts which queries break each retriever before running them.

existing.note: Drop definitions of inverted index, embeddings, ANN and metrics; keep BM25 IDF, the Postgres gotchas, pgvector filtering and the index limits table (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: Permissions, freshness and the ANN index
lessons.brief: Per-user access control, deletes and freshness all fight the ANN index, because filtering after the scan returns fewer than k rows. The lesson covers pgvector's post-filter behaviour and iterative scans, per-tenant namespaces and their limits, and how Microsoft 365 Copilot scopes retrieval to the user's permissions. The decision is filter placement and index partitioning for a corpus with mixed permissions.

lessons.title: pgvector or a dedicated vector database
lessons.brief: The choice turns on index size in RAM, filter selectivity, write rate and who operates it, not on benchmark queries per second. The lesson covers pgvector index limits and the version floor (0.8.3 or later; the README now shows 0.8.7), HNSW memory per vector, and when a managed service pays for itself. The reader can defend the choice for a stated corpus and growth rate.

problems.brief: Permissions, freshness and the ANN index for a mixed-permission corpus: filter placement, partitioning, delete handling and the recall you accept.
problems.reported: Scale AI, Atlassian (candidate reports via Hello Interview community)

problems.brief: BM25 from scratch; hidden property tests check IDF saturation and length normalisation rather than one ranking.
Flat, IVF or HNSW for three stated corpora and update rates, with the parameter you would tune first.
LIMIT 10 returns 3 rows from a filtered vector query; the arithmetic is no longer in the correct option.
Does an index of 50 million chunks fit in memory, and which quantisation or partitioning makes it fit?
Enterprise search with RAG over 5M documents searchable within 5 minutes, at 300 QPS and p95 under 1.2 s, with ACLs, offline NDCG@k and recall@k and an online A/B.

modules.title: Ingestion, parsing and chunking
modules.brief: Choosing a parsing route for documents, chunking decided by eval, and ingestion as a batch pipeline with quality gates.

lessons.title: Playbook: OCR pipeline, VLM parsing or page-image retrieval
lessons.brief: Documents can be parsed to text, parsed by a vision-language model, or retrieved as page images, and each route has different failure modes and costs. ColPali embeds page images as multi-vectors and reports beating text-extraction pipelines on its ViDoRe benchmark, while Claude and Gemini price pages as images with documented token rates. The worked case is 200-page contracts with tables and stamps, with what to measure after choosing.

existing.note: Parsing routes become a playbook; chunking stays; pipeline engineering becomes its own lesson.

lessons.title: Chunking as a retrieval decision
lessons.brief: Chunk size and boundaries decide what one retrieved unit can answer, so chunking defaults should come from an eval rather than a blog post. The lesson covers fixed, recursive and structure-aware splitters, Chroma's chunking evaluation, Anthropic's contextual retrieval and late chunking. The reader picks defaults for two corpora and shows the eval that justified them.

lessons.title: Ingestion as a batch pipeline with quality gates
lessons.brief: Ingestion is a batch pipeline with contracts: idempotent re-runs keyed on content hash, lineage from every chunk to its source version, and stage gates that fail the batch instead of dropping documents silently. The lesson uses NeMo Curator's stages (language detection, rule filters, exact, fuzzy and semantic dedup, model-based quality filtering) as a reference, with Presidio for PII at ingest. The reader writes the gate thresholds for empty text, duplicates, PII hits and chunk-length drift.

problems.brief: Chunk a 200-page PDF with tables and headers, and say what you would measure to know the chunking is right.
The bot cites a deleted policy: find the gap in delete propagation among other real ingestion defects.
Per-user access control in retrieval when permissions change hourly and the index rebuild takes a day.
Keep an index fresh when source documents change daily: idempotent re-ingest keyed on content hash, deletes, lineage and a quality gate.
Parse 200-page contracts with tables and stamps: tokens and cost per document for text extraction versus page images on two providers.
Critique an ingestion job that silently skips documents that fail parsing and reports success.

modules.title: Fusion, reranking and query transformation
modules.brief: Rank fusion without score calibration, choosing and training rerankers, and transformations that pay for their extra model call.

lessons.title: Fusion: RRF, score normalisation and when hybrid wins
lessons.brief: Reciprocal rank fusion merges rankings without calibrating scores, which is why it is the default when lexical and dense scores live on different scales. The lesson covers RRF's constant, weighted fusion, and identifier-heavy queries where hybrid beats dense-only retrieval. The reader implements fusion and tunes it against an eval set.

existing.note: Reranker training is added as its own lesson; query transformation becomes its own lesson.

lessons.title: Rerankers: choosing and training
lessons.brief: Cross-encoder rerankers trained with binary cross-entropy on mined hard negatives are a strong default, and the Sentence Transformers write-up shows a fine-tuned 150M reranker lifting NDCG@10 on its domain well above the retriever alone. Distillation from a larger teacher helps only when the teacher is stronger, and LLM listwise rerankers trade latency for quality. The decision is how many candidates to rerank inside a latency budget and whether to train your own.

lessons.title: Query rewriting, HyDE and decomposition: when transformation pays
lessons.brief: Transformation adds a model call before retrieval, so it pays only when queries are underspecified or need several hops. The lesson covers HyDE, multi-query and decomposition, and routing away from retrieval when it is the wrong tool. The reader measures the gain per added call before shipping it.

problems.brief: Merge two rankings with RRF and a weighted variant; hidden tests check ties and missing documents.
How many candidates can you rerank inside a latency budget: the reader specifies how to measure reranker latency, then computes with their own numbers.
Cross-encoder, ColBERT or LLM reranker for a stated latency, corpus and update rate.
Fine-tune a small reranker for a domain: training data, negative mining, evaluation and the rule for stopping.
A ranking system combining BM25, dense retrieval and LLM reranking across several indexes, with the latency budget split per stage.
HyDE raised offline recall and hurt the latency SLO and answer quality on short navigational queries; decide the routing rule.

modules.title: Late interaction, GraphRAG and agentic retrieval
modules.brief: Advanced patterns judged by what they cost: late interaction storage, GraphRAG indexing, agentic retrieval loops, and long context as the alternative.

lessons.title: Late interaction, walked through
lessons.brief: ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim, and the storage blow-up is what decides whether late interaction is affordable. ColBERTv2 cuts the footprint with residual compression, PLAID cuts search latency, and MUVERA reduces multi-vector search to single-vector MIPS. The walkthrough ends with the storage arithmetic for a stated corpus and what to say when asked whether late interaction is worth it.

lessons.title: GraphRAG: when relationships earn their indexing cost
lessons.brief: GraphRAG builds an entity graph and community summaries at indexing time so global questions can be answered, at an indexing cost that ordinary RAG does not pay. The lesson covers the original method, LazyGraphRAG's deferred summarisation, and the question types where a graph changes the answer. The reader decides when the indexing bill is justified.

existing.note: Late interaction becomes a paper walkthrough; GraphRAG, agentic RAG and long context versus RAG become separate lessons.

lessons.title: Agentic RAG: retrieve, judge, retry
lessons.brief: Agentic retrieval lets the model decide whether it has enough context and retry, which helps on multi-hop questions and loops on unanswerable ones. The lesson covers Self-RAG, corrective RAG and a LangGraph agentic retrieval loop with a retry budget and an abstain path. The reader caps the loop and measures the cost per answered question.

lessons.title: Long context, RAG or cache-augmented generation
lessons.brief: Stuffing a corpus into a long window trades retrieval errors for position effects and context rot, at a cost per query that retrieval does not pay. The lesson uses Lost in the Middle, Chroma's context-rot results and HELMET to show where long context underperforms its advertised size. The decision is per workload, with prompt caching changing the arithmetic.

problems.brief: Long context, RAG or cache-augmented generation for three stated workloads, with the cost per query of each.
When does GraphRAG earn its cost? Answer, then respond to a vendor's cost ratios presented as proof.
Implement MaxSim scoring over token vectors and compute storage for a stated corpus with and without residual compression.
Model search when documents and pasted queries exceed the context window: chunking misses, cross-document synthesis, permissions in caches and a 200-page summary.
An agentic RAG loop retries unanswerable questions until the budget ends and the bill per question jumps.
Critique a design that sends a whole policy corpus in a long window on every query because the model supports it.

modules.title: Locating RAG failures
modules.brief: A failure taxonomy by stage, oracle-context ablations, and the 50-document take-home solved and critiqued.

lessons.title: Locating a RAG failure: chunk, query, rank, context or generation
lessons.brief: Every wrong RAG answer has a first failing stage, and finding it is a bisection over the pipeline. The lesson uses the seven failure points paper and a triage function that labels the first upstream failure. The reader can classify twenty failed answers by stage in an hour.

existing.note: Cut the opening scenario and the subtraction predict; keep the taxonomy table, the triage function, oracle context and the field guide.

lessons.title: Oracle context and ablations: separating retrieval from generation
lessons.brief: Giving the generator the correct passages tells you whether the generation step can succeed at all, which separates retrieval failures from generation failures. The lesson covers oracle runs, context ablations and contextual retrieval as a fix for chunks that lose their context. The reader designs the ablation that decides where the next week of work goes.

lessons.title: The 50-document take-home, solved and critiqued
lessons.brief: The reported take-home asks for Q&A over 50 markdown documents, a 20-question eval set, and recall@5 and faithfulness. The lesson solves it with the scoping choices, the README and the eval report a reviewer wants, then critiques the common submissions. The reader can finish one in three hours and know what was cut.

problems.brief: Right documents, wrong answers: the code comment that named the bug is gone, and a chunker change is a real secondary defect to rank.
Score the take-home: compute recall@5 and a faithfulness check over a provided run, with hidden tests on edge cases.
Enterprise RAG over a company wiki where freshness and permissions conflict.
