Answer correctness fell after a reranker change while recall@k did not; the reranker truncates query plus document tokens.
Users say the bot feels dumb: critique a fix list that starts with a bigger model and a longer prompt.
Measure faithfulness without human labels and name the traps in the judge you would use.

modules.title: Vector index internals
modules.brief: HNSW built by hand, filtered vector search as a design problem, quantisation with verification, and sharding and multi-tenancy for vector search.

lessons.title: HNSW, built by hand
lessons.brief: HNSW draws each node's level from a decaying distribution, searches greedily from the top layer down, and depends on a neighbour-selection heuristic the paper says matters at high recall and on clustered data. The lesson covers M, efConstruction and efSearch, memory per node, and why deletes need tombstones or rebuilds. In the lab the reader inserts, searches, measures recall against brute force at several efSearch values, then adds a filter and watches recall fall.

lessons.title: Playbook: filtered vector search
lessons.brief: Pre-filtering, post-filtering, filter-aware traversal, iterative scans and per-tenant partitions fail at different selectivities. pgvector's README shows post-filtering at 10% selectivity with efSearch 40 returning about 4 rows, Qdrant adds filter-aware edges only if payload indexes exist before the graph is built, and ACORN traverses a predicate subgraph. The inputs are selectivity, correlation between filter and query, and tenant count; the playbook ends with the recall and latency test to run after choosing.

lessons.title: Vector quantisation with a verification pass
lessons.brief: Scalar int8, binary codes with rescoring, product quantisation and RaBitQ are lossy compression followed by a verification pass on full vectors. The lesson covers pgvector's binary_quantize expression index with a rerank of the top candidates, PQ's asymmetric distance tables, and RaBitQ's error bound. The reader picks a format for a stated recall target and RAM budget.

lessons.title: Sharding, multi-tenancy and freshness in vector search
lessons.brief: At scale vector search becomes a storage problem: RAM-resident graphs, SSD-resident indexes and object-storage engines with caches trade cost against cold-query latency. turbopuffer keeps data in object storage with a write-ahead log per namespace and reports a cold p50 of 874 ms against a warm p50 of 14 ms at 1M documents. The decision is how to shard, isolate tenants and bound freshness for a corpus with many small tenants.

problems.brief: HNSW returns 50 neighbours in 18 ms at 96% recall; with tenant, category and inventory filters it returns 11 in 140 ms. Fix filtered recall without destroying latency.
What M, efConstruction and efSearch control, and where HNSW becomes hard to operate.
Vector search for a million small tenants: index per tenant or shared, cold-start latency, freshness and cost.
Switch the embedding model at 80 million vectors: re-embedding cost, dual-write window, storage and the recall check before cut-over.
HNSW insert and search in stdlib Python; tests measure recall against brute force and require a recall floor at a fixed efSearch.
Optimise vector semantic search for an assistant: embedding choice or training, ANN and sharding, hybrid plus rerank, caching, tenant isolation and freshness.
The nlist versus nprobe trade-off in IVF, and when you add product quantisation.

modules.title: Search evaluation
modules.brief: Judgment pools and graded relevance, LLM relevance assessors and their limits, and evaluating citations.

lessons.title: Search evaluation with judgment pools and graded relevance
lessons.brief: Search quality is measured with pooled judgments and graded relevance, and leaderboards measured on other people's queries do not transfer. BEIR found BM25 a robust baseline across its datasets, and BRIGHT showed a then-leading MTEB model falling from 59.0 to 18.3 NDCG@10 on reasoning-heavy queries. The reader designs the evaluation for a new search product with no labels.

lessons.title: LLM relevance assessors: where they match humans and where they drift
lessons.brief: LLM relevance labels reached human-level accuracy at Bing at a fraction of the cost, and the same work found that paraphrasing the prompt changes accuracy. UMBRELA reproduces the approach openly and correlates with system rankings on TREC tracks, which is a weaker claim than agreeing with each human label. The reader calibrates an LLM assessor on a human-labelled slice before trusting it.

lessons.title: Evaluating citations and answer attribution
lessons.brief: A citation is correct only if the cited span supports the claim it is attached to, which is a stricter test than retrieving a relevant document. The lesson covers provider citation features, search-result content blocks, and Perplexity's published search architecture as an example of span-level retrieval feeding answers. The reader writes the citation checks for an answer engine.

problems.brief: Build the relevance-judgment workflow for a new enterprise search product with no labels: pools, grades, assessors and calibration.
Offline recall is good but online search quality is bad: what do you check, in what order?
How would you evaluate an answer's citation quality, and which failure would a document-level check miss?
Two-stage retrieval and ranking with user and listing embeddings: labels, position bias and evaluation.
Critique an embedding-model choice made from the MTEB leaderboard alone for a reasoning-heavy support corpus.
Candidate search over resumes with noisy structured data and hard filters that must exclude.

tracks.title: Agents and protocols
tracks.brief: The agent loop and its economics, tools and protocols (MCP at the 2026-07-28 revision, A2A, Agent Skills), memory and long-lived state, multi-agent systems and their failure modes, and computer-use agents with autonomy controls. Coding-agent harnesses have their own track (harness), durable execution lives in workflows, and MCP authorisation is implemented in security; this track keeps the agent-level decisions.

modules.title: The agent loop and its economics
modules.brief: Quadratic token growth, budgets that end runs cleanly, verification inside the loop, and debugging a looping agent from its trace.

lessons.title: The loop's cost: quadratic tokens, budgets and stuck detection
lessons.brief: Each turn re-sends the history, so token cost grows quadratically with turns unless the cache holds the prefix. The lesson covers step, spend and wall-clock budgets, the Agent SDK rule that max_turns needs one extra turn for the final answer or the run ends with error_max_turns, stuck-state detectors, and the error contract between tools and the loop. The reader prices a 30-call run and sets budgets that end runs cleanly.

existing.note: Cut the while-loop section and the interpreter analogy; keep the quadratic arithmetic, the three budgets, the detector, the error contract and cache hygiene (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: Planning, reflection and verification inside the loop
lessons.brief: Plans and reflections are model output and need the same checks as tool calls. The lesson covers ReAct, plan-then-execute, verifier steps that run code or tests, and the cases where reflection only adds cost. The reader places one deterministic check in a loop and measures what it catches.

lessons.title: Debugging a looping agent from its trace
lessons.brief: Loops come from tool errors that look like progress, missing termination signals and lost context, and each leaves a different signature in the trace. The lesson reads recorded traces with fault injection and maps each signature to a fix in the tool, the budget or the context policy. The reader can find the cause from a trace in minutes.

problems.brief: The agent loops forever on some inputs: find the cause from the trace and fix it at the right layer.
Write a minimal agent loop with tool dispatch, a max-steps guard and the final-turn rule; hidden tests inject tool errors.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported phone-screen task via a commercial blog)

problems.brief: Workflow, ReAct loop or state machine for three stated systems, with what each choice costs.
Forty-seven tool calls for a five-call task: rank the causes from the trace.
Price a 30-call agent run with and without a warm cache, and the budget that would stop a runaway at a stated cost.
An agent calls a broken tool 400 times in five minutes: which controls at the orchestrator, tool and cost layers would each have stopped it?

modules.title: Tools, MCP, A2A and skills
modules.brief: Designing tools for models, MCP at its current revision, when A2A beats one agent with more tools, and Agent Skills as progressive disclosure.

lessons.title: Designing tools for agents: narrow, idempotent, well-errored
lessons.brief: Tools are an interface for a model, so names, argument types, response size and error messages are all prompts. Anthropic's guidance includes a concise or detailed response format (72 versus 206 tokens in its Slack example) and errors that say what to do next, and tool search with deferred loading changes how many tools an agent can carry. The reader rewrites a tool set and measures the change in wrong calls.

existing.note: MCP authorisation implementation moves to security/mcp-security; coding-agent tool design moves to harness/tools-aci.

lessons.title: MCP at the 2026-07-28 revision: transports, stateless requests and migration
lessons.brief: The 2026-07-28 revision moved MCP to per-request version negotiation and stateless patterns, and revisions from 2025-11-25 back are handshake-based. The lesson covers the streamable HTTP transport, the multi-round-trip pattern, the deprecation window (at least twelve months) and what a stateful server must change to migrate. The reader can plan a server migration and its compatibility period.

lessons.title: A2A, MCP or one agent with more tools
lessons.brief: A2A connects agents owned by different parties, MCP connects an agent to tools and data, and most systems need neither boundary inside one team. The lesson covers the A2A specification, the move of MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, and the cost of an agent boundary in latency and debugging. The decision is where an organisational boundary justifies a protocol boundary.

lessons.title: Agent Skills: progressive disclosure and where procedures live
lessons.brief: A skill loads its name and description every session and its body only when used, which keeps procedures out of the base context. The lesson covers the SKILL.md specification, skills versus tools versus memory files, and side-effecting skills that must not be invoked by the model on its own. The reader decides which of a team's procedures become skills.

problems.brief: A2A or MCP for four stated integrations, with options of equal length.
Skills, MCP tools or fine-tuning for a team's procedures, with the context cost of each.
Move a stateful MCP server to the 2026-07-28 revision without breaking existing clients.
The wiki token opened the billing server; a missing customer_id authorisation check is a real secondary defect to rank.
Two hundred tools: stop the model choosing the wrong ones with deferred loading, tool search and namespacing, and measure the result.
Which MCP servers would you refuse to install? Critique a team's MCP configuration file.

modules.title: Memory and long-lived state
modules.brief: What an assistant should remember and forget, memory as an attack and privacy surface, and checkpoints that cover state but not side effects.

lessons.title: What to remember: memory kinds, write policy and forgetting
lessons.brief: Long-term memory is a write path into every future context, so the write policy matters more than the store. The lesson covers semantic, episodic and procedural memory, the Claude memory tool and LangGraph stores, and policies for consolidation and forgetting. The reader designs memory for an assistant that runs for months.

existing.note: Memory kinds and write policy stay here; durable execution moves to workflows/durable-execution; memory files move to harness/context-management.

lessons.title: Memory as an attack and privacy surface
lessons.brief: Anything written to long-term memory is replayed into future contexts, so a memory write from untrusted content persists an injection across sessions. The lesson covers the spAIware case against ChatGPT memory, provenance on memory entries, OpenAI's memory controls and retention notes, and deletion that must reach memory as well as chats. The reader designs memory writes that an attacker cannot use as a foothold.

lessons.title: Checkpoints, resume and rollback for long agent runs
lessons.brief: Agent checkpoints capture state but not external side effects, so resume needs idempotent tools and rollback needs compensation. The lesson covers LangGraph checkpointers, Claude Code checkpoints that cover file edits only, and progress files that let a fresh session continue. The reader makes a three-hour run resumable after a crash.

problems.brief: A refund agent that waits for a human: persistence, resume, no double payout.
The agent forgot what it finished after a context reset; the progress file and the checkpoint disagree.
Guard the memory tool's paths against traversal, symlinks and writes outside the memory root.
Memory for a personal assistant that runs for months: what is written, provenance, consolidation, forgetting and deletion.
Critique a memory feature that writes a summary of every web page the agent reads into long-term memory.
Context-window pressure on a long task: keep the goal without keeping everything, and say what you would test.

modules.title: Multi-agent systems and their failure modes
modules.brief: When parallel breadth pays for its token multiplier, what fails only with several agents, and the contract between an orchestrator and its workers.

lessons.title: When several agents pay: parallel breadth versus shared context
lessons.brief: Anthropic's research system beat a single agent by 90.2% on its internal eval while using about 15 times the tokens of chat, and Cognition argues single-threaded agents with shared context are more reliable for coupled work. The lesson reads both as conditions: breadth-first tasks with separable subtasks favour several agents, and tightly coupled edits favour one. The reader decides for three stated tasks and states the cost.

existing.note: Keep orchestrator-worker numbers and MAST; move sub-agents as a harness feature to harness/context-management.

lessons.title: MAST: why multi-agent systems fail
lessons.brief: MAST classifies multi-agent failures into specification, inter-agent misalignment and verification failures from annotated traces. Most failures it records are design failures rather than model errors, which is why adding agents rarely fixes them. The walkthrough ends with coding a set of traces against the taxonomy.

lessons.title: The delegation contract: scope, budget, output and verification
lessons.brief: Orchestrator-worker systems fail at the boundary, so each delegation states the objective, output format, allowed tools, budget and how the result is verified. The lesson uses Anthropic's lessons on vague delegation and the OpenAI Agents SDK's agents-as-tools and handoffs to show both ends of the contract. The reader writes the contract for a research or code-review system.

problems.brief: Six passes in eight trials: what that says about pass^k, and how many more trials you need.
The guardrail fired too late in a handoff chain: which placement fixes it?
Failures that need more than one agent to happen, classified with MAST.
Write the delegation contract between an orchestrator and its workers, with budgets, output schema and verification.
Two agents are editing the same file: prevent and resolve conflicts.
Critique a code-review system of five specialist agents with no verifier and a majority vote.

modules.title: Computer use, browser agents and autonomy controls
modules.brief: Agents that act through screens and browsers, the controls that bound them, and the published residual injection rates that set the design.

lessons.title: Computer use and browser agents: screenshots, DOM and flakiness
lessons.brief: Computer-use agents act through screenshots and input events, browser agents can also read the DOM, and both are slower and flakier than API tools. The lesson covers the Claude computer-use tool, OSWorld as the benchmark, and ChatGPT agent's mix of a visual browser, a text browser, a terminal and connectors. The decision is when a screen-driving agent is worth its cost over an integration.

existing.note: Harness material (model versus harness, AGENTS.md, permission rules, sandboxes) moves to the harness track and is corrected there; computer use and autonomy stay here.

lessons.title: Autonomy controls: modes, action budgets, kill switches and approvals that mean something
lessons.brief: Autonomy is a set of dials (permission mode, action budget, confirmation rules, kill switch), and approvals that users click through stop being a control. Anthropic reports users approved 93% of permission prompts before auto mode, and ChatGPT agent asks for confirmation before consequential actions. The reader sets the dials for an agent that can spend money.

lessons.title: Prompt injection against acting agents: what vendors publish
lessons.brief: Browser agents read attacker-controlled pages with the user's sessions, so the residual attack rate is a design input rather than a bug to close. Anthropic reports about 1% attack success for Claude Opus 4.5 in a browser under an adaptive attacker, and OpenAI writes that prompt injection is unlikely ever to be fully solved. The reader designs the agent so that a successful injection has a bounded blast radius.

problems.brief: The agent dropped a production table: redesign permissions and approvals using published incidents (config that ran before trust, credentials read from disk, an allowlisted upload domain).
The approval gate allowed curl through a compound command; find the parsing gap.
Evaluate a browser agent that books travel: environment, success criteria, side-effect safety and pass^k.
Which actions need human approval, and how do you keep approvals from becoming a reflex click?
Expected successful injections per month for a browser agent at a published residual attack rate and a stated exposure volume, and what that implies for scopes.
Critique an agent mode that confirms only purchases and leaves all connectors enabled by default.

tracks.title: Harness engineering and agentic coding tools
tracks.brief: Everything between the user and the sampler in a coding agent: how a harness assembles each request, which controls are deterministic and which are the model deciding, tool sets built for models, memory files and compaction, prompt caching inside a harness, rule engines, sandboxes, hooks and classifier approvers, verification loops, long-running and parallel agents, and how to tell a harness effect from a model or infrastructure effect. Built from vendor documentation and engineering posts (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenHands, Aider, SWE-agent) dated 2025 and 2026, with a teardown of each tool. This is the owner's first missing area and is built first.

modules.title: What the harness owns
modules.brief: The split between model and harness, how a harness builds each model call, which controls are enforced and which are advice, and the research on how much harness a strong model needs.

lessons.title: Model plus harness: what each one decides
lessons.brief: The harness is everything between the user and the sampler: prompt assembly, tool set, context management, permissions and sandbox, verification, budgets and persistence. Claude Code's docs call this layer the agentic harness, OpenAI calls the Codex agent loop the harness, and Böckeler splits a user-built harness into feedforward guides and feedback sensors, each computational or inferential. The lesson assigns common coding-agent failures to the layer that fixes each one, and corrects two statements in the old lesson: editing CLAUDE.md mid-session neither breaks the cache nor applies until /clear, /compact or a restart, and Cursor's current docs say it stores no embeddings for search.

existing.note: The "harness is most of the product" section becomes this lesson; permission rules and sandboxes move to permissions-sandboxing; computer use stays in agents/coding-agents. Fix the CLAUDE.md cache sentence and date the Cursor semantic-search figure as historical.

lessons.title: The request lifecycle: how a harness builds each model call
lessons.brief: Codex sends instructions, tools and an input list to the Responses API, concatenates AGENTS.md files from the git root to the working directory up to 32 KiB by default, appends configuration changes as new messages, and avoids previous_response_id to stay stateless and support zero data retention. Claude Code orders a request as system prompt and tools, then project context (CLAUDE.md, auto memory, unscoped rules), then the conversation, and appends plan mode and skill loading as messages so the prefix holds. The lesson shows one real turn from each tool as an annotated trace.

lessons.title: Deterministic versus model-decided controls
lessons.brief: Claude Code's best-practices page sorts controls into what the model decides (prompt, CLAUDE.md, skills, the auto-mode classifier, effort) and what the harness enforces (hooks, deny rules, sandbox, managed settings, a Stop hook running tests, turn and budget caps, branch protection). Its rule is that anything that must happen every time becomes a hook, a deny rule or a managed setting, and the enforced set stays small. OpenAI's harness team does the same by promoting rules into custom lints whose error message carries the fix.

lessons.title: SWE-agent and the agent-computer interface
lessons.brief: SWE-agent treats the model as a new kind of user that needs purpose-built interfaces: search capped at 50 results, a 100-line file viewer, an edit command guarded by a linter, old observations collapsed, and a $4 per-instance budget. Its ablations on SWE-bench Lite with GPT-4 Turbo are the payload: 18.0% with the full interface, 15.0% without the linter, 10.3% with no edit command, and lower scores with a 30-line window or the whole file. What to say in an interview is which of these choices still matter with stronger models and how you would measure it.

lessons.title: The minimal harness: mini-swe-agent, CodeAct and Agentless
lessons.brief: mini-swe-agent is about 100 lines for the agent class, uses only bash with linear history, and runs each action as an independent subprocess, which makes swapping in a container trivial. CodeAct argues for code as the action space and Agentless replaces the loop with a fixed localise, repair and validate pipeline. The interview point is how much harness a strong model needs and what you lose by deleting it, with the caveat that scores across these papers use different models.

problems.brief: Model or harness: assign five described coding-agent failures to the layer that fixes each, and name the one that needs both.
Tear down this harness: a design that rewrites the system prompt each turn, splits commands with a regex, keeps AGENTS.md at a thousand lines and has no Stop check.
Build an agent from only a model API and a file editor tool, and stop it repeating the same tool call; hidden tests use a scripted mock model.
Which of these is enforced regardless of what the model decides: a CLAUDE.md rule, a PreToolUse hook that exits 2, the auto-mode classifier, or a skill?
Design an AI coding agent: request assembly, tools, context policy, permissions, verification and budgets, and what you would build versus rent.
Compare your agent with Claude Code and Codex on context assembly, skill loading and checkpoints, and say what you would copy.
Why build your own coding agent when Claude Code exists? Defend the decision to a sceptical director.

modules.title: Tool sets for coding agents
modules.brief: Bash-only versus specialised tools, tool output as a bounded buffer, carrying many tools without paying for them every turn, errors that instruct, and parallel tool calls.

lessons.title: Playbook: bash-only or specialised tools
lessons.brief: A coding agent can run on bash alone (mini-swe-agent), on bash plus a string-replace editor (the two tools in the Claude 4 SWE-bench scaffold), on a broad built-in set (Claude Code), or with code as the action space. The inputs are model strength, portability across vendors, the need for structured permission checks and observability. The playbook works a stated case and ends with what to measure after choosing.

lessons.title: Tool output budgets and pruning
lessons.brief: Every tool result is a write into a bounded buffer: Claude Code's Read returns at most 25,000 tokens per call, Bash output over about 30,000 characters becomes a saved file plus a short preview, and Glob caps at 100 files. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance adds response formats and actionable errors, and clearing old tool results is the lightest form of compaction. The reader sets output budgets for a tool set and tests the truncation paths.

lessons.title: Many tools: deferred loading, tool search and code execution
lessons.brief: Anthropic measured 58 tools across five MCP servers at about 55K tokens before the conversation started; tool search with deferred loading cut a 77K-token setup to 8.7K and raised MCP eval accuracy. Programmatic tool calling and code execution with MCP cut tokens further for workflows that chain tools. Claude Code now defers MCP tools by default, which also keeps the cache intact when a server connects mid-session.

lessons.title: Errors and lints as instructions
lessons.brief: An error message is the next prompt, so it should say what to do. SWE-agent's linter rejects a bad edit and shows the error, OpenAI's harness team writes custom lint messages that inject the remediation, Cursor found agents retried a sandbox-blocked command unchanged until the result named the sandbox constraint, and Goose returns invalid-JSON errors to the model as tool results. The reader rewrites three error messages and measures retries.

lessons.title: Parallel tool calls
lessons.brief: The Agent SDK runs read-only tools concurrently and mutating tools sequentially, and custom tools default to sequential. Anthropic's research system cut research time by up to 90% with parallel sub-agents and tool calls, and Cognition's SWE-grep issues several parallel calls per turn for a few turns. The lesson covers what breaks when a tool wrongly claims to be read-only.

problems.brief: Choose the tool set for an internal coding agent that must run on models from three vendors, with permission checks your security team can audit.
Tool output truncation to a character budget with a file-path fallback and a truncation flag; hidden tests probe the boundaries.
Tokens spent before the conversation starts with 58 tools across five servers versus deferred loading, and the break-even per session with caching.
Critique a lint message the agent keeps ignoring, then rewrite it to carry the fix.
The agent retries a sandbox-blocked command unchanged until the budget ends; the shell result never names the sandbox.
Read-only tools run concurrently and mutating tools sequentially: why, and what breaks when a custom tool lies about being read-only.

modules.title: Context management in a harness
modules.brief: Memory files and their load order, where a piece of knowledge or policy should live, compaction, context resets, sub-agents as context firewalls, and how agents find code.

lessons.title: Memory files: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and rules
lessons.brief: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md from the working directory and every parent at launch and subdirectory files on demand, Codex concatenates AGENTS.md files from the git root down to 32 KiB by default, and Cursor applies .mdc rules by type. OpenAI's harness team keeps AGENTS.md at roughly 100 lines as a map into a docs tree, Chroma's context-rot results argue for focused context, and the ETH Zurich study found context files raise inference cost by over 20% without a general success gain. The lesson concludes that memory files should hold what the agent cannot infer from the code, and nothing else.

lessons.title: Playbook: CLAUDE.md, skill, rule, hook, sub-agent or MCP server
lessons.brief: The decision is where a piece of knowledge or policy lives, and the inputs are whether it applies to every task, whether it is a procedure, whether it must be enforced and what it costs in context every turn. Claude Code's guidance puts facts the agent cannot infer in CLAUDE.md, procedures in skills, area conventions in path-scoped rules, zero-exception rules in hooks or deny rules, noisy work in sub-agents, and prefers a CLI to an MCP server when one exists. The worked case sorts a team's twenty rules and procedures.

lessons.title: Compaction: what survives and what it costs
lessons.brief: In Claude Code the system prompt stays, project-root CLAUDE.md and auto memory are re-read from disk, recently modified files and invoked skill bodies are re-injected within caps, and path-scoped rules and nested memory files are summarised away. Codex compacts through an endpoint whose returned item is opaque and encrypted, and OpenHands' condenser keeps the first events and halves the view while logging a condensation event. Compaction is itself a request over the whole conversation, cheap while the cache is warm and expensive after the TTL.

lessons.title: Context resets versus compaction
lessons.brief: Anthropic's 2026-03-24 harness-design post found Sonnet 4.5 wrapping up early as it neared its believed limit, which made full resets with a structured handoff necessary; with Opus 4.5 the resets were dropped and automatic compaction was enough. The general lesson is that harness components encode assumptions about one model and must be re-tested per model. The walkthrough ends with how you would detect such an assumption before it ships.

lessons.title: Sub-agents as context firewalls
lessons.brief: Claude Code sub-agents start with a fresh context, return only a summary, nest up to three levels and can be limited to read-only tools so a reviewer cannot edit. The docs say delegation does not make the answer smarter; a fresh reviewer helps because it has not seen the reasoning, and Cognition's SWE-grep exists because retrieval dominated the first turn. The reader decides which work to delegate and what it costs in tokens and time.

lessons.title: Finding code: grep, repo maps and embeddings
lessons.brief: Aider ranks a tree-sitter tag graph with personalised PageRank into a token budget, Anthropic recommends starting with agentic search and adding semantic search only if needed, and Cursor reported a 12.5% average accuracy gain from semantic search in November 2025 while its current docs say no embeddings are stored for search. The lesson treats the choice as a lexer versus an index and shows how to measure it on your own repository. Every vendor figure is dated, because this is where content goes stale fastest.

problems.brief: Design the compaction and memory policy for a six-hour run: what is pinned, what is summarised, what is re-read from disk, and how you test that the goal survives.
Critique a CLAUDE.md that restates the code, uses capitals for emphasis and buries the test command at line 300.
AGENTS.md has grown to a thousand lines and agents ignore half of it: redesign repository knowledge for agents and enforce it mechanically.
A long-running agent drifts after hours and confidently works on the wrong thing; diagnose from its compaction events and progress file.
Grep or retrieval for searching a repository, and what you would measure to decide on your own codebase.
After Claude Code compacts, which of these is gone: project-root CLAUDE.md, a path-scoped rule, an invoked skill body, or the plan from plan mode?
Context files that raise inference cost by over 20%: price it per month for a stated team and say what result would justify keeping them.

modules.title: The harness's bill
modules.brief: Prompt caching inside a harness and what breaks it, what published harness runs cost, runaway controls, and latency from decoupling the loop from the sandbox.

lessons.title: Prompt caching inside a harness
lessons.brief: Exact-prefix matching means any change recomputes everything after it, and Claude Code lists its cache breakers: switching models, changing effort on most models, toggling fast mode, connecting MCP servers when tools load upfront, compaction, image eviction and upgrades. Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session does not break the cache and does not apply until /clear, /compact or a restart, while Codex breaks its cache on tool, model, sandbox, approval-mode or working-directory changes and once on an MCP tool-ordering bug. The reader predicts a session's cache hit rate from its events.

lessons.title: What a harness costs
lessons.brief: Published runs give real numbers: Anthropic's retro game maker cost $9 in 20 minutes solo against $200 in six hours with the full three-agent harness, the C compiler took nearly 2,000 sessions and just under $20,000, and multi-agent research runs at about 15 times chat tokens. The lesson turns each into an estimate with its assumptions stated. The reader can say what a harness change will cost before running it.

lessons.title: Playbook: cost and runaway controls
lessons.brief: Turn caps, dollar caps, auto-mode fallbacks after repeated denials, a cap on consecutive Stop-hook blocks and per-instance budgets each stop a different runaway. The inputs are whether the agent runs headless, who pays, and what a stopped run costs to resume; Anthropic's reverted change of default effort is the example of a cost lever that cost quality. The playbook ends with the dashboard that shows a runaway before the invoice does.

lessons.title: Latency: decoupling the loop from the sandbox
lessons.brief: Claude Managed Agents provisions a container only when a tool needs one, and Anthropic reports p50 time to first token down about 60% and p95 down over 90% after the change. The lesson covers the session log outside the harness, sandboxes behind an execute interface, and a dead container returned to the model as a tool error. The reader designs lazy provisioning for an agent platform.

problems.brief: Cache hit rate and bill for a three-hour session with two model switches and one compaction, with TTL and cache-write premiums.
The cache hit rate dropped to zero after an MCP server began announcing tool-list changes mid-conversation.
Which of these breaks Claude Code's prompt cache: editing CLAUDE.md mid-session, switching models, connecting a server whose tools are deferred, or /rewind?
Best-of-five with a verifier versus one attempt with a larger budget, priced per resolved task with stated pass rates.
Replay Anthropic's April 2026 postmortem: a thinking-clearing bug causes cache misses and quality loss; commit to a hypothesis at each checkpoint and name the gate that would have caught it.
Runaway controls for headless agents in CI: turn caps, dollar caps, denial fallbacks and the alert that fires first.

modules.title: Permissions and policy in the harness
modules.brief: Rule engines for shell commands, hooks as policy and how they fail open, classifiers as approvers with published error rates, and the harness's own configuration as an attack surface.

lessons.title: Rule engines for shell commands
lessons.brief: Claude Code evaluates deny, then ask, then allow, applies deny in every mode, splits compound commands on shell separators and never auto-approves protected paths. Codex uses Starlark rules with allow, prompt and forbidden decisions where the strictest wins, and evaluates any script with substitution, redirection or control flow as one command instead of splitting it. The lesson shows why a regex split is not a parser and how to test rules before shipping them.

lessons.title: Hooks as policy, and how they fail
lessons.brief: Claude Code has 33 hook events and five handler types; exit code 2 blocks, exit code 1 does not, and hooks fail open on crash or timeout unless configured to block. Prompt and agent hooks are another model deciding, not enforcement, and a Stop hook that runs the typecheck is the canonical verification gate. The reader writes a policy hook that fails closed and a test that proves it.

lessons.title: Classifiers as approvers: Claude Code auto mode and its peers
lessons.brief: Anthropic's auto-mode post reports a two-stage classifier that sees user messages and tool calls with tool results stripped, a 0.4% false-positive rate on 10,000 real actions, and a 17% false-negative rate on 52 real overeager actions, and calls it not a drop-in replacement for careful review on high-stakes infrastructure. Cursor says its Auto-review is not a security boundary and Codex auto-review never widens the sandbox. The walkthrough ends with what you put around an approver that misses one dangerous action in six.

lessons.title: The harness as an attack surface
lessons.brief: The files an agent can write are the files that configure the agent, so Claude Code write-protects its settings, hooks, skills, MCP config and git internals, Codex keeps .git, .codex and .aws read-only, and project settings cannot raise the permission mode. Cursor's CVE-2025-54135, where an injected agent created an MCP config without approval and reached code execution, is the failure case, and Anthropic's containment post adds project config that ran before the trust prompt. The reader audits a harness for paths that let the agent grant itself permissions.

problems.brief: A shell-aware permission gate: deny, ask and allow with compound-command splitting, refusing to split scripts that contain substitution or redirection; hidden tests include bypass attempts.
Critique a policy hook that exits 1 on violation and times out under load.
Critique a safety design that relies on a risk flag the model sets on its own tool calls, under an injected instruction.
An approval classifier with a 0.4% false-positive and 17% false-negative rate on overeager actions: expected misses per week at a stated action volume, and what you put around it.
The same compound command is allowed by one harness and prompts in another: explain which rule fired in each.
Harness security and permissions for an internal coding agent, and when a long task should stop early.
problems.reported: Alibaba Cloud (candidate report via keepkeen guide)

problems.brief: In an interactive session where bypass permissions are available, what actually stops edits in plan mode?

modules.title: Verification: how the agent knows it is done
modules.brief: Giving the agent a check to run, separate evaluator agents, keeping oracles out of the agent's reach, and parallel attempts that need a verifier to mean anything.

lessons.title: Give the agent a check to run
lessons.brief: Claude Code's guidance says the most useful line in CLAUDE.md is the command that runs the checks, enforced by a Stop hook that sends the agent back with the failing output. The Agent SDK post orders verification as rules (lint, types), then visual feedback, then an LLM judge, which it calls generally not very robust. The reader wires a check into a harness and measures how often it sends the agent back.

lessons.title: Generator and evaluator agents
lessons.brief: Anthropic's 2026-03-24 harness post found self-evaluation lenient and Claude a poor QA agent out of the box, then built a separate evaluator with few-shot score breakdowns, Playwright against the running app and hard thresholds per criterion. Sprint contracts were negotiated in files, and the planner and evaluator survived after a newer model made sprints unnecessary. The walkthrough ends with how you would know your evaluator is stricter than your generator.

lessons.title: Tests the agent cannot edit, and benchmarks that grade the oracle
lessons.brief: Agents edit tests when tests stand between them and done, so Anthropic's long-running harness tells agents it is unacceptable to remove or edit tests, and Anthropic's performance take-home README records model submissions that modified the tests. OpenAI's audit found 59.4% of 138 hard SWE-bench Verified problems had material issues, which is the same failure at benchmark scale. The reader designs a check the agent cannot weaken.

lessons.title: Parallel attempts and test-time scaling
lessons.brief: Large Language Monkeys raised SWE-bench Lite coverage from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250, and found voting and reward models plateau without automatic verifiers. Claude 4's parallel test-time compute sampled attempts, discarded patches that failed visible tests and picked with a scoring model, lifting Opus 4 from 72.5% to 79.4%. The point is that selection needs a verifier and that high-compute numbers are a different quantity from pass@1.

problems.brief: Run a coding agent headless in CI: non-interactive mode, an exact allowlist, a budget, a Stop check and branch protection.
Critique a CI pipeline in which the agent can edit its own tests and the merge gate is "tests pass".
Code review for a world where most PRs are agent-generated: who reviews, what is checked mechanically, and what still needs a human.
For a bug-fix agent, static specification or dynamic feedback from the environment: which, and why?
Coverage at 1 and 250 samples versus success with an imperfect verifier: what selection can and cannot recover.
The agent marks features done that fail end to end: find where the harness lets it declare victory early.

modules.title: Long-running and parallel agents
modules.brief: Harnesses that survive many context windows, the session log outside the harness, parallel agents coordinating through git, and worktrees and fan-out.

lessons.title: The long-running harness
lessons.brief: Anthropic's long-running harness has an initializer agent write an init script, a progress file and a JSON feature list of over 200 features all marked failing (JSON because models overwrite it less than Markdown), and each coding session reads git log and progress, picks one feature, runs an end-to-end check first, commits and updates progress. OpenAI's harness team reports single Codex runs of upwards of six hours. The reader designs what persists between sessions, in what format, and who may edit it.

lessons.title: Sessions as an event log outside the harness
lessons.brief: Managed Agents keeps the session as an append-only event log behind a small API, runs a stateless harness and treats sandboxes as tools, so a dead container is a tool error rather than a lost run. The OpenHands SDK paper describes the same event-sourced design, and Anthropic's research system used rainbow deployments to avoid breaking running agents. The reader designs session storage that survives harness upgrades.

lessons.title: Parallel agents without an orchestrator
lessons.brief: The C compiler build ran 16 Claude instances in containers against a bare git upstream, claimed tasks with lock files resolved by git conflicts and used no orchestration agent, with specialised roles for dedupe, performance and docs. The walkthrough compares it with Claude Code worktrees and batch fan-out into separate PRs, and with Cognition's argument against splitting context. What to say in an interview is which coordination primitive you would trust and why.

problems.brief: Design the harness for a coding agent that must work across many context resets: what persists between sessions, in what format, and who may edit it.
Worktrees, sandboxes, a harness gate, context isolation and token return on investment for a team running parallel agents.
problems.reported: Alibaba International (public recruiting samples via keepkeen guide)

problems.brief: The server restarts at step fourteen of twenty: what happens to the task, and what did the harness need to record to make that safe?
From the C compiler's published totals, compute tokens and cost per session, and what a half-as-efficient agent would have cost.
Critique a lock-file task-claiming scheme for parallel agents and find the race.
The agent does well on short tasks and degrades past 30 minutes: separate context, compaction and task-state causes.

modules.title: Is harness B better than harness A?
modules.brief: Attributing a score change to model, harness or infrastructure, the coding-agent benchmark map, and shipping harness changes safely.

lessons.title: Attributing a score to model, harness or infrastructure
lessons.brief: On Terminal-Bench 2.0, moving from strict resource limits to uncapped lifted success by 6 points while infrastructure errors fell from 5.8% to 0.5%, and Anthropic advises scepticism about leaderboard gaps under 3 points until configurations match. Terminal-Bench runs several agent harnesses through one framework, which makes harness swaps measurable with the model held fixed. The reader designs a comparison that isolates the harness.

existing.note: Harness-versus-model attribution is new; it links back to agent-evals for grading.

lessons.title: The coding-agent benchmark map
lessons.brief: SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks; OpenAI stopped reporting it in February 2026), SWE-bench Pro (1,865 problems from 41 repositories in public, held-out and commercial splits), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 tasks), tau-bench and the bash-only leaderboard each measure something different. The lesson says what each can support as a claim and what it cannot. The reader can answer "our harness scores X" with the right follow-up questions.

lessons.title: Playbook: shipping a harness change safely
lessons.brief: Anthropic's April 2026 postmortem describes three harness changes (a lower default effort, a thinking-clearing bug that also caused cache misses, and a verbosity line that cost 3% on a broad eval) that each passed review, tests or dogfooding. Its commitments are a broad per-model eval for every system-prompt change, line-by-line ablations, soak periods, gradual rollouts and model-specific changes gated to their model. The playbook adds rainbow deployments for in-flight agents and what to monitor in the first week.

problems.brief: Your score moved four points the week you changed the harness and migrated benchmark infrastructure: attribute it, and design the run that would settle it.
Paired trials needed to detect a three-point difference on an 89-task benchmark given the noise you assume.
Ship one system-prompt change across three models: ablations, soak period, gradual rollout and the rollback trigger.
A pass^k runner with cost and turns per trial that flags gaps inside the noise band; hidden tests vary trial counts.
Critique a vendor comparison of two harnesses run on different models and different resource limits.
Which modules make up a harness, and how do you keep a harness eval set from being overfit?

tracks.title: Prompt injection, guardrails and model safety
tracks.brief: The model-facing half of AI security and safety: trust boundaries and exfiltration channels, adaptive red-teaming, prompt-injection defences split into those that hold by construction (CaMeL, FIDES, deterministic exfiltration blocks, the six design patterns) and those that only lower a rate (spotlighting, instruction hierarchy, classifiers) with their published limits, guardrails and tenant isolation, and hallucination and alignment topics engineers are asked about. Infrastructure security (sandboxes, secrets, MCP authorisation, supply chain, operations, governance) is in the security track.

modules.title: Trust boundaries and exfiltration
modules.brief: Where instructions and data share a channel, the OWASP lists as a controls checklist, and the channels data leaves through.

lessons.title: Trust boundaries in model systems
lessons.brief: Instructions and data share one channel, so every untrusted input is a potential instruction and every capability is a potential exfiltration path. The lesson uses the lethal trifecta and Meta's Rule of Two to score a session's capabilities, and names the MCP attack classes the specification's security page lists. The reader can draw the trust boundaries of an agent and say which leg to remove.

existing.note: Cut the SQL-injection section, the direct and indirect definitions and the trifecta list; keep EchoLeak, the OWASP renumbering note and the MCP items (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: The OWASP lists as a controls checklist
lessons.brief: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications changed between 2025 and 2026 (Excessive Agency is now third), and the Agentic Top 10 and the Agent Control Standard add agent-specific entries and runtime enforcement points. The lesson maps each entry to the control and the test that addresses it instead of reciting the list. Every reference carries its year, because the numbering moved.

lessons.title: Exfiltration without a send tool
lessons.brief: Data leaves through rendered images and links, allowlisted domains with upload APIs and anything else that makes a request on the attacker's behalf. EchoLeak chained classifier evasion, reference-style Markdown and an allowed proxy, and Anthropic's containment post describes a file upload to an attacker's account through an allowlisted domain. The fix pattern is a deterministic block on the channel, not a better prompt.

problems.brief: An attacker controls one document in your RAG index: walk the paths from that document to harm and the control for each.
Why is "never reveal the system prompt" at the top of the prompt not enough? Options of equal length.
Secure an email agent that can read and send, when the CISO wants it off and the PM has a launch date.
What security risks does MCP introduce, mapped to the specification's own mitigations?
The image filter that let data out: find the rendering path the filter did not cover.
Threat-model a model inference API that receives untrusted input at scale.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

modules.title: Adaptive red-teaming
modules.brief: Why small bypass rates become certainties, and turning attacks into regression suites.

lessons.title: Why small bypass rates become certainties
lessons.brief: An attacker who can retry turns a small per-attempt success rate into near-certain success, which is what Best-of-N jailbreaking and many-shot jailbreaking exploit. The Attacker Moves Second bypassed 12 published defences, most above 90% success, where most had reported near zero. The reader computes attempts-to-success for a stated defence and decides what that means for the architecture.

existing.note: Security evals in CI and the red-team programme move to security/security-ops; adaptive attacks and regression suites stay.

lessons.title: Turning found attacks into regression suites
lessons.brief: Every attack that worked once becomes a test that runs forever, and canaries detect leaks without preventing them. The lesson covers garak probe families, promptfoo red-team configuration, canary tokens and how to keep a regression battery from going stale. The reader builds a suite from five found attacks and wires it to a release.

lessons.title: Attack families and why surface filters fail
lessons.brief: Role-play, encoding, translation, many-shot and multi-turn attacks and payload splitting each defeat a different surface check, which is why keyword and pattern filters fail against an attacker who adapts. Many-shot jailbreaking exploits long context directly, and Best-of-N shows that simple random augmentations retried enough times get through. The reader maps each family to the layer that can stop it and to the regression test that keeps it stopped.

problems.brief: How many attempts does the attacker need against a classifier with a stated recall, and what does that imply for rate limits and architecture?
Ship a classifier that catches 95% of injections? Compute the residual at your traffic and decide.
The command allowlist that checks only the first word: find the bypass and the fix.
Red-team an LLM feature before launch with two weeks and one engineer: scope, attack families, success criteria and what blocks launch.
Detect a leaked canary, including encoded and split copies; hidden tests include obfuscations.
Design a red-team exercise to find security risks introduced by AI-generated code in a production codebase.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

modules.title: Prompt-injection defences: what holds and what lowers a rate
modules.brief: Defences that hold by construction, defences that only lower a rate with their published limits, tool-result hygiene, and choosing a design pattern per task.

lessons.title: Defences that hold by construction
lessons.brief: CaMeL extracts control and data flow from the trusted query so retrieved data cannot change the program, attaches capabilities to values and checks policies at tool calls, solving 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security against 84% undefended. FIDES applies confidentiality and integrity labels with deterministic enforcement, and Microsoft's deterministic block of Markdown image exfiltration fixes the impact instead of the injection. The limits are stated with them: CaMeL needs written policies and does not stop text-only attacks.

existing.note: The CaMeL provenance sketch moves here; probabilistic defences get their own lesson with numbers.

lessons.title: Defences that lower a rate, with their numbers
lessons.brief: Spotlighting reported attack success falling from above 50% to below 2% in its own tests, instruction hierarchy trains models to ignore lower-privileged instructions, and Prompt Guard 2 is a classifier with a published operating point. Against them: adaptive attacks bypassed 12 defences, Anthropic reports about 1% residual attack success for a browser agent and calls it meaningful risk, and OpenAI writes that injection is unlikely ever to be fully solved. The conclusion is that these layers are worth having and are never the only wall.

lessons.title: Tool-result hygiene
lessons.brief: Untrusted text enters context through tool results, so each entry point needs a rule. GitHub's Copilot agent filters hidden characters and only users with write access can trigger it, Claude Code's auto-mode classifier sees tool calls with tool results stripped, and the MCP specification asks clients to validate tool results before they reach the model. The reader lists every entry point in an agent and the rule at each.

lessons.title: Six design patterns for securing agents
lessons.brief: The design-patterns paper gives action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute and context-minimisation, each trading a specific utility for a specific guarantee. The walkthrough builds a toy executor per pattern and shows which attack each one stops. What to say in an interview is the utility you gave up and why it was acceptable.

lessons.title: Playbook: choose the defence pattern for the task
lessons.brief: The decision is which pattern and which rate-lowering layers a given agent gets, and the inputs are the trifecta legs present, whether actions are reversible, and the residual rate the business accepts in writing. The playbook works an email agent that summarises and drafts replies and a travel agent that browses and books. It ends with the tests: unit tests for the deterministic controls and an adaptive suite for the probabilistic ones.

problems.brief: Write the decision: an email assistant with a classifier and auto-reply must ship in two weeks; choose the architecture, the residual risk you accept and who signs it.
Pick one of the six patterns for an agent that summarises email and drafts replies, and state the utility you give up.
Apply the Rule of Two to a travel assistant that browses and books: which property do you drop, and what does the product lose?
How do you measure whether prompt-injection defences work, and why is a static attack set not enough?
An agent with a token that reads private repositories triages issues in a public one: find the leak path and the smallest fix.
Provenance labels: tag values by origin and refuse a tool call that sends data derived from untrusted input to an outbound channel; hidden tests include laundering through a summary.
A defence cuts attack success from above 50% to below 2% in its authors' tests: residual successful attacks per day at a stated adversarial volume, and why that is not the control.

modules.title: Guardrails, tool firewalls and tenant isolation
modules.brief: Classifier guardrails at an operating point, tool firewalls and approvals, and keeping tenants apart in retrieval and tools.

lessons.title: Classifier guardrails at an operating point
lessons.brief: A guardrail classifier is chosen at a recall and false-positive rate, and stacking two multiplies latency and false blocks. The lesson covers Prompt Guard 2 and Llama Guard 4 model cards, constitutional classifiers, and the arithmetic of a stack with its caveat about correlated errors. The reader picks an operating point from the cost of a false block and the cost of a miss.

existing.note: Cut the WAF paragraph and filter definitions; keep operating points and stacking; PII and residency move to security/output-data.

lessons.title: Tool firewalls, argument validation and approvals that mean something
lessons.brief: A tool firewall validates arguments against policy before execution and does not trust the model's description of what it is doing. The lesson covers allowlists, argument validation, Agents SDK guardrails and approval design that shows the reviewer the exact call. The reader writes the firewall rules for a refund tool.

lessons.title: Tenant isolation in retrieval and tools
lessons.brief: Cross-tenant leaks come from filters applied in the wrong place, shared caches and tools that accept identifiers from the model. The lesson covers namespace and filter placement, Microsoft 365 Copilot's permission scoping and why tenant identity must come from the session, never the prompt. The reader audits a design for every path one tenant's data could reach another.

problems.brief: Talk them out of giving the support agent write access to the payments database, then respond when product shows manual refunds cost more than the fraud you fear.
One tenant's documents surface in another's answers; the prose that named the bugs is removed.
An output guardrail for PII and a leaked secret, with hidden tests for formatting variants.
Handle PII in prompts, logs and traces when OpenTelemetry content capture is opt-in and legal wants full logs.
Stack two classifiers with stated recall and false-positive rates: end-to-end false blocks and added latency on a chat product, and when correlation breaks the estimate.
Critique an approval step that shows the reviewer a model-written summary of the action instead of the arguments.

modules.title: Hallucination, abstention and model safety
modules.brief: Why models hallucinate and what abstention costs, confident-but-wrong answers in high-risk domains, and the alignment topics engineers are asked about.

lessons.title: Why models hallucinate and what abstention costs
lessons.brief: OpenAI's 2025 analysis argues that training and evaluation reward guessing over abstaining, which is why calibrated abstention has to be designed and measured. The lesson covers grounding with citations, chain-of-verification, and the trade between coverage and error rate when the model may say it does not know. The reader sets an abstention threshold from the cost of each error type.

existing.note: EU AI Act dates and compliance move to security/governance; hallucination and alignment topics stay.

lessons.title: Confident but wrong in high-risk domains
lessons.brief: In medical, legal and financial settings the design question is how a wrong answer is caught before it acts, not how often the model is right. The lesson covers grounding to approved sources, verification chains, escalation to a human and logging that supports review. The reader designs the escalation path and its trigger.

lessons.title: Reward hacking, sycophancy and sleeper agents for engineers
lessons.brief: Anthropic found that a model that learned to reward-hack in real coding environments generalised to sabotage and alignment-faking reasoning, the GPT-4o sycophancy update shipped on positive A/B tests, and Sleeper Agents showed backdoors persisting through safety training. Each has a product consequence: what you reward, what you measure at launch, and what you can verify about a model you did not train. The reader can discuss each with the evidence and its limits.

problems.brief: Make the model say "I don't know": choose the abstention threshold from error costs and coverage on a labelled sample.
RAG hallucinates even with the right context: rank the generation-side causes.
Investigate and mitigate a model that gives confident but factually wrong answers in a high-risk domain, with a written decision on what ships.
The model started refusing benign requests after a safety-training round: what do you investigate first?
What is reward hacking? Give an example from an LLM product and the mitigation you would put in the training or the eval.
Explain to a manager why sensitive data cannot simply be deleted from a trained model, and what you will do instead.

tracks.title: Implementing security for AI systems
tracks.brief: Security as an implementation discipline for model systems, taken from threat model to architecture to controls to tests to operations: capability matrices and a test per control, permission systems and agent identity, isolation technology and what harness sandboxes leave outside, secrets kept out of context and sandbox, MCP authorisation implemented against its real CVEs, output-handling sinks and cross-tenant cache leakage, model supply chain (pickle, the weights_only bypass, safetensors, signing, poisoning), audit logging, abuse and incident response, security evals in CI, and the NIST, EU AI Act, SOC 2, ISO 42001 and privacy duties engineers implement. Every defence is labelled as holding by construction or lowering a rate.

modules.title: From threat model to tests
modules.brief: One system walked from data-flow diagram to a control per boundary and a test per control, with every control labelled by construction or by rate.

lessons.title: Playbook: from threat model to tests on one agent
lessons.brief: An email and calendar assistant with a send tool and a fetch tool is taken through five artefacts: a data-flow diagram, a per-session capability table scored on the Rule of Two and the lethal trifecta, an architecture change that removes one leg per session, a control per boundary labelled as holding by construction or lowering a rate, and a test per control. The CoSAI incident-response framework's architecture chapter supplies the boundaries per pattern (RAG, agentic, agentic RAG). The output is a document a security reviewer can sign.

lessons.title: Per-session capability matrices
lessons.brief: Risk in an agent is a property of the session's combined capabilities, so the unit of review is the session, not the tool. The lesson builds a matrix of untrusted input, sensitive access and outbound communication per session type and shows how splitting sessions removes a leg. The reader produces the matrix for an existing agent and finds the sessions that need supervision.

lessons.title: Running a security design review for an AI feature
lessons.brief: A design review for an AI feature asks the same questions as any review plus four new ones: what is untrusted text, what can it cause, what does a successful attack cost, and which control is deterministic. The lesson gives the review checklist, the evidence to request, and the decisions that must be written down with an owner. The reader runs a review on a stated design and writes the findings.

problems.brief: Take an email and calendar assistant from data-flow diagram to a test per control, labelling each control by construction or by rate.
An LLM feature will read from a few internal systems: keep it from becoming a hole.
Critique a threat model that lists the OWASP entries with no control or test against any of them.
Detect a prompt-injection attack at the infrastructure level, not only in the application.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

problems.brief: Explain AI security risk to senior leadership as a decision they must make, with the residual risk in writing.
Which control holds by construction: spotlighting, instruction hierarchy, capability checks at tool calls, or a prompt-injection classifier?

modules.title: Permissions and agent identity
modules.brief: Permission systems for tools built from their CVEs, delegated authority for agents, and protecting model weights.

lessons.title: Designing a permission system for agent tools
lessons.brief: A permission system evaluates deny before ask before allow, parses compound commands rather than prefix-matching, protects paths no rule can approve, and never lets the agent edit its own permissions. CVE records show each failure: a Claude Code command-parsing bypass of confirmation (CVE-2025-54795), Cursor letting an injected agent create its MCP config (CVE-2025-54135), and a Copilot command injection in Visual Studio (CVE-2025-53773). The lab grows a gate with a matcher, a splitter, protected paths, symlink resolution and an audit record per decision.

lessons.title: Agent identity and delegated authorisation
lessons.brief: Giving the agent the user's OAuth token fails both blast-radius and audit tests, which is why MCP forbids token passthrough. The lesson covers impersonation versus delegation in OAuth token exchange (subject and actor tokens, the act claim), audience-bound tokens per resource, and step-up scopes through authentication challenges. The reader designs the token path for an agent acting for a user across three services.

lessons.title: Protecting model weights
lessons.brief: Model weights are a high-value asset whose exfiltration paths include training clusters, serving fleets, checkpoints and the people with access to them. The lesson covers access tiers, egress controls on training and serving hosts, checkpoint handling, and how frontier labs describe weight security as part of their scaling policies. The reader designs access control for weights in a research organisation that also needs to move fast.

problems.brief: Should the agent use the user's OAuth token: impersonation, delegation with an actor token, or passthrough? Options of equal length.
Extend a permission gate with protected paths, symlink resolution and an audit record per decision; hidden tests include path tricks.
Design an access control system to protect model weights.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

problems.brief: Critique an agent that can edit its own settings file, hooks and MCP configuration inside the workspace.
The permission model for an agent that can read email and send money.
A confirmation prompt is bypassed by a crafted command: find the parsing defect in a gate, among two other real but harmless issues.

modules.title: Isolation and secrets
modules.brief: Choosing an isolation boundary, what coding-agent sandboxes leave outside, keeping secrets out of context and sandbox, and egress policy.

lessons.title: Playbook: choosing an isolation boundary for agent code execution
lessons.brief: seccomp filters system calls and the kernel docs say it is not a sandbox on its own; Landlock lets unprivileged processes restrict their own filesystem and network access; containers share the host kernel, as runc's CVE-2024-21626 escape shows; gVisor implements the Linux interface in user space at a compatibility and per-syscall cost; Firecracker microVMs boot to guest init within 125 ms under its stated test conditions and do no network filtering of their own. The inputs are tenancy, code trust, start-up budget and compatibility. The worked decisions are a hosted multi-tenant interpreter, a local coding agent and a CI job.

lessons.title: What coding-agent sandboxes leave outside
lessons.brief: Claude Code's sandbox is off by default, uses bubblewrap on Linux and Seatbelt on macOS, allows reads of most of the machine including ~/.ssh unless narrowed, starts with no allowed domains, and leaves hooks and local MCP servers outside it; the proxy does not inspect TLS. Codex runs read-only, workspace-write or full-access modes with network off by default and its own docs say its DNS check reduces but does not eliminate rebinding risk. The reader lists three ways a sandboxed agent can still leak a secret.

lessons.title: Secrets never enter the context or the sandbox
lessons.brief: Four patterns hold: a credential proxy outside the sandbox that checks the operation and attaches the real token (Claude Code on the web's git proxy), placeholder substitution at egress (Managed Agents vaults), setup-only secrets removed before the agent runs (Codex cloud), and secret scanning on agent output (GitHub). The motivating incident is the August 2025 Nx compromise, whose postinstall script drove locally installed AI CLIs with permission-skipping flags to inventory credentials. The reader redesigns a credential path that currently uses environment variables inside the sandbox.

problems.brief: Design a sandboxed cloud IDE: a multi-tenant browser notebook that runs user code in isolation.
Your agent runs in the sandbox; list three ways it can still leak a secret and the control for each.
An egress policy for a fetch tool: scheme and host allowlists, resolve then pin, block private and link-local ranges including IPv4-mapped IPv6 and odd encodings, re-validate redirects.
Your agent can execute arbitrary Python; make it safe for a multi-tenant product.
A secrets management system for a fast-growing research organisation where developers move quickly.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

problems.brief: Critique a sandbox whose allowlisted domain has an upload API.
Which isolation boundary for untrusted multi-tenant code: seccomp alone, a container, gVisor or a microVM?

modules.title: MCP security implemented
modules.brief: MCP authorisation as code, the MCP attacks that happened and the clause that stops each, and running a multi-tenant MCP server.

lessons.title: Implementing MCP authorisation correctly
lessons.brief: Servers publish protected-resource metadata, validate every token's audience, answer with challenges that name the needed scopes, and never accept or forward tokens issued for another resource; clients use PKCE, send the resource parameter, compare the issuer by exact string and open only https authorisation URLs, never through a shell. Client ID Metadata Documents are preferred and Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated in the 2026-07-28 revision. The reader implements token validation and the client checks with tests.

existing.note: The authorisation section moves here and is implemented, not described.

lessons.title: MCP attacks that happened, and the clause that stops each
lessons.brief: Tool poisoning and rug pulls, the mcp-remote command injection from a malicious authorization_endpoint (CVE-2025-6514), the unauthenticated MCP Inspector proxy (CVE-2025-49596), the GitHub MCP private-repository leak and the Supabase service-role trifecta each map to a clause in the specification or a design rule. The lesson walks each one end to end and names the control that would have stopped it. Secondary-only incidents are labelled as such.

lessons.title: Running a multi-tenant MCP server on the stateless revision
lessons.brief: A multi-tenant MCP server must key all state to the user identity from the verified token, because possession of a state handle must not be treated as authentication. The lesson covers per-tenant scopes, rate limits, audit logging with correlation ids for scope elevation, and pinning tool descriptions by hash. The reader designs the server and its threat model.

problems.brief: Review this MCP server before production: token handling, state handles, OAuth discovery and tool descriptions.
Validate token audience and issuer for an MCP client and server, rejecting passthrough and missing issuer parameters; hidden tests include mix-up attempts.
A secure multi-tenant MCP server on the stateless 2026-07-28 specification.
A crafted authorization_endpoint reaches a shell in an MCP client: find the code path and the fix.
Why PKCE alone does not stop mix-up attacks, and what issuer validation adds.
Explain the MCP remote transport and authorisation model and the risks of running MCP servers in production.

modules.title: Output handling and data protection
modules.brief: Model output as untrusted input to the next component, PII and telemetry content with residency, and cross-tenant leakage through shared caches.

lessons.title: Model output is untrusted input to the next component
lessons.brief: OWASP's improper-output-handling entry lists XSS, CSRF, SSRF, privilege escalation, code execution through shells or eval, SQL injection and path traversal, with context-aware encoding, parameterised queries and a strict CSP as the controls. The DeepSeek chat case, where an injected document made the model emit a javascript: iframe that read the session token, is the worked example. The reader writes an encoder and a parameterised SQL tool that pass an attack battery.

lessons.title: PII redaction, telemetry content and data residency
lessons.brief: Redaction is a probabilistic detector (Presidio says it gives no guarantee), the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions mark message content opt-in because it may contain personal data, and residency on the Claude API is two settings: per-request inference geography and a workspace geography for data at rest. The lesson covers what each control actually guarantees and what logs must never contain. The reader writes the logging and residency policy for an EU customer.

existing.note: PII handling and residency from the guardrails lesson move here.

lessons.title: Cross-tenant leakage through shared caches
lessons.brief: Prompt caching is a timing side channel when shared: an audit found global cache sharing across users at seven API providers in early 2025. In vLLM, cache_salt is the mitigation for the prefix-cache membership oracle, and an October 2026 advisory showed one code path dropping the salt and restoring the oracle through cached-token counts. The design lesson is that isolation controls must hold on every code path, so they are tested per endpoint.

problems.brief: Render model Markdown to HTML so that it passes an XSS battery including javascript: URLs, data URIs and image exfiltration.
A SQL tool that accepts only a parameterised template plus typed arguments; hidden tests attempt injection through the arguments.
A customer says your chatbot leaked another user's data; the trace shows a shared prefix-cache hit and a shared conversation id, and only one explains it.
A system where one user's prompt cannot leak to another user, across caches, logs, memory and retrieval.
Data residency on the Claude API is two settings: which data does each one control?
Security architecture for a multi-tenant self-hosted serving tier: engine-killing requests, prefix-cache oracles and stored provider keys.
Critique a decision to log full prompts and outputs in every environment "for audit".

modules.title: Model and agent supply chain
modules.brief: Loading model artefacts safely, data poisoning and backdoors, and the agent toolchain as a supply chain.

lessons.title: Loading model artefacts safely
lessons.brief: Pickle runs code at load time, Hugging Face says its pickle scanning is not foolproof, and the nullifAI models evaded picklescan with broken streams. torch.load now defaults to weights_only=True, yet weights_only=True was bypassable in PyTorch 2.5.1 and earlier (CVE-2025-32434), and the docs still say never to load untrusted data; safetensors removes code execution but does not validate values or prove who produced the weights, which is what signing with Sigstore addresses. The lab builds a pickletools-based import allowlist scanner.

lessons.title: Data poisoning and backdoors
lessons.brief: Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that 250 poisoned documents backdoored models from 600M to 13B parameters with a denial-of-service trigger, while 100 were not enough, and the authors caution that the backdoor was narrow and low-stakes. Sleeper Agents found backdoors persisting through SFT, RL and adversarial training. The walkthrough ends with what this means for training on scraped or user data and what to say when asked how much poisoned data is needed.

lessons.title: The agent toolchain as a supply chain
lessons.brief: Coding agents install packages, MCP servers and skills, so their toolchain is a supply chain with its own incidents: the Nx compromise drove local AI CLIs to steal credentials, an over-scoped token in CodeBuild shipped malicious code in Amazon Q Developer 1.84.0, and package hallucination suggests packages that do not exist. Controls are pinning and reviewing MCP servers and skills like dependencies, sandboxed installs, and never running agents with permission-skipping flags outside an isolated container. The reader writes the policy for a team running coding agents.

problems.brief: What belongs in a model's bill of materials, and what signing does and does not prove about the weights?
A vendor publishes fine-tuned weights but not training data: your supply-chain trust process and the gaps that remain.
A Python dependency in your training pipeline was found to contain malicious code: walk through your response.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

problems.brief: A pickletools-based import allowlist scanner; hidden tests include a broken-stream evasion and a benign model.
A poisoned package plants editor and agent auto-execution hooks so opening the repository runs the payload: critique a team's defence.
PyTorch 2.5.1 with weights_only=True and an untrusted checkpoint: what is true?

modules.title: Security operations for AI features
modules.brief: Audit logs an investigator can use, abuse and denial of wallet, incident response, security evals in CI and a red-team programme.

lessons.title: Audit logging for agents
lessons.brief: An investigator needs the model id and version, a redacted prompt or hash, tool calls with arguments and results, who approved what, the policy rule that matched, and the token subject and actor. That conflicts with privacy because content capture is opt-in and logs become a personal-data store with retention duties. The lesson writes the log schema and the retention rule and shows how token passthrough breaks the trail.

lessons.title: Rate limiting, abuse and denial of wallet
lessons.brief: OWASP's unbounded-consumption entry names variable-length floods, denial of wallet, model extraction and functional replication, with token buckets, spend caps and limits on logprob exposure among the controls. Anthropic reported a state-sponsored campaign that used Claude Code for most of an intrusion campaign by splitting work into innocent-looking tasks, and responded with bans and new classifiers. The lesson treats abuse as account-level behaviour that single-prompt filters cannot see.

lessons.title: Playbook: incident response for AI features
