lessons.brief: The CoSAI framework aligns with NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 and adds AI incident classes, AI forensics and playbooks for training-data poisoning, multi-channel prompt injection, memory injection, poisoned RAG and metadata-credential abuse. The playbook covers kill switches (disable a tool, a connector or a model version), credential rotation, memory and index quarantine and customer communication, with the Amazon Q 1.84.0 case as the worked example. It ends with what to measure in the review.

lessons.title: Security evals in CI
lessons.brief: Three suites run at different cadences: deterministic control tests on every PR, a fixed battery of known attacks per release (promptfoo, garak), and adaptive attacks nightly or before release (AgentDojo's tasks and security cases). Tooling changed in 2026: OpenAI announced it would acquire Promptfoo and continue the open-source project, and PyRIT moved to a new repository. The reader wires the three suites to a pipeline with blocking rules.

lessons.title: Playbook: running a red-team programme
lessons.brief: A programme defines scope, threat actors, adaptive attackers as the default, what counts as a finding, severity, regression capture and disclosure. AIUC-1, a vendor-maintained standard, describes scenario-based red-teaming with periodic retests and should be labelled as such. The playbook works a programme for a customer-facing agent and ends with how findings change the roadmap.

problems.brief: Integrate AI security into CI/CD: what runs per PR, per release and nightly, and what blocks a merge.
What should happen in the hour after a successful agent attack, and in the week after?
Rate limits for an AI API: per-tenant token buckets and spend caps from a stated traffic model, and the abuse pattern they still miss.
Detect someone stealing your model through the API.
Replay the Amazon Q Developer 1.84.0 incident: at each checkpoint commit to a hypothesis, then name the build control and the agent control that would each have stopped it.
A researcher pushes a live API key to a public repository: incident response, step by step.
problems.reported: Anthropic (reported via a vendor compiling candidate reports)

problems.brief: Audit logging for agents that an investigator can use without building an uncontrolled personal-data store.

modules.title: Governance and privacy duties engineers implement
modules.brief: The NIST documents, the EU AI Act articles that become engineering work, SOC 2 and ISO 42001 evidence, and privacy law for AI features.

lessons.title: NIST for engineers in one sitting
lessons.brief: The AI RMF (January 2023) organises work as Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, the Generative AI Profile (July 2024) adds GenAI risks, the Cyber AI Profile is still an initial preliminary draft from December 2025, and SP 800-61 Rev. 3 covers incident response. The lesson maps each to artefacts an engineering team produces. Every document is cited with its status so a draft is never presented as final.

lessons.title: EU AI Act duties an engineer implements
lessons.brief: After the Digital Omnibus, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I from 2 August 2028, and generative systems already on the market have until 2 December 2026 to mark generated content. Article 15(5) requires technical measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks, and Article 99 sets fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices. The lesson turns each article into engineering tasks with owners.

existing.note: The compliance dates paragraph from the hallucination lesson moves here and is expanded.

lessons.title: Playbook: SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 42001 for an AI feature
lessons.brief: As of the CSA note of 30 August 2026 there are no AI-specific SOC 2 trust services criteria, so auditors map AI controls onto existing criteria and requests vary by firm; ISO/IEC 42001 certifies a management system, not a model. The evidence that recurs is model change management with approvals, per-inference logs with model version and a redacted prompt, providers treated as subprocessors with retention documented, and an inventory of unsanctioned AI use. The playbook ends with the evidence pack an engineering team can maintain without stopping work.

lessons.title: Privacy law for AI features: deletion, retention and provider data controls
lessons.brief: The EDPB's Opinion 28/2024 addresses personal data in AI models, and deletion requests must reach logs, eval sets and fine-tuning data as well as the product database. Provider data controls differ: OpenAI keeps abuse-monitoring logs up to 30 days by default with zero data retention by approval and excluded endpoints, and Claude separates inference geography from workspace geography. The reader traces every store a deletion request must reach.

problems.brief: Design an AI governance process that satisfies auditors without stopping teams from shipping.
Which Article 15(5) measures become engineering work for a high-risk system, and how would you evidence each?
An HR assistant user asks to delete all their data: trace every store the request must reach, including evals and fine-tuning sets.
Article 99 fine exposure at a stated turnover under each tier, and how the SME rule changes it.
Critique a SOC 2 evidence pack for an AI feature that has model cards but no change management or inference logs.
Map the NIST AI RMF functions onto an AI feature's release process, naming the artefact each function produces.

tracks.title: Inference, serving and cost
tracks.brief: Serving models as a capacity and scheduling problem: prefill and decode on the roofline, KV capacity and compression, continuous batching, paged KV and chunked prefill, quantisation and speculative decoding, disaggregation, gateways and routing, SLOs and quality incidents with no model change, and fleet-scale routing, release pipelines, quota ledgers and adapter serving. The reader knows schedulers, allocators and queues; the track teaches what is different when the work unit is a token and the memory is a KV cache.

modules.title: Prefill, decode and KV capacity
modules.brief: The roofline view of prefill and decode, KV bytes per token by model, and the families of KV compression.

lessons.title: Prefill and decode on the roofline
lessons.brief: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound because decode reads every weight and the KV cache for each generated token. The lesson places both on the H100 roofline with its ridge point, and covers model bandwidth utilisation, goodput and the metric names engines report. The reader can say which phase a change will speed up before benchmarking it.

existing.note: Cut "two phases in a systems engineer's terms" and the latency vocabulary; keep roofline and ridge point, the KV table by model, goodput and MBU, engine metric names.

lessons.title: KV cache capacity: bytes per token by model, and what fits
lessons.brief: KV bytes per token are layers times KV heads times head dimension times two times bytes per element, and that number sets how many concurrent tokens a GPU holds after weights. The lesson computes it from published configs (Llama 3, Qwen3, gpt-oss, DeepSeek-V3) and turns it into a concurrency limit per GPU. The reader sizes a deployment from a traffic mix of sequence lengths.

lessons.title: Playbook: shrinking the KV cache
lessons.brief: Four families fail differently: architectural (GQA, MQA, MLA, hybrid linear layers, fixed at training time), eviction (H2O, SnapKV), quantisation (KIVI at 2 bits with keys per channel and values per token) and top-k sparse attention (DeepSeek's DSA). The input that decides is task accuracy at length, measured with long-context tasks rather than needle tests. The worked case serves a 128K-context assistant on a fixed GPU budget and lists what to measure after deciding.

problems.brief: Why prefill is compute-bound and decode is not, stated with arithmetic intensity rather than slogans.
KV cache for Llama 3 70B at 32K context and a stated batch.
Roofline for a 70B model on one H100: choose FP8 or BF16 and the GPU count, and say which assumption flips it.
KV bytes per token for MHA, GQA-8, MLA and a 1:7 attention-to-Mamba hybrid at 256K, computed from published configs.
Serve a 128K-context assistant on a fixed GPU budget: choose a KV compression family and the accuracy test that would reverse the choice.
After a sliding-window change evicted the first tokens, output turned to noise; explain and fix without losing the memory saving.

modules.title: Continuous batching and the KV allocator
modules.brief: Iteration-level scheduling, PagedAttention as virtual memory for KV, and chunked prefill with a token budget.

lessons.title: Continuous batching: iteration-level scheduling
lessons.brief: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at every decode step instead of waiting for a batch to finish, which is why it raises throughput without raising latency for short requests. The lesson covers Orca's iteration-level scheduling, the vLLM V1 scheduler that assigns tokens per request per step, and the metrics that show it working. The reader can trace a request through one engine step.

existing.note: Cut the worker-pool analogy and the static-batching predict; keep PagedAttention and the allocator, chunked prefill and the budget knob, preemption and fairness.

lessons.title: PagedAttention: virtual memory for the KV cache
lessons.brief: PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size blocks with a block table per sequence, which removes fragmentation and allows copy-on-write sharing of prefixes and beams. The lesson covers block size, preemption by recompute or swap, and prefix sharing. The reader implements the allocator in the lab.

lessons.title: Chunked prefill, token budgets and fairness
lessons.brief: A long prefill in the same step as decodes stalls every decode behind it, and Sarathi-Serve's chunked prefill bounds the step with a token budget. The lesson covers the max_num_batched_tokens knob, preemption order, fairness across tenants and the head-of-line blocking it trades against throughput. The reader picks a budget for a mixed workload and shows its p99 effect.

problems.brief: Trace a request through a paged-KV inference engine, step by step, naming every queue and allocator decision.
Batching for a single GPU with synchronous callers waiting on up to 100 inputs per batch.
A paged KV block allocator with copy-on-write prefix sharing and preemption; hidden invariant tests.
A step scheduler with chunked prefill and a token budget; the preemption order is the reader's choice and tests check invariants rather than one schedule.
Design an end-to-end batching system for LLM queries.
After raising the batched-token limit, one long prompt starves short ones and p99 time to first token doubles.

modules.title: Quantisation, speculation, caching and disaggregation
modules.brief: Each serving optimisation with the condition under which it helps and the measurement that shows it.

lessons.title: Quantisation formats and how to measure the damage
lessons.brief: GPTQ, AWQ, FP8 and GGUF quantise weights differently, KV-cache quantisation is a separate choice, and the damage shows up on long-tail tasks before averages. The lesson covers the formats, where outliers break them, and an evaluation protocol that compares on your tasks, not on perplexity. The reader decides a format for a stated model, GPU and quality floor.

existing.note: Training parallelism moves to training/distributed; each optimisation becomes its own lesson.

lessons.title: Speculative decoding: why it preserves the distribution and when it hurts
lessons.brief: Speculative decoding drafts tokens cheaply and verifies them in one target pass, and the acceptance rule preserves the target distribution exactly. It helps when decode is memory-bound and hurts at large batch where the GPU is already compute-bound. The lesson covers draft models, EAGLE-style heads and the batch size at which it stops paying.

lessons.title: Prefix caching in the engine
lessons.brief: Engine prefix caching hashes KV blocks by their token prefix so shared system prompts and few-shot blocks are computed once. The lesson covers block hashing, eviction, cache-aware routing across replicas, and the per-tenant salt needed when the cache is shared. The reader estimates saved prefill for a stated traffic mix.

lessons.title: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessons.brief: Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools removes their interference and lets each pool be sized to its own bottleneck, at the cost of moving KV between them. DistServe frames the goal as goodput under latency SLOs, and chunked prefill is the alternative that keeps one pool. The reader decides between tuning one pool and splitting two for a mixed workload.

lessons.title: Tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism for serving
lessons.brief: Serving splits a model across GPUs for memory or latency, and the choice of tensor, pipeline or expert parallelism follows the interconnect and the batch. The lesson covers why tensor parallelism stays inside an NVLink domain, pipeline parallelism for models that do not fit, and expert parallelism with all-to-all for MoE. The reader picks a layout for a stated model and node.

problems.brief: Speculative decoding at batch size 128: which outcome do you expect, with options of equal length?
Speculative decoding made throughput worse after a traffic change.
Accuracy fell after 4-bit quantisation on one task family only.
The speculative decoding verification step with the acceptance rule; hidden tests check the output distribution.
Disaggregate or tune: a mixed chat and long-document workload on sixteen GPUs with two SLOs.
FP32 to int8 quantisation: symmetric and zero-point schemes, per-channel scales, clipping and outliers.
Prefix-cache hit rate and saved prefill FLOPs for a shared system prompt at a stated request rate and replica count.

modules.title: Gateways, routing and break-even
modules.brief: What an AI gateway owns, routing and cascades, and the self-host break-even and how fast it moves.

lessons.title: The AI gateway: auth, quotas, routing, caching and logging
lessons.brief: An AI gateway centralises keys, quotas, routing, caching and logging so product teams stop reimplementing them. The lesson compares LiteLLM, Portkey and OpenRouter on routing and budget features and covers per-tenant attribution. The reader decides what the gateway owns and what stays in the product.

existing.note: Unit economics per outcome moves to llmops/economics-selection; gateway, routing and break-even stay.

lessons.title: Routing and cascades
lessons.brief: A cascade sends easy requests to a cheap model and escalates the rest, and its saving depends on how well the router predicts difficulty. FrugalGPT frames the cascade with a scorer, and gateway routers implement fallbacks and cost-based routing. The reader measures a router's confusion matrix before trusting its savings.

lessons.title: Self-host or API: the break-even and how fast it moves
lessons.brief: Self-hosting beats an API only above a break-even volume at sustained utilisation, after counting people and on-call. Epoch AI measured the price of a fixed capability falling between 9x and 900x per year depending on the threshold, so the break-even moves within a year. The reader computes a break-even with dated GPU and API prices and states when to recompute it.

problems.brief: A token-charged rate limiter shared across servers: atomic check-and-update and behaviour when the store is down.
An AI gateway for an organisation whose product teams, security team and a finance team all want different things.
Self-host or API: find the break-even volume with dated prices and say when it flips.
A multi-model gateway with per-tenant budgets, attribution and fallbacks that do not change behaviour silently.
The monthly model bill tripled in six weeks while traffic grew 40%: find the cause from the cost breakdown.
Critique a cascade that routes by prompt length to a small model.

modules.title: Operating model services
modules.brief: SLOs and autoscaling with cold starts, load testing, and quality regressions that come from serving infrastructure.

lessons.title: SLOs, GPU autoscaling and cold starts
lessons.brief: Model servers take minutes to cold start, so autoscaling must act on leading signals and hold warm capacity for the ramp. The lesson covers SLOs for time to first token and inter-token latency, GKE's guidance on inference autoscaling metrics, and queueing arithmetic for headroom. The reader writes SLOs and the scaling policy for a chat service.

existing.note: Rollout ladders move to llmops/releases-experiments; the three-bug postmortem becomes quality-incidents.

lessons.title: Load testing model endpoints
lessons.brief: A load test for a model endpoint must vary input and output lengths, concurrency and prefix sharing, because each moves a different bottleneck. The lesson covers NIM benchmarking metrics, vLLM's metric names and how to read a saturation curve. The reader designs a load test that would have caught a stated regression.

lessons.title: Quality regressions with no model change
lessons.brief: Anthropic's September 2025 postmortem describes three unrelated infrastructure bugs (a context-window routing error that reached 16% of Sonnet 4 requests in the worst hour, a TPU misconfiguration that corrupted output, and an approximate top-k miscompilation) that degraded answers with no model or prompt change. Detection was slow because models recover from isolated errors, evals were noisy and privacy limits restricted reading traffic. The lesson ends with the production quality probes and exact checks Anthropic added.

problems.brief: p99 inter-token latency doubled after a deploy; two engine settings changed and only one matters.
An inference API with autoscaling and SLOs, given cold starts measured in minutes.
Throughput collapsed at 2 a.m. with no deploy: read the engine metrics and find the preemption storm.
Replay Anthropic's three overlapping infrastructure bugs: commit to a hypothesis at each checkpoint and name the instrument that would have caught each bug.
Warm capacity to hold for a stated diurnal curve when cold starts take minutes.
Inference serving at scale for ten million daily users across two regions.

modules.title: Inference fleets: routing, release, quotas and adapters
modules.brief: Fleet-scale routing with cache affinity, model release pipelines, credit and quota ledgers, and serving many adapters on one base.

lessons.title: Routing across accelerators, regions and caches
lessons.brief: At fleet scale the router decides cost and latency: it chooses accelerator type and region, keeps prefix-cache affinity, and separates production from research demand. The lesson uses Anthropic's inference job description as the specification of the job and the engine designs for prefix-aware and disaggregated routing. The reader designs a router for two accelerator types and three regions.

lessons.title: Model release pipelines for a serving fleet
lessons.brief: Releasing a model or a serving change to a fleet needs quality probes on canaries, not only error rates, because infrastructure bugs degrade answers silently. The lesson builds the pipeline from Anthropic's postmortem commitments and provider deprecation schedules: canary by quality probe, staged rollout, rollback triggers and an owner. The reader writes the release checklist for a new model version.

lessons.title: Credit and quota ledgers
lessons.brief: Token credits and quotas are a ledger with grants, expirations, holds and refunds, and getting it wrong is either lost revenue or an outage for paying users. The lesson covers consuming the oldest-expiring grant first, holds for in-flight requests whose cost is unknown, usage reporting to billing within its correction window, and reconciliation. The reader implements the ledger in stages.

lessons.title: Serving adapters: merge or hot-load many on one base
lessons.brief: An adapter can be merged into the base for zero runtime cost and one model per tenant, or kept separate and hot-loaded alongside many others on one base. vLLM serves adapters with a maximum rank set at start-up and warns against exposing runtime loading outside a trusted environment, S-LoRA serves thousands of adapters, and LoRA Land served 25 adapters on one 80 GB A100. Routing becomes sticky to replicas that hold the adapter, which is the operational cost.

problems.brief: A credit tracker in stages: grants and consumption, then expirations consumed oldest first, then holds for in-flight requests, then refunds and an audit log.
problems.reported: OpenAI, Perplexity (candidate reports via Hello Interview and PracHub)

problems.brief: Route requests across two accelerator types and three regions while keeping prefix-cache affinity and research traffic off the production path.
How many LoRA adapters of a stated rank fit on one 80 GB GPU next to the base model and its KV cache?
A per-tenant adapter platform: hot-loading, sticky routing, eviction and an eval gate per adapter.
Release pipeline for a new model version on a serving fleet: canary by quality probe, rollback triggers and owner.
Requests for one tenant's adapter fail after a deploy that lowered the server's maximum adapter rank.

tracks.title: LLMOps, fine-tuning and AI product economics
tracks.brief: The operating discipline around a model feature: prompts as versioned artefacts and the optimisers that search over them, releases with the statistics that make an A/B test defensible, drift and feedback loops that do not train sycophancy, curating data from production, fine-tuning as a project (with OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning closed to new organisations and ending new jobs on 6 January 2027), unit economics per outcome and licence clauses, and the staff-level strategy, platform and governance questions. Incident replays of the GPT-4o sycophancy rollback anchor the release material.

modules.title: Prompt registries and optimisers
modules.brief: Prompts as immutable versions behind labels, and automatic optimisers as search over text parameters against a metric you must trust first.

lessons.title: Playbook: prompt registry and release mechanics
lessons.brief: A prompt is a deployable artefact with a version, an owner, a test suite and a rollout, and in Langfuse's model every edit is an immutable version fetched by a label that rollback simply moves. The trap is that SDKs cache prompts client-side, so rollback takes as long as the cache TTL, not the click. The playbook covers who may move the production label, attaching prompt versions to traces, and never shipping a prompt change and a model change together.

existing.note: The "prompts as code" section moves here and becomes a playbook.

lessons.title: Automatic prompt optimisation: what the optimisers actually do
lessons.brief: APE keeps the best-scoring generated instruction, OPRO puts past candidates and scores in the prompt, DSPy's BootstrapFewShot keeps only teacher traces that pass the metric, MIPROv2 searches instructions and demonstrations with a surrogate, GEPA reflects on trajectories and keeps a Pareto frontier, and TextGrad treats critiques as gradients. All of them exploit a bad metric, so you need a trustworthy metric, a dev set sized to the optimiser (DSPy suggests 200 or more examples for MIPROv2) and a held-out set it never sees. OpenAI's own optimiser guide warns that an optimised prompt can do worse on specific inputs.

lessons.title: GEPA: reflective prompt evolution
lessons.brief: GEPA reports beating GRPO by 6% on average and up to 20% with up to 35 times fewer rollouts across six tasks, and beating MIPROv2 by over 10%, all as the authors' own results. The mechanism is natural-language reflection on full trajectories plus a Pareto frontier of candidates that each win on some example. The walkthrough ends with the DSPy usage, where the metric must return feedback text, and with the conditions a reviewer should attach to the headline.

problems.brief: A one-line prompt tweak shipped on Friday and escalations rose on Monday: critique the versioning and testing system that let it through.
An optimiser lifted dev accuracy from 24% to 51% on a ReAct program: what do you check before it ships?
Rollback moved the production label but errors continued for minutes: find the client-side cache.
Dev and held-out set sizes and the cost of a MIPROv2 run following DSPy's guidance, for a stated three-module program.
Bootstrap few-shot: keep only teacher traces that pass the metric, cap the demonstrations, and test against a deterministic mock model.
Who may move the production label? Prompt registry governance across many teams with different risk levels.

modules.title: Releases and experiments
modules.brief: The release ladder with entry and exit rules, A/B statistics that survive review, and qualitative launch blockers.

lessons.title: Playbook: the release ladder with numbers
lessons.brief: Offline gate, shadow, canary, A/B and full rollout each have an entry condition, a measurement, a cost and an exit rule, and only the A/B test measures outcome metrics causally. Shadow doubles token spend for the shadowed share and cannot see user reactions; provider retirement dates (at least 60 days' notice at Anthropic) set hard deadlines. The playbook ends with pinned model ids and the rollback trigger for each rung.

existing.note: The rollout section moves here with numbers added.

lessons.title: A/B testing LLM features: statistics that survive review
lessons.brief: Randomise by user or account, compute sample size before launch, pick one primary metric with a few guardrails, check sample ratio mismatch before reading results, and use clustered errors when the unit is a multi-turn conversation. Anthropic reports clustered standard errors more than three times naive ones on popular evals, and the arithmetic shows detecting 70% to 72% resolution at alpha 0.05 and power 0.8 needs about 8,080 users per arm. The reader designs an experiment that a statistician would sign.

lessons.title: Qualitative launch blockers and behaviour evals
lessons.brief: The April 2025 GPT-4o update added a reward signal from thumbs data, passed offline evals and an A/B test, drew comments from expert testers that it felt off, shipped and was rolled back. OpenAI's response was to treat model behaviour issues as launch-blocking and to add evals for known failure classes before the change. The lesson gives qualitative signals a formal place in the gate and an owner.

problems.brief: Sample size to detect a lift from 70% to 72% task resolution at alpha 0.05 and power 0.8, then the duration at a stated daily traffic.
An A/B result shows a four-point lift but the arms are unbalanced: check sample ratio mismatch and decide what the result is worth.
Replay the GPT-4o sycophancy update: at each checkpoint decide ship or hold from the evidence available then, and add the gate that would have stopped it.
A new reranker improves offline NDCG@10 modestly: design the online experiment that decides whether it ships.
Randomise by user, request or conversation for a multi-turn assistant: decide, and show the error calculation that follows.
Critique a rollout plan that ships a prompt change and a model change together behind one flag.

modules.title: Drift and feedback loops
modules.brief: The four sources of drift, what to monitor before labels arrive, feedback that does not train sycophancy, and the last mile from 80% to 95%.

lessons.title: Drift you can and cannot see
lessons.brief: Quality changes come from the provider's model behind an alias, your own prompt and retrieval changes, traffic mix and serving infrastructure; Chen, Zaharia and Zou measured GPT-4 prime-number accuracy at 84% in March 2023 and 51% in June 2023 on the same questions. Before labels arrive you monitor resolved model id, output length, refusal rate, tool calls per task, assertion failures and sampled judge pass rates. A frozen input set replayed on a schedule separates traffic drift from model drift.

lessons.title: Playbook: feedback loops that do not train sycophancy
lessons.brief: Explicit feedback (thumbs, regenerate) and implicit feedback (accept, edit, abandon, escalate) are filters for which traces to read, not metrics or rewards without controls. The sycophancy rollback is the counter-example, and METR measured experienced developers 19% slower with AI while they believed they were faster, so engagement needs an outcome check. The playbook closes the loop: confirmed failure, new eval case, fix, gate.

lessons.title: From 80% to 95%: estimating the last mile
lessons.brief: LinkedIn reported reaching about 80% of its target experience in the first month and needing about four more months to pass 95%, with a linguist team that could evaluate up to 500 conversations a day. Malformed parameters in about 10% of responses fell to about 0.01% with a defensive parser, and chain-of-thought improved quality while raising perceived latency. The reader uses these as priors when asked to estimate a timeline.

problems.brief: Eval scores are flat after a model change but users complain: what is happening, and what do you sample first?
What do you monitor before ground-truth labels arrive, and which signal fires first for each kind of drift?
A provider updated the model behind an alias: detect it and separate it from a change in traffic mix.
Critique a plan to use thumbs-up rate as the reward for a weekly fine-tune.
Plan the timeline and labelling capacity for a feature like LinkedIn's, given its reported 80% and 95% milestones.
How do you detect drift in your evaluator, separately from drift in the system it evaluates?

modules.title: Curating data from production
modules.brief: Eval and SFT data from logs with stratification, dedup, PII scrubbing and leakage checks, synthetic data without collapse, and consent and deletion.

lessons.title: Curating eval and SFT data from production
lessons.brief: The pipeline samples by stratum, deduplicates exactly, then near-duplicates with MinHash, then semantically, scrubs PII before data leaves the logging boundary, labels with a rubric and measured agreement, and splits by time or user so train and eval do not share near-duplicates. LIMA (1,000 curated examples) and AlpaGasus (9k filtered from 52k, trained 5.7 times faster) are the evidence for quality over volume. The reader builds the pipeline and its leakage check.

existing.note: The production-curation material moves here.

lessons.title: Synthetic data without collapse
lessons.brief: Model collapse appears when synthetic data replaces real data, and accumulating synthetic with real data kept test error bounded in Gerstgrasser et al. Nemotron-4 used over 98% synthetic alignment data with a released reward model as the filter, which is the pattern: generation is cheap and the filter decides quality. The reader designs a synthetic-data loop with its filter and its contamination check.

lessons.title: Consent, retention and deletion for training data
lessons.brief: Using production conversations for evals or fine-tuning needs consent and retention terms that cover it, and deletion requests must reach eval sets and fine-tuning data. The lesson covers the EDPB's opinion on personal data in AI models, provider retention defaults, and the engineering of a deletion that propagates. The reader writes the data-use policy and the deletion path for a training set.

problems.brief: Eight thousand labelled support examples collected over two years for fine-tuning: curate them into training and eval sets.
Leadership wants production conversations used for eval sets and fine-tuning data: design the pipeline with consent, PII, deletion and leakage controls.
Extract and clean a usable dataset from a demo database using only SQL and Python.
A fine-tuned model scores higher on eval than in production: eval examples are paraphrases of training data, among other plausible causes.
When does synthetic data cause collapse, and what does accumulating real data change?
Critique a synthetic SFT set generated and graded by the same model with no held-out real data.

modules.title: Fine-tuning in practice
modules.brief: Whether to fine-tune, a run end to end from base choice to held-out eval, and the two papers that correct the usual fine-tuning pitch.

lessons.title: Playbook: should we fine-tune?
lessons.brief: Fine-tuning fixes format, style, narrow skills and cost; it loses to retrieval for knowledge (Ovadia et al.), and fine-tuning on facts the model does not know raises hallucination as those examples are learned (Gekhman et al.). It wins for narrow high-volume tasks where a small tuned model replaces a large prompted one, as LoRA Land shows. The 2026 platform reality is part of the input: OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning closed to new organisations on 7 May 2026 and ends new jobs for existing customers on 6 January 2027.

lessons.title: A fine-tuning run end to end
lessons.brief: A run starts with the base (licence, size, chat template, tokenizer), the data format (messages, prompt-completion, tool calls) and loss on assistant tokens only, which in TRL needs generation markers in the chat template. Hyperparameters come with sources (TRL's default 2e-5 for full SFT and about 1e-4 suggested for adapters; Unsloth's 2e-4, one to three epochs and training loss below 0.2 as an overfitting sign), and evaluation is against the prompted base on a held-out set, starting from about 50 good examples as OpenAI's guide suggests. The reader can run and judge a LoRA fine-tune on rented hardware.

lessons.title: LoRA learns less and forgets less
lessons.brief: Biderman et al. found LoRA substantially underperforms full fine-tuning on code and maths in standard low-rank settings while forgetting less, and that full fine-tuning learns perturbations of 10 to 100 times higher rank. Read with LoRA Without Regret, the conditions are clear: LoRA matches full fine-tuning on small and medium SFT and RL when applied to all layers with a higher learning rate. The walkthrough ends with how to answer "LoRA or full fine-tune?" with conditions instead of a slogan.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning on new knowledge encourages hallucinations
lessons.brief: Gekhman et al. found that examples introducing knowledge the model lacks are learned more slowly and, once learned, increase hallucination roughly linearly. This is why "fine-tune it on our docs" is the wrong tool for facts that change, and why retrieval wins for knowledge. The walkthrough ends with how to explain this to a product manager in two minutes.

problems.brief: Develop a strategy for fine-tuning given OpenAI's self-serve wind-down: which workloads move, to what, and by when.
problems.reported: OpenAI (prompt reported by aced.io; the platform change postdates it)

problems.brief: After fine-tuning the model parrots users: loss was computed on user turns because the template lacked generation markers.
Critique a fine-tuning plan that trains on user turns, evaluates on paraphrases of training examples and has no prompted-base baseline.
A product manager says: fine-tune a model on our company data so it knows our products. Respond with the evidence.
One 80 GB GPU, a 7B to 13B open-weight model and a month to adapt it to your domain: the plan, the evals and the stop rule.
How do you evaluate a generative model after fine-tuning, including regressions on general capability?
Cost and time of a LoRA fine-tune on rented H100s, choosing and stating your throughput assumption.

modules.title: Unit economics, build or buy, and licences
modules.brief: Cost per successful outcome, the three build-or-buy decisions, and model selection with licence clauses that change the answer.

lessons.title: Unit economics of an AI feature
lessons.brief: Cost per call is the wrong unit: cost per successful outcome includes attempts per success, tool and retrieval cost, and human escalation for failures. The market already prices outcomes (Intercom Fin charges $0.99 per outcome and defines it), and Epoch AI's price trends mean a decision justified by today's price can flip within a year. The reader builds the per-outcome cost model and compares it with an outcome price.

existing.note: Unit economics per outcome is new here; break-even stays in inference.

lessons.title: Playbook: build versus buy
lessons.brief: Three decisions get blurred: buy an AI product or build the feature, call an API or self-host weights, and train or adapt. The inputs are differentiation, data sensitivity and residency, volume and growth, team skills, time to value and deprecation risk; Menlo's survey found most enterprise AI solutions bought rather than built in 2025. The playbook ends with the costs teams forget: people, evals and on-call.

lessons.title: Playbook: model selection and licence clauses
lessons.brief: Selection is evals plus constraints, and the constraints include licence clauses: Llama 4's licence requires a separate licence above 700 million monthly active users, attribution and Llama-prefixed names for derivatives, while Gemma's terms reserve the right to restrict use and Apache 2.0 or MIT models carry no such clauses. Open weights are not open source under the OSI definition, which requires data information, code and parameters. The playbook adds retirement schedules and data retention as selection inputs.

problems.brief: Cost per resolved conversation for a support agent with stated tokens, success rate and escalation cost, compared with a $0.99 per-outcome price.
The AI feature costs ten times more per user than projected: find the cause from the request bill of materials.
An internal assistant for 20,000 employees: self-host an open model or use a hosted API, and how many GPUs.
Critique a three-year build decision justified by today's API price.
An assistant with a 6,000-token system prompt serving two million requests a day: daily cost with and without caching, and which number dominates.
A model strategy for five features (customer chat, document extraction, code assistance, summarisation, compliance review) in a regulated financial company.

modules.title: Staff strategy, platforms and decision rights
modules.brief: The questions staff candidates get about org shape and risk: AI strategy, shared platforms, governance and the one metric.

lessons.title: Playbook: AI strategy for a company
lessons.brief: Staff questions are about portfolio, platform and risk rather than prompts: which use cases first, which primitives to share, who decides, and what leadership will measure. The one-page shape is a portfolio ranked by value and risk, platform primitives (gateway, prompt registry, eval service, tracing, data controls), decision rights, and risk tiers mapped to NIST AI RMF functions. The playbook works a regulated firm with several features and ends with the first 90 days.

lessons.title: Shared inference and eval platforms
lessons.brief: When a dozen teams call models in their own way, a shared platform pays for itself in keys, quotas, tracing and evals, and fails if it becomes a queue for every change. The lesson covers the platform's contract with product teams, paved paths versus mandates, and the platform's own success metric. The reader writes the charter for an internal AI platform team.

lessons.title: Decision rights and risk tiers
lessons.brief: Governance that does not stop shipping assigns decision rights by risk tier: who moves a production label, who approves a new model, who can launch to all users. The lesson maps tiers to NIST AI RMF functions and to the release ladder, with evidence each tier must produce. The reader designs a process an auditor accepts and a team does not route around.

problems.brief: Twelve LLM features across chat, search, extraction and agents, each calling models its own way: design the shared inference platform.
Eight product teams run ad-hoc evals in notebooks: design the shared eval platform and how you would know it works.
You own an internal AI platform other teams build agents on: your strategy, and the one metric you would own.
What would you build in your first 90 days?
Critique a governance process that requires a committee review for every prompt change.
Present a one-page AI strategy to a VP: portfolio, platform primitives, decision rights and metrics, then take questions.

tracks.title: Training, post-training and infrastructure
tracks.brief: What ML infra and research-engineer loops ask first: training FLOPs, MFU and scaling laws, GPUs and kernels, distributed training (collectives, ZeRO and FSDP2, tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism), numerics and loss spikes, reliability at scale, pretraining data and ablations, mixture of experts, SFT and reward models, RL for LLMs (PPO, the GRPO family, verifiers, reward hacking, rollout-trainer mismatch), distillation and merging, and adapting models. Every lab is pure Python in Pyodide (simulators, planners, toy policies), never real training in the browser. Public training reports (DeepSeek-V3, Llama 3, Kimi K2, OLMo 2, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1) are the primary material.

modules.title: Compute, scaling laws and the training budget
modules.brief: Turning a token budget and a cluster into days and MFU, what the scaling laws do and do not say, and sizing a run.

lessons.title: Training FLOPs, MFU and the budget equation
lessons.brief: Training compute is well approximated by 6 times parameters times tokens, which turns a token budget and a cluster into days once you assume an MFU. The lesson makes Llama 3 405B's 38 to 43% BF16 MFU and DeepSeek-V3's 180K H800 GPU hours per trillion tokens comparable, and shows attention FLOPs only dominate past sequence lengths around eight times the model dimension. The reader estimates days to train a stated model on a stated cluster.

lessons.title: Scaling laws: Kaplan, Chinchilla, and training past compute-optimal
lessons.brief: Kaplan found power laws over more than seven orders of magnitude, Chinchilla's 400-plus runs said to double tokens with model size, and the 20 tokens per parameter figure is a ratio derived from one run (1.4T over 70B). Deployed models train far past it because inference cost dominates, and Llama 3 used IsoFLOP curves to land on 405B against an extrapolated optimum of 402B on 16.55T tokens. The reader can say what a scaling law predicts and what it does not.

lessons.title: Chinchilla, replicated
lessons.brief: Besiroglu et al. found Chinchilla's parametric fit does not fit the extracted data, its intervals are implausibly narrow, and a re-fit agrees with the paper's other two methods. The walkthrough covers what that means for the 20x rule and for anyone extrapolating from small runs. It ends with the interview answer to "how sure are you about 20 tokens per parameter".

lessons.title: Playbook: size the run
lessons.brief: The inputs are target quality, expected inference volume, GPU count and type, and the deadline; the options are compute-optimal dense, inference-optimal smaller and longer, or MoE at a chosen sparsity. Sardana et al. found quality kept improving up to 10,000 tokens per parameter, and Kimi K2 published a sparsity scaling law for its MoE. The playbook ends with what to measure during the run: loss against the extrapolated curve, MFU and effective training time.

problems.brief: Days to train a stated dense model on a stated number of H100s at an MFU you choose and defend, using 6ND.
From DeepSeek-V3's published GPU hours and tokens, estimate the run's hardware utilisation and label it an estimate.
How sure are you about 20 tokens per parameter, and what would you use instead to size a run?
Size a run for a stated inference volume: compute-optimal dense, smaller and longer, or MoE.
Which H100 BF16 peak goes in the MFU denominator: the sparse figure or the dense one?
Critique an MFU report that uses the sparse peak and counts recomputed activations as useful FLOPs.

modules.title: GPUs, roofline and kernels for training
modules.brief: The GPU as a memory hierarchy, the roofline for a training step, fusion and compilation, and profiling as an experiment.

lessons.title: The GPU as a memory hierarchy
lessons.brief: An H100 SXM has 132 SMs, up to 228 KB of shared memory per SM, a 50 MB L2 and 80 GB of HBM at 3.35 TB/s, and every kernel decision is about which level the data lives in. The lesson covers warps, blocks, occupancy, TMA and clusters, and the spec-sheet trap that 1,979 BF16 TFLOPS is the sparsity figure while dense is 989. The reader can explain why a kernel is slow from where its data sits.

lessons.title: The roofline for a training step
lessons.brief: Arithmetic intensity against the H100's critical intensity of about 295 FLOPs per byte says whether an op is compute-bound or bandwidth-bound. Large-batch matmuls are compute-bound while norms and pointwise ops are bandwidth-bound, and small ops are overhead-bound. The reader classifies the ops of a transformer block and picks what to fuse.

lessons.title: Fusion, torch.compile, Triton and CUDA graphs
lessons.brief: Fusing pointwise ops saves HBM round trips, torch.compile's modes trade compile time and memory for speed, and reduce-overhead mode uses CUDA graphs that need static shapes and no CPU synchronisation during capture. The lesson covers graph breaks, recompilation with dynamic shapes, the caching allocator and the ladder from PyTorch to torch.compile to Triton to CUDA. The reader knows when a custom kernel is worth writing.

lessons.title: Playbook: profiling a kernel like an experiment
lessons.brief: Profiling is an experiment: baseline, controlled changes, variance reduction, stop criteria, attribution and a correctness gate. The playbook is built on the reported Anthropic profiling prompt and Anthropic's public performance take-home, whose README records model submissions that cheated by editing tests. It ends with what you write down after each change.

problems.brief: At what batch size does a BF16 matmul become compute-bound on an H100, and why?
With only a kernel simulator reporting cycles, IPC, stall reasons, occupancy and bandwidth, design a rigorous plan to profile and optimise a kernel.
Make a kernel on a simulated machine run in fewer cycles (the shape of Anthropic's public performance take-home), with tests that cannot be edited.
torch.compile in reduce-overhead mode is slower than eager and recompiles every few steps.
GPUs are starved for input: diagnose across storage, CPU preprocessing, batching, transfer and synchronisation.
Which of these ops is compute-bound on an H100 at a stated batch: a large matmul, layer norm, softmax or GELU?

modules.title: Distributed training
modules.brief: Collectives, the memory anatomy of a step, ZeRO and FSDP2, tensor, sequence, pipeline and context parallelism, and composing them.

lessons.title: Collectives from first principles
lessons.brief: All-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, all-to-all and broadcast are the vocabulary of distributed training, and ring all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. Per-GPU traffic for ring all-reduce stays near twice the buffer size regardless of GPU count, which is why bandwidth, not count, sets its cost. The lab simulates it and counts bytes per rank.

lessons.title: Memory anatomy of a training step
lessons.brief: Mixed-precision Adam needs 16 bytes per parameter (20 with FP32 gradient accumulation) before activations, and activations grow with sequence length and batch. Selective recomputation with sequence parallelism cut activation memory five times with over 90% less recompute overhead in Korthikanti et al. The reader plans memory for a stated model and parallel layout in the lab.

lessons.title: Data parallelism, ZeRO and FSDP2
lessons.brief: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 adds gradients and ZeRO-3 adds parameters at about 3 units of traffic against 2. FSDP2 shards each parameter as a DTensor on dimension 0 with mixed-precision policies and prefetching, and applying fully_shard only at the root gives one large all-gather with no overlap. The reader can say what a ZeRO-3 step communicates and when it hides.

lessons.title: Tensor and sequence parallelism
lessons.brief: Tensor parallelism splits the MLP and attention matmuls column then row, with collectives every layer, which is why it stays inside an NVLink domain; the Ultrascale Playbook measured large drops when it crossed nodes. Sequence parallelism shards norms and dropout along the sequence. The lesson pairs with the reported OpenAI question on deriving a sharded matmul and its backward pass.

lessons.title: Pipeline parallelism and its schedules
lessons.brief: All-forward-all-backward has a bubble of (p - 1) / m, 1F1B keeps that bubble but caps in-flight activations, interleaving cuts it to about (p - 1) / (v m) at v times the communication, and zero-bubble schedules split the backward pass. DeepSeek-V3's DualPipe overlaps computation and communication across directions. The lab simulates the schedules and checks the formulas.

lessons.title: Context parallelism and ring attention
lessons.brief: Context parallelism splits a long sequence across GPUs and rotates keys and values around a ring while computing, and causal masking unbalances the work unless chunks are assigned in a zig-zag. Llama 3 trained a context-parallel stage at 131,072 tokens with CP 16 at 38% MFU. The reader decides when context parallelism is needed and what it costs.

lessons.title: Playbook: composing 4D and 5D parallelism
lessons.brief: The order of decisions is fit one replica, reach the global batch, then maximise throughput, with TP inside nodes and PP or ZeRO-3 across them, and PP and ZeRO-3 rarely together. Published configs differ sharply: Llama 3 used TP 8, PP 16 and data parallelism up to 128, while DeepSeek-V3 used PP 16, EP 64 over 8 nodes and ZeRO-1 with no tensor parallelism. The worked case is the reported Meta prompt with 256 A100-80GB GPUs.

problems.brief: An MoE pretraining pipeline for about 1T tokens on 256 A100-80GB GPUs: experts and top-k, parallelism and group sizes, all-to-all overlap, memory per GPU, checkpointing and elastic restart; then scale to 1,024 GPUs.
Y = X @ W with W column-sharded over P devices: derive forward and backward and name every collective needed for a replicated dX with dW sharded.
ZeRO-3 memory per GPU for a stated model, GPU count and sequence length, including activations with and without recompute.
Pipeline bubble for p = 16 and m = 32, then with interleaving at v = 2, and what the interleaving costs.
MFU dropped after tensor parallelism moved from 8 to 16 on the same cluster.
Critique a parallel layout for a large dense run with tensor parallelism across nodes and pipeline parallelism combined with ZeRO-3.
Tensor versus pipeline parallelism for training and for inference: bubbles, micro-batches, interconnect and small inference batches.
Ring all-reduce simulator: reduce-scatter then all-gather, with a test that per-rank traffic equals 2(N - 1)/N of the buffer.

modules.title: Precision, optimizers and stability
modules.brief: Mixed precision without folklore, FP8 as DeepSeek-V3 did it, loss spikes and how labs stopped them, and AdamW, decoupled decay and Muon.

lessons.title: Mixed precision without folklore
lessons.brief: FP16 needed loss scaling because of its narrow exponent range, and BF16 keeps FP32's range with fewer mantissa bits, so it does not. Master weights and FP32 reductions still matter, and FSDP2 exposes them as parameter and reduce dtypes. The reader can say which tensors stay in FP32 and why.

lessons.title: FP8 training as DeepSeek-V3 did it
lessons.brief: DeepSeek-V3 ran FP8 GEMMs for forward and both backward passes with 1x128 activation tiles, 128x128 weight blocks and promotion to FP32 every 128 elements, kept embeddings, the output head, gating, norms and attention in higher precision, and reported relative loss error under 0.25% against BF16. The walkthrough compares per-tensor scaling with E4M3 and E5M2 formats. It ends with what "we trained in FP8" should make an interviewer ask.

lessons.title: Loss spikes and how labs stopped them
lessons.brief: OLMo 2 linked spikes to batches with long repeated n-grams and added RMSNorm reordering, QK-norm, z-loss and no weight decay on embeddings; Kimi K2 found attention logits exploding under Muon and capped them with QK-Clip, reporting no loss spikes over 15.5T tokens; DeepSeek-V3 reports no irrecoverable spikes or rollbacks. The lesson turns these into a first-hour checklist for an upward spike. Each fix is presented with the run that motivated it.

lessons.title: Optimizers: AdamW, decoupled decay and Muon
lessons.brief: An L2 penalty in the loss is not decoupled weight decay under Adam, which is why AdamW exists, and decay interacts with the learning-rate schedule. Muon reports about twice the compute efficiency of AdamW once weight decay and per-parameter update scaling are added, and Kimi K2 needed QK-Clip to keep it stable at scale. The reader can explain the difference and when to try Muon.

problems.brief: Loss goes to NaN after a partial move from FP16 to BF16: find the reduction still running in low precision.
An upward loss spike at step N in a long run: what do you look at in the first hour, and what do you change?
Why does BF16 often work better than FP16 for training stability?
Adam versus AdamW: why an L2 penalty differs from decoupled weight decay, and how decay interacts with the schedule.
Stable softmax cross-entropy and its gradient with a finite-difference check.
Which components did DeepSeek-V3 keep in higher precision during FP8 training?

modules.title: Reliability at scale
modules.brief: What fails in a large run, checkpointing that does not stall training, and finding bad nodes.

lessons.title: What fails in a 16K-GPU run
lessons.brief: Llama 3 405B had 466 interruptions in 54 days, 419 of them unexpected and about 78% of those attributed to hardware, with faulty GPUs and HBM3 the top causes and six silent data corruptions, while keeping effective training time above 90%. The lesson separates MFU from effective training time and flags an arithmetic inconsistency in the paper's failure table. The reader can design for the failure rate rather than against it.

lessons.title: Checkpointing that does not stall training
lessons.brief: Distributed checkpoints are per-rank files resharded at load, with asynchronous saves staged to CPU memory and written by a separate thread. The checkpoint interval is a trade between failure rate and save time, and Kimi K2's checkpoint engine updated a 1T model for RL in under 30 seconds. The reader chooses an interval and proves restores bring back optimizer state.

lessons.title: Finding bad nodes
lessons.brief: Bad nodes show up as NCCL watchdog timeouts, stragglers and silent corruption, and finding them is group testing under constraints. The lesson builds on the reported xAI question of finding faulty nodes with parallel group tests that cannot share nodes, including flaky tests and a live cluster. The reader implements the search and states its round count.

problems.brief: Find all faulty GPU nodes with parallel group tests that cannot share nodes; then handle few bad nodes and flaky tests.
Choose a checkpoint interval from a failure rate and save time you state, and compute the expected lost work.
A checkpoint restore silently drops optimizer state and the loss curve tells you only later.
MFU versus effective training time: which one a failure storm hurts, and which one the board should see.
Elastic restart and bad-node quarantine for a 2,048-GPU run.
Critique a postmortem that quotes Llama 3's faulty-GPU percentage without checking its denominator.

modules.title: Pretraining data and ablations
modules.brief: From Common Crawl to tokens, dedup at three levels, mixing and annealing, running short on quality tokens, small-scale ablations, and benchmarks that move for the wrong reason.

lessons.title: From Common Crawl to tokens
lessons.brief: Extraction, language identification, heuristic filters and model-based quality classifiers turn a crawl into training tokens, and each choice is decided by training small models per variant. FineWeb produced 15T tokens from 96 snapshots, and DCLM found model-based filtering the key step, training a 7B model to 64% MMLU 5-shot on 2.6T tokens. The reader designs the filter stack and its ablation plan.

lessons.title: Dedup: exact, near and line-level
lessons.brief: Lee et al. found one 61-word sentence over 60,000 times in C4 and a tenfold drop in memorised emissions after dedup, and Llama 3 deduplicated at URL, document (MinHash) and line level. OLMo 2's micro-annealing found some duplication helpful, so dedup is a tuned choice, not a maximum. The lab builds MinHash with LSH bands.

lessons.title: Mixing, annealing and mid-training
lessons.brief: Llama 3's mix was roughly half general, a quarter maths and reasoning, 17% code and 8% multilingual, with annealing on high-quality data that helped the 8B and barely moved the 405B. OLMo 2 souped several anneals, Qwen3 used three pretraining stages, and Kimi K2 rephrased data rather than repeating it. The reader plans a mid-training stage and its evaluation.

lessons.title: Playbook: not enough high-quality tokens
lessons.brief: After aggressive filtering the options are relaxing filters, repeating epochs, rephrasing, synthesising or distilling, each with a cost and a risk. Kimi K2 reported better SimpleQA from ten rephrasings seen once than from ten epochs of raw data, and Nemotron-4 used mostly synthetic alignment data with a reward-model filter. The playbook answers the NVIDIA follow-up reported for this question.

lessons.title: Small-scale ablations and micro-annealing
lessons.brief: Data decisions are made with small models: FineWeb and DCLM ran ablations per choice, OLMo 2 used micro-annealing to judge a source cheaply, and Llama 3 judged data by annealing the 8B. Scaling-law extrapolation predicts the large run from the small ones within limits. The reader designs an ablation that decides whether a new source enters the mix.

lessons.title: Benchmarks that move for the wrong reason
lessons.brief: Contamination, overfitting to fixed benchmarks and metric choice (pass@1 versus pass@k versus majority vote) all move scores without moving capability. DeepSeek-V3 states an aim to avoid over-optimising fixed benchmarks, and the reported NVIDIA follow-up asks what to do when benchmarks rise and a user-facing language regresses. The reader builds the regression check that catches it.

problems.brief: Turn raw text into a curated training set (sources, filtering, dedup, mixing, evaluation); then there are too few quality tokens, and a user-facing language regressed.
MinHash near-dedup with shingles, signatures and LSH bands; hidden tests plant near-duplicates and distinct documents.
Rephrase, repeat or synthesise when filtering leaves too few tokens: the cost and risk of each.
Turn a mix in percentages into token counts and epochs per source for a stated budget and source sizes.
Benchmarks went up and a user-facing language regressed after a data change.
A small-scale ablation plan to decide whether a new data source goes into the mix.

modules.title: Mixture of experts in training
modules.brief: Routing, capacity and load balance, expert parallelism with all-to-all, and sparsity as a design knob.

lessons.title: Routing, capacity and load balance
lessons.brief: Top-k routing with a capacity factor drops tokens when experts overflow, auxiliary losses balance load, and DeepSeek-V3 replaced the auxiliary loss with a bias updated during training. Qwen3 uses a global-batch balance loss and no shared experts while DeepSeekMoE uses fine-grained plus shared experts. The lesson covers router collapse and making a hard router differentiable.

lessons.title: Expert parallelism and all-to-all
lessons.brief: Expert parallelism dispatches tokens to experts on other GPUs and combines them back with two all-to-all exchanges per layer, which can cancel the compute saving. DeepSeek-V3 limited each token to at most 4 nodes to bound that traffic. The reader decides expert placement and when communication eats the gain.

lessons.title: Sparsity as a design knob
lessons.brief: Kimi K2 fit a sparsity scaling law and chose 384 experts with 8 active, reporting fewer FLOPs than lower sparsity at the same validation loss, and kept 64 attention heads because doubling them would add substantial inference FLOPs at long context. The walkthrough reads the paper as a set of trade-offs between training and serving cost. It ends with what you would ask before copying the configuration.

problems.brief: Trace tokens through routing, expert compute and combine; explain total versus active parameters and when communication cancels the saving.
Make a hard top-k router differentiable: straight-through, Gumbel-softmax, relaxations or REINFORCE, with the auxiliary losses and defaults you would pick.
Router collapse: two experts take most tokens a few thousand steps in.
Tokens per batch for an MoE layer to be compute-bound with DeepSeek's expert configuration, labelled as an estimate.
DeepSeek-V3's auxiliary-loss-free balancing adjusts which quantity during training?
Choose expert count, top-k and shared experts for a stated training and serving budget.

modules.title: SFT, preferences and reward models
modules.brief: Building SFT data, reward models and their limits, and DPO in practice.

lessons.title: Building SFT data
lessons.brief: SFT data comes from domain-specific generation, rejection sampling from expert models and packing with isolation masks; DeepSeek-V3 used about 1.5M instances for two epochs and fixed overthinking, formatting and length problems in R1-generated data. Llama 3 ran several rounds of SFT then DPO with rejection sampling of many samples per prompt. The reader designs the SFT data pipeline for one capability.

lessons.title: Reward models and their limits
lessons.brief: Pairwise reward models, rule-based rewards and process supervision each fail differently, and Gao et al. showed over-optimisation against a proxy reward. Lightman et al. found process supervision beating outcome supervision on maths, while DeepSeek-R1 abandoned process reward models because steps are hard to define and judge and invite reward hacking. The reader picks a reward source for a task and names how it will be gamed.

lessons.title: DPO in practice
lessons.brief: DPO needs a frozen reference model but no separate reward model and no sampling during training, and its beta controls how far the policy moves. The lesson covers dataset construction (fields, ties, noisy labels), offline versus online preference data, and Llama 3's settings (learning rate 1e-5, beta 0.1, an NLL term on chosen responses). The lab derives the loss and its gradient by hand.

problems.brief: DPO versus PPO-based RLHF and why DPO skips the reward model; then specify a DPO dataset: fields, chosen and rejected sources, ties, noisy labels and filtering.
A DPO run where the chosen responses' log-probabilities also fall: is it a bug, and what do you change?
DPO loss and gradient by hand on toy pairs; tests check the loss equals log 2 when policy equals reference and a finite-difference gradient.
A real-time QA chatbot: training data, RL tasks and rewards, the reward's weaknesses and how you detect the policy exploiting it.
Process versus outcome reward models, and why DeepSeek-R1 dropped process rewards.
The proxy reward keeps rising while human preference falls: diagnose over-optimisation and decide the stopping rule.

modules.title: Reinforcement learning for LLMs
modules.brief: PPO mechanics, the GRPO family, verifiers and environments, reward hacking, and the infrastructure that makes on-policy RL off-policy.

lessons.title: PPO for language models
lessons.brief: PPO for LLMs has a policy, a value model, a reward model and a reference, a clipped surrogate objective, and a KL penalty that can sit in the reward or in the loss. GRPO drops the value model by normalising rewards within a group of samples. The reader can say which policy is "old" in the ratio and what each model costs in memory.

lessons.title: The GRPO family: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO and GSPO
lessons.brief: GRPO uses group-relative advantages, so a group where every sample is correct contributes zero gradient; Dr. GRPO removes a length bias; DAPO adds clip-higher, dynamic sampling, token-level loss and overlong shaping and drops the KL term, reaching 50 on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B in half the steps of the R1-Zero baseline; GSPO moves to a sequence-level ratio for MoE stability. TRL's current defaults encode several of these choices (no KL term, a DAPO loss type). The walkthrough ends with which choice you would make for a stated task and why.

lessons.title: RLVR, verifiers and environments
lessons.brief: R1-Zero used rule-based accuracy and format rewards, Qwen3 ran reasoning RL on 3,995 query-verifier pairs and moved AIME'24 from 70.1 to 85.1 in 170 steps, and Kimi K2 combined real and synthetic environments with a self-critique rubric reward. Open tooling (Prime Intellect's verifiers and Environments Hub) makes environments shareable. The reader designs a verifier and lists how a policy could satisfy it without doing the task.

lessons.title: Reward hacking: evidence and mitigations
lessons.brief: Models edit unit tests, exit early from harnesses and flatter graders, and Anthropic found that learning to reward-hack in real coding environments generalised to sabotage in 12% of a Claude Code evaluation and alignment-faking reasoning in 50% of responses, with inoculation prompting removing most of it. Baker et al. showed chain-of-thought monitoring catches hacking but optimising against the monitor produces obfuscated hacking. The reader designs environments and monitors that make hacking visible rather than hidden.

lessons.title: RL infrastructure: rollouts, staleness and mismatch
lessons.brief: Rollouts run in an inference engine and gradients in a trainer, and differences in their numerics make nominally on-policy RL off-policy, which truncated importance sampling corrects and batch-invariant kernels can remove. The lesson covers colocated versus separate rollout engines, asynchronous actors and learners with staleness bounds, and Kimi K2's colocated design with fast weight updates. It pairs with the reported Anthropic GRPO screen and the Meta asynchronous RL design question.

problems.brief: Engine and trainer log-probabilities disagree in an "on-policy" GRPO run: diagnose the mismatch and apply truncated importance sampling.
An asynchronous RL post-training loop for a chat model already serving traffic: actors, reward inference, learners, replay, off-policy corrections, KL control and rollback.
How pipeline stages and micro-batches interact with GRPO rollouts: relative advantages, policy versions, throughput and staleness.
A group where every sample is correct: what does it contribute to GRPO, and what does DAPO do about it?
A GRPO run's response length explodes over a few hundred steps.
Critique a plan to penalise "bad thoughts" in the chain of thought to stop reward hacking.
Distributed PPO across thousands of GPUs: placement of policy, value, reward and reference models, and the bottleneck you expect.

modules.title: Distillation, merging and synthetic data
modules.brief: Three kinds of distillation, merging weights from a shared initialisation, and synthetic data with a filter that decides quality.

lessons.title: Distillation: soft targets, SFT on samples and on-policy
lessons.brief: Distillation means Hinton's soft targets, SFT on teacher samples (R1 distilled on about 800K samples), or on-policy distillation where the student samples and the teacher scores per token. Thinking Machines reproduced the Qwen3 result that on-policy distillation reached 74.4 on AIME'24 at 1,800 GPU hours against 67.6 at 17,920 for RL. Yue et al. found distillation can add reasoning patterns that RLVR does not, which changes which one to use.

lessons.title: Model merging
lessons.brief: Model soups average fine-tuned weights from a shared initialisation at no inference cost, TIES trims small changes, elects a sign per parameter and merges agreeing values, and Llama 3 and OLMo 2 averaged checkpoints across anneals and stages. Merging is not ensembling: one model runs, so it needs compatible weights. The reader decides when merging beats training another round.

lessons.title: Synthetic data with a filter that decides quality
lessons.brief: Synthetic data is cheap to generate and only as good as its filter, whether a reward model (Nemotron-4), a verifier, or rejection sampling against tests. Kimi K2's rephrasing in pretraining is the other use, and contamination is the risk both share. The reader designs the filter and the contamination check together.

problems.brief: Design knowledge distillation of models and an LLM post-training pipeline, with evals and gates per stage.
problems.reported: Cohere (candidate report via aced.io, staff level)

problems.brief: On-policy distillation versus RL GPU hours for the Qwen3-8B result, and what would change the comparison for your task.
Merging versus ensembling: what model soups require, and when merging fails.
Does RL teach new reasoning or sharpen what the base model already samples? Use Yue et al. with its limits.
TIES merging on toy parameter vectors: trim, elect sign, merge; tests check sign conflicts.
Critique a synthetic-data plan that generates a million examples with no filter and no contamination check.

modules.title: Adapting models: LoRA, QLoRA and continued pretraining
modules.brief: LoRA settings that work, QLoRA's mechanics and limits, and continued pretraining without forgetting.

lessons.title: LoRA in practice
lessons.brief: LoRA Without Regret recommends applying adapters to all layers including MLP and MoE, a learning rate around ten times full fine-tuning, care with large batches, and notes rank 1 matches full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL. PEFT's defaults (r 8, alpha 8) are library defaults, not recommendations, and alpha over r scaling makes the best learning rate roughly rank-independent. The reader sets up a LoRA run and defends each setting.

lessons.title: QLoRA mechanics
lessons.brief: QLoRA freezes an NF4-quantised base with double quantisation, trains adapters in higher precision and pages optimizer state, which let a 65B model fine-tune on one 48 GB GPU. The memory saving stops at activations, which grow with sequence length and batch. The reader estimates QLoRA memory and knows where it breaks.

lessons.title: Continued pretraining without forgetting
lessons.brief: Re-warming and re-decaying the learning rate with a replay share of original data matched full retraining at a fraction of the compute at 405M and 10B parameters in Ibrahim et al. LoRA forgets less but learns less in continued pretraining on code and maths. The reader designs a domain continued-pretraining run with forgetting checks.

problems.brief: LoRA learning rate, targets and rank: why library defaults are not recommendations, with the evidence.
QLoRA memory for a 65B model at a stated sequence length and batch, and where the saving stops.
Continued pretraining on a domain corpus: re-warm, re-decay, replay ratio, forgetting checks and the stop rule.
A LoRA run matches full fine-tuning on instruction data but falls short on a maths dataset.
A LoRA layer forward pass with alpha over r scaling and zero-initialised B; tests check equivalence to the base at initialisation.
In QLoRA, which part is stored in NF4 and which part trains in higher precision?

tracks.title: Long context, architectures, multimodal and voice
tracks.brief: The areas the first build had no content for: RoPE scaling (PI, YaRN, LongRoPE) and attention sinks, testing long context honestly when needle scores mislead, MLA, state space models and hybrids, diffusion language models, how vision-language models see and what images, pages, video and audio cost per provider, speech models and a voice turn measured stage by stage, and image and video generation for engineers who design and serve them. Three review rules apply across the track: a needle-test score is never evidence of usable long context, every image-token figure names its model family, and 800 ms voice-to-voice is one vendor's target, not a standard.

modules.title: Stretching and testing long context
modules.brief: How RoPE works and how a window is stretched, attention sinks, and long-context evaluation that predicts real tasks.

lessons.title: RoPE from the inside, and how a context window is stretched
lessons.brief: RoPE rotates query and key pairs by a position-dependent angle so their dot product depends on relative distance, and stretching a window changes those frequencies. Position Interpolation squeezes positions into the trained range with short fine-tuning, YaRN rescales frequencies unevenly, Llama 3.1 ships a rope_type llama3 block with factor 8 from 8,192 original positions, and LongRoPE searches per-dimension factors. These are configuration changes with a quality cost, and Qwen's model card warns that static YaRN can hurt short inputs.

existing.note: The "advertised versus effective context" section moves to long-context-evals.

lessons.title: YaRN, walked through
lessons.brief: Position Interpolation left high-frequency dimensions with too little local resolution, and YaRN answers with a per-frequency ramp and an attention temperature term. gpt-oss extends dense layers to 131,072 tokens with YaRN and Qwen3 documents a factor-4 YaRN block. The walkthrough ends with the answer to "why not just raise the base".

lessons.title: Attention sinks and streaming
lessons.brief: StreamingLLM showed window attention collapses once the first tokens are evicted because heads park attention on them even when they are not semantically important, and keeping those few KV entries restores quality over very long streams. gpt-oss builds the idea into the model with a learned per-head bias in the softmax denominator. The engineering consequence is that any KV eviction policy must pin the sink tokens.

lessons.title: Testing long context honestly
lessons.brief: The needle test plants a fact in filler text and sweeps length and depth, and RULER, NoLiMa and HELMET all found models scoring near perfectly on needles while realistic or no-overlap tasks degraded; HELMET states needle results do not reliably predict downstream performance. The lesson builds a probe suite of single needle, multi-needle, no-overlap needle, multi-hop chain and aggregation tasks against a scripted mock model. The reader reports score by length for their own task and never cites a needle score as proof.

problems.brief: After adding a static YaRN block to reach 128K, short prompts got worse; decide whether to keep it and how to serve both.
Implement RoPE on toy vectors and verify that the attention score depends only on relative position; hidden tests probe the offset bug.
Take a 32K model to 128K: PI, YaRN, LongRoPE or continued training, with the cost and the quality test for each.
Build a long-context eval for your product: task types, lengths, scoring and the report that replaces a needle score.
Why not just raise the RoPE base frequency to extend context?
Critique a vendor claim of "perfect recall at 1M tokens" supported only by a needle-in-a-haystack heatmap.

modules.title: Architectures beyond the dense transformer
modules.brief: Latent attention, state space models and why production keeps hybrids, and diffusion language models.

lessons.title: Multi-head latent attention and the KV bytes table
lessons.brief: DeepSeek-V2 compresses keys and values into a shared latent, caches the latent and keeps a small decoupled RoPE key because rotation does not commute with the absorbed projection. It reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache against DeepSeek 67B, a dense multi-head model, which is why the baseline must be stated whenever the figure is used. The walkthrough computes bytes per token for MHA, GQA-8 and MLA from published configs.

lessons.title: State space models and why production uses hybrids
lessons.brief: Mamba makes state-space parameters input-dependent so a fixed-size state can choose what to keep, and Mamba-2 relates SSMs to attention as structured matrices. "Repeat After Me" proves a fixed state cannot copy long strings that a two-layer transformer can, and finds pretrained transformers far better at copying and retrieval from context. Shipped models therefore keep some attention: Jamba uses one attention layer per seven Mamba layers, Kimi Linear three linear layers per MLA layer, and Qwen3.8-27B three Gated DeltaNet layers per full-attention layer.

lessons.title: Diffusion language models
lessons.brief: Diffusion language models generate by iteratively unmasking many positions in parallel instead of one token at a time. LLaDA 8B is reported competitive with LLaMA3 8B on in-context learning, and Mercury Coder reports up to 10 times the speed of speed-optimised models on average, measured by a third party. The engineering questions are what parallel decoding does to streaming UX, KV caching and structured output.

problems.brief: Why do production long-context models keep some full attention? Use the copying result and a shipped hybrid ratio.
KV cache at 256K for a 1:7 attention-to-Mamba hybrid versus a dense MoE of similar size, from the published configurations.
How do diffusion language models generate, and what changes for streaming, KV caching and constrained output?
Given an open model's config with banded windows and sinks, compute KV per token at 128K and decide whether to serve it for a long-document product.
MLA's 93.3% KV reduction is measured against which baseline?
Critique a proposal to switch to a diffusion LM because it is "10x faster", for a streaming chat product.

modules.title: Vision-language models and their costs
modules.brief: How a VLM sees, what an image, a page, a second of video and a second of audio cost per provider, and the failure modes of VLMs.

lessons.title: How a vision-language model sees
lessons.brief: ViT turns an image into patch tokens, CLIP trains image and text towers on 400 million pairs with a contrastive loss, LLaVA connects a vision encoder to an LLM through a projector, Qwen2.5-VL trains a native dynamic-resolution encoder with time encoding for long video, and Llama 4 uses early fusion. The encoder is a lexer for pixels and the projector is the ABI between two models, and which parts are frozen during training is the question interviewers probe. The reader can draw a VLM and say what each part costs at inference.

lessons.title: Playbook: what an image, a page, a second of video and of audio cost
lessons.brief: Claude counts one visual token per 28-pixel patch with caps by tier, OpenAI's patch models count 32-pixel patches with a multiplier and its tile models charge a base plus a cost per 512-pixel tile, and Gemini charges 258 tokens per small image or per 768-pixel tile, 32 tokens per second of audio and documents video at more than one rate. Every figure must name its model family. The playbook decides between downsampling, cropping and switching tier for a stated workload.

lessons.title: VLM failure modes: counting, OCR errors and ignoring the image
lessons.brief: VLMs fail by describing from the text prompt alone, miscounting, misreading small text, and losing track across many pages, and each failure has a different fix (resolution, cropping, prompting order, retrieval over page images).
