The lesson pairs each failure with the test that detects it and the change that addresses it. The reader can debug a VLM product from a sample of failures.

problems.brief: Design a video vision-language model end to end: data, architecture, objectives, evaluation and serving.
Image tokens and cost for a 1920 by 1080 screenshot on three providers, naming the model family for each figure.
What is a vision encoder, how is it trained, what bottlenecks VLM inference, and how would you cut memory and latency?
The multimodal model ignores the image and answers from the text: rank causes and fixes.
The VLM answers single-image questions well and fails on multi-page documents.
Walk through your VLM project: encoder, LLM, where fusion happens, what was frozen, leakage, latency and failure modes.

modules.title: Speech models and voice agents
modules.brief: ASR, TTS, turn detection and full-duplex models, a voice turn measured millisecond by millisecond, and pipeline versus speech-to-speech.

lessons.title: Speech models for engineers
lessons.brief: Whisper was trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual, multitask audio, TTS is judged by time to first byte, and Moshi models user and agent audio as parallel streams with 160 ms theoretical and 200 ms practical latency. Turn detection is its own model: plain VAD, OpenAI's semantic VAD with an eagerness setting, or Pipecat's Smart Turn. The reader picks components for a voice agent and knows which one sets the latency floor.

existing.note: The voice section of the real-time case lesson moves to this module; the 800 ms widget default is relabelled as one vendor's target.

lessons.title: A voice turn, millisecond by millisecond
lessons.brief: The Pipecat maintainers publish a round-trip table from microphone through encoding, network, jitter buffer, transcription and endpointing, LLM time to first byte, sentence aggregation and TTS to playback that sums to about 1.3 seconds, and their June 2026 update sets 1,500 ms as the target and says to avoid spikes. ElevenLabs' 800 ms figure is one vendor's target and must be labelled that way. The lab is a discrete-event simulator where the reader adds streaming TTS, speculative LLM start on interim transcripts, filler phrases for slow tools and barge-in, with tests on p50 and p95.

lessons.title: Playbook: cascaded pipeline or speech-to-speech
lessons.brief: A cascaded ASR, LLM and TTS pipeline gives control, tool use and logging per stage, while speech-to-speech models give lower latency and prosody at the cost of observability and per-minute pricing. The inputs are latency target, tool calls per turn, compliance logging and cost per minute from the provider's published realtime costs. The playbook ends with what to measure in the first week of a pilot.

problems.brief: Design a real-time AI voice system: ingestion, ASR, orchestration, TTS, session state, interruptions, safety, latency and cost.
Budget voice-to-voice latency by stage and find where the time goes, using a published stage table and your own assumptions.
Critique a voice-agent design that waits for the full LLM reply before starting TTS.
Speculative LLM start on interim transcripts: how it cuts latency, what it costs, and when it is wrong.
Cascaded ASR, LLM and TTS versus native speech-to-speech: the trade-offs for a support line with tool calls.
Users get cut off mid-sentence after a VAD change: plain VAD threshold or semantic VAD eagerness?

modules.title: Image and video generation for engineers
modules.brief: Enough of diffusion, latent diffusion, guidance, DiT and flow matching to design and serve generation systems.

lessons.title: Image and video generation for the AI engineer
lessons.brief: Latent diffusion moves denoising into an autoencoder's latent space, classifier-free guidance trades diversity for quality with one model trained conditional and unconditional, DiT replaces the U-Net with a transformer, and flow matching and rectified flow (Stable Diffusion 3) straighten the sampling path and cut steps. Movie Gen is a 30B transformer generating 16-second 1080p video from up to 73K video tokens. The reader can explain each component's effect on quality and serving cost.

lessons.title: Serving generation models: steps, distillation and batching by resolution
lessons.brief: Generation cost scales with sampling steps, resolution and frames, so the serving levers are fewer steps (flow matching, distillation), caching the text encoder output, and batching requests by resolution. The lesson costs a generation request and shows which lever moves latency most. The reader designs the serving path for an image product with a latency target.

lessons.title: Diffusion transformers, walked through
lessons.brief: DiT replaces the U-Net in latent diffusion with a transformer over latent patches and reports FID 2.27 on ImageNet 256, with quality improving as compute per image grows. Stable Diffusion 3 extends the idea with separate weights per modality and rectified flow. The walkthrough ends with what the move to transformers changed for serving (batching, parallelism, the same kernels as language models) and what to say when asked to explain a recent generation paper.

problems.brief: Design an image generation system (data, diffusion or autoregressive, conditioning, safety, evaluation, inference), extend it to text and image in and out, then explain a recent paper.
The diffusion model takes too long per image: speed up sampling without a visible quality drop, and prove it.
Design a text-to-video generation service: queueing, GPU allocation, safety filtering and cost per second of video.
What does the classifier-free guidance scale trade, and how would you choose it for a product?
Video tokens and compute scale for a 16-second clip at the published Movie Gen settings, and why latent compression decides feasibility.
Flow matching versus DDPM-style sampling: why the step count drops and what that does to serving.

tracks.title: AI system design
tracks.brief: The design round taught as decisions under conflicting constraints: the delivery framework as a reference, capacity and cost with every assumption labelled, retrieval-centric, agentic and real-time cases, and platform cases (coding-agent platforms, agent platforms, shared eval platforms) that staff loops ask for. Each case ends with what the design gives up and a written artefact (a rollout plan, a risk note), and rubrics are checklists the reader ticks rather than paragraphs to read.

modules.title: Design answers as decisions
modules.brief: Decisions under conflicting constraints, the scoping reference, and the eval and fallback plan every design needs.

lessons.title: Design answers as decisions under conflicting constraints
lessons.brief: Staff-level design rounds reward a decision under conflicting constraints with its cost stated, not a complete diagram. The lesson works a support assistant whose resolution rate rose while re-contacts also rose, and shows how the answer changes with a regulator, a deadline and a system that cannot be rewritten. Hello Interview's level rubric (senior goes deep in about two places, staff leads almost the entire interview) frames what changes between levels.

existing.note: The rubric and five scoping questions survive as a one-page reference (scoping-reference); the lesson becomes a decision-under-conflict lesson (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: Scoping reference: the questions that change the design
lessons.brief: A short list of scoping questions changes an AI design more than any component choice: who the user is, what a wrong answer costs, latency and cost targets, data access and residency, and how success is measured. The lesson is a reference page with each question and the design branch it opens. It replaces the old framework lesson's body.

lessons.title: The eval plan and the human fallback inside a design
lessons.brief: Every AI design needs an eval plan before launch, an online measurement after, and a fallback when the model is wrong, and interviewers ask for all three. The lesson covers outcome metrics with guardrails, pass^k for agents, escalation paths and how the fallback is staffed. The reader adds these to any design in five minutes.

problems.brief: Resolution rate is up and re-contacts are up after a launch: decide whether to roll back, with the analysis and the owner.
Design a support assistant with one operating constraint (an incumbent ticketing system that cannot change) and a stated "what you give up".
Design ChatGPT: the parts that matter for an interview and the decisions a staff candidate drives.
problems.reported: OpenAI (aggregated candidate reports via Hello Interview)

problems.brief: Critique this design document for a multi-tenant chat backend with billing and moderation.
Drive a full AI design round while the interviewer adds a new constraint at intervals; self-rate against the probe list.
A support assistant for a bank under a regulator, with a fixed launch date and a system that cannot be rewritten: the design and the risk note.

modules.title: Capacity and cost
modules.brief: The request bill of materials and break-evens, latency budgets across hops, and traffic to GPU fleet.

lessons.title: The request bill of materials and cache break-even
lessons.brief: A design's cost is a bill of materials per request (tokens in and out, cache reads and writes, retrieval, tools, retries) times traffic, and the prompt-cache break-even decides whether caching pays. The lesson derives the break-even from current price tables and shows which term dominates for three workloads. The reader can produce a cost line in a design round in two minutes.

existing.note: Cut the bill-of-materials opener and "history is re-sent"; keep the break-even derivation, Little's law sizing and rate limits as capacity.

lessons.title: Latency budgets across hops
lessons.brief: A latency budget is split across hops (network, retrieval, rerank, model time to first token, generation, post-processing), and percentiles do not add, so the budget is checked by simulation. The lesson uses Little's law for concurrency and labels published voice targets as vendor targets. The reader can cut a design that is three times over budget.

lessons.title: Traffic to GPU fleet
lessons.brief: Converting traffic into GPUs takes tokens per request, a throughput per GPU measured or estimated at the target latency, peak-to-average ratio and headroom for failures. The lesson works one case from a stated traffic model with a published model config and GPU specification. The reader states which assumption dominates the fleet size.

problems.brief: What a 1M-token context promise costs per request and per day at stated traffic, from list prices and a published model config.
From traffic to a GPU fleet for a stated model, latency target and peak ratio.
Latency doubled after a deploy; the diff touched retrieval, prompt length and the model id.
Daily cost of a RAG assistant at a million queries a day with caching tiers, stating which assumption flips the answer.
Your design is three times over the latency budget: where do you cut, and what does each cut cost in quality?
GPU compute cost for serving a chat product at a stated scale, including peak load and a failure-domain reserve.

modules.title: Retrieval-centric cases
modules.brief: Enterprise search with permissions, a support assistant with escalation, and document-heavy workflows.

lessons.title: Enterprise search with permissions
lessons.brief: Enterprise search fails on permissions, freshness and identifier-heavy queries before it fails on model quality. The lesson designs it end to end with permission-scoped retrieval as Microsoft 365 Copilot describes, per-tenant namespaces and their limits, contextual retrieval and an eval plan. It ends with the cost per query and what the design gives up.

existing.note: Document-heavy workflows move to workflows/batch-pipelines; enterprise search and support stay.

lessons.title: A support assistant with escalation
lessons.brief: A support assistant is retrieval plus policy plus escalation, and its success metric must include re-contacts and escalations, not only resolution. The lesson covers policy grounding, escalation triggers, tau-bench-style evaluation and the human handoff. The reader can show how they would know it helps and not harms.

lessons.title: Claims and compliance documents as a design case
lessons.brief: Insurance claims and compliance review mix retrieval over heterogeneous documents with a workflow that writes decisions, so most of the right answer is a workflow with model steps. The lesson costs PDF pages as text plus images, adds review routing and an audit trail of document versions. The reader designs it with token cost control.

problems.brief: Enterprise RAG with per-user permissions; the rubric becomes a checklist and the answer includes what you give up.
An insurance-claims system with token cost control, designed as a workflow with model steps rather than an agent.
A support assistant with escalation, and how you prove it helps rather than shifting work to re-contacts.
Multilingual retrieval for a global support corpus: one index or several, and the eval per language.
Critique an enterprise-search design that caches answers across users to save cost.
Embedding and storage cost for 100 million documents with permission metadata, and the re-index cost on a model change.

modules.title: Agentic cases
modules.brief: Customer-service agents with policy tools, coding-agent products, and computer-use automation.

lessons.title: A customer-service agent with policy tools
lessons.brief: An agent that can refund money needs deterministic policy limits outside the model, tools that enforce them, and evaluation by end state over repeated trials. The lesson designs it with tau-bench's policy domains as the test, approvals for out-of-policy requests and a human handoff. It ends with what happens when a model upgrade changes the escalation rate.

existing.note: The coding-agent platform material moves to case-platforms; policy agents and computer-use automation stay.

lessons.title: A coding agent product, end to end
lessons.brief: A coding agent product is a job system with an untrusted planner: sessions, sandboxes, credentials, verification and a review path into the repository. The lesson draws on the Copilot cloud agent's published limits (one branch, a firewall that covers only its Bash tool, the requester cannot approve the PR) and Anthropic's containment incidents. The reader designs the product and its security review.

lessons.title: A computer-use automation product
lessons.brief: Computer-use automation is slow, flaky and exposed to injection from every page it reads, so the product design is about narrowing scope, confirming consequential actions and recovering from failure. The lesson uses ChatGPT agent's published controls and the residual injection rates vendors report. The reader decides which customer tasks it should and should not take.

problems.brief: An agent for a streaming service's customer support, with refunds, policy limits and a model upgrade that doubles escalations.
Multi-tenant model deployment with an eval harness; the rubric becomes a checklist.
A code-review bot that runs headless in CI with budgets, a check and branch protection.
A customer-service agent that follows policy and can refund money, with the deterministic limits outside the model.
A multi-agent fintech chat backend with planning, retrieval, calculation, compliance and response agents, including failure handling.
Chat over SEC filings with agent orchestration, streaming, cancellation and token-budget enforcement.

modules.title: Real-time and specialised cases
modules.brief: Moderation pipelines, multi-tenant chat with metered billing, and multimodal intake.

lessons.title: A moderation pipeline with a model cascade
lessons.brief: Moderation is a cascade: cheap classifiers first, a model for the ambiguous middle, humans for appeals, each at an operating point chosen from the cost of errors. The lesson uses published moderation and guard models and constitutional classifiers as components. The reader sets the thresholds and the review capacity together.

existing.note: Voice moves to multimodal/speech-voice; moderation, chat billing and multimodal intake stay.

lessons.title: Multi-tenant chat with conversation state and metered billing
lessons.brief: A multi-tenant chat backend needs conversation state, per-tenant limits and billing that counts cache reads, cache writes and uncached input correctly. The lesson covers usage fields, rate limits as capacity, and billing systems that accept corrections only within a window. The reader designs the metering path and its reconciliation.

lessons.title: Multimodal intake: uploads, OCR and VLMs
lessons.brief: A file uploader for a chat product must handle large files, choose text extraction or page images per file type, and feed the model within a context and cost budget. The lesson covers chunked uploads, parsing routes, page-image costs and background processing with progress. The reader designs it for a stated mix of documents and images.

problems.brief: A real-time voice assistant with sub-second response as the product requirement, with the 800 ms figure labelled as a vendor target.
Content moderation with a model cascade and an appeals queue sized from the thresholds.
A multi-tenant chat backend with metered billing that counts cache reads and writes correctly.
Rolling out a new model version: the mechanics, with a retirement deadline and regressions on two prompts.
Rate limits at peak hour: separate a token-bucket limit from a concurrency limit in the evidence.
A file uploader for an AI chat app that handles large multimodal uploads and feeds them into the model's context.

modules.title: Platform cases
modules.brief: Coding-agent platforms, multi-tenant agent platforms and shared eval platforms, as staff loops ask them.

lessons.title: A coding-agent platform: session log, sandboxes and credential paths
lessons.brief: Managed Agents keeps the session as an event log outside a stateless harness, provisions sandboxes only when a tool needs them, and keeps credentials out of reach of generated code with vaults and egress substitution. Anthropic's containment post adds what failed: project config that ran before trust, credentials read and posted, and an allowlisted domain used for upload. The reader designs a hosted coding-agent platform and its security review.

lessons.title: A multi-tenant agent platform with harness regression gates
lessons.brief: Staff job descriptions define the work: Decagon's agent platform role names routing, execution logic, tool orchestration and control-plane systems, and Perplexity's agent-evals role names cost per successful task and regression gates for model, connector, tool, skill and harness changes. The lesson designs the platform against that specification. The reader can explain how a harness change is gated before it reaches customers.

lessons.title: A shared eval platform
lessons.brief: An eval platform runs many datasets asynchronously with code and model graders, versions everything and reports results teams trust. Duolingo runs its evals as Temporal workflows with deterministic graders first and a judge only where diffs are too brittle. The reader designs the platform and its own success metric.

problems.brief: A coding-agent platform: session log, lazily provisioned sandboxes, credential proxy, egress policy and cost per task.
Prevent one product's misuse of a shared agent capability from degrading the platform for everyone.
A coding agent as a CI component for automated bug fixing.
Telemetry for your own coding agent that can never upload repositories or secrets.
The review and distribution pipeline for internal plugins that bundle skills and MCP servers.
Critique a hosted agent platform in which sandboxes hold customers' OAuth tokens as environment variables.

tracks.title: Coding rounds, work samples, behavioural and customer craft
tracks.brief: The formats 2026 loops actually use: hand-written ML code with invariants, progressive multi-stage coding (in-memory database, KV store, file system, credit ledger) and integration exercises, take-homes and build-and-defend work samples (Sierra's Plan, Build and Review), repository bug squash and PR review, AI-assisted rounds scored on verification, customer discovery, product sense and FDE decomposition with regulated and government constraints, project deep dives and paper presentations, and staff behavioural stories with a dated loop atlas. Company attributions are labelled official, candidate report or vendor, with dates, and reported exercises are taught with original material.

modules.title: Hand-written ML code
modules.brief: Invariants that hidden tests check, and backpropagation by hand as the reported rounds ask.

lessons.title: Hand-written ML code: the invariants hidden tests check
lessons.brief: Attention, samplers, BPE and losses written by hand are graded by invariants (masking, normalisation, numerical stability, equivalence of a cached decode to a full recompute), not by matching a reference. The lesson lists the invariants per algorithm and the online softmax normaliser that keeps long rows stable. The reader writes tests before code for each one.

existing.note: Cut the practical notes and the top-p predict; keep the invariants table without the junior rows and the online normaliser (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: Backpropagation by hand, as the rounds ask
lessons.brief: Reported OpenAI and Anthropic rounds ask for hand-derived backprop with a finite-difference check, a minimal reverse-mode autograd engine, and a linear-time prefix-product backward pass with zeros in the input. The lesson derives each with shapes and the check that proves it. The lab builds a scalar then matrix autograd engine in stdlib Python.

lessons.title: A small decoder with bugs, then a KV cache
lessons.brief: A reported OpenAI onsite hands over a small decoder-only transformer and its training step with four bugs, then asks for a KV cache whose logits match the full sequence. Defects worth testing for in code like this include mask direction, position offsets under caching, loss computed on padded positions and a shape that broadcasts silently. The lesson teaches the tests that find each one before reading the code, including KV cache size for a stated layer count, hidden size and context.

problems.brief: A KV-cache decode step for a toy decoder whose output equals the full recompute, with grouped-query heads.
AUC without a library, with ties handled; hidden tests compare against a brute-force pair count.
How many long requests fit in the KV cache of one GPU for a stated model and context mix?
A minimal reverse-mode autograd engine (add, mul, matmul, ReLU, sum) with broadcasting in the backward pass.
Prefix-product backward pass in linear time without division, when inputs may contain zeros.
A one-hidden-layer binary classifier with hand-derived backprop, stable cross-entropy and a finite-difference check.
Top-k decoding without a tensor library, then batched with a different k per row and a temperature per row.
problems.reported: Cohere (candidate report via aced.io, staff level)

modules.title: Progressive-spec and integration coding
modules.brief: Multi-stage coding where requirements arrive per stage, integration exercises against a mock service, and model-client patterns.

lessons.title: Progressive-spec coding: state that survives stage three
lessons.brief: Progressive rounds (an in-memory database, a KV store with transactions, a file system, a credit ledger) add a requirement per stage, and the candidate who designed state for stage one rewrites everything at stage three. The lesson covers choosing data structures that admit filtered scans, TTL with an injected clock, snapshots and restore, and the habit of writing the next stage's test first. Candidates report this format at Anthropic, OpenAI, Ramp and Perplexity; the lesson teaches the skill with original specifications.

existing.note: The lesson named the in-memory database and KV store rounds without drilling them; it now teaches the progressive format; the duplicated rate limiter moves to ai-collab-coding.

lessons.title: Integration rounds: multi-part API exercises
lessons.brief: Integration exercises unlock parts in order (paginate, collect auth headers while crawling, reconcile payments idempotently, handle retries and partial failure), and reports from Stripe say completing three of five parts can be enough. The lesson practises reading an unfamiliar API quickly and keeping each part's code shippable. The lab runs against a deterministic mock HTTP service in the browser.

lessons.title: Model-client patterns the coding rounds test
lessons.brief: Rounds that involve a model API test the same few patterns: classify errors before retrying, bound concurrency, parse streams incrementally, batch requests within a time window, and keep a provider pool healthy. The lesson writes each pattern once with tests. The reader can do any of them in 30 minutes.

problems.brief: In-memory database in four stages: set, get and delete; then filtered scans; then TTL with an injected clock; then backup and restore.
In-memory file system in stages: mkdir, touch and ls; then cd and relative paths; then move with conflict rules.
A KV store with set, begin, commit and abort; then nested transactions; then serialisation and restore.
A time-versioned KV store: get at a timestamp, then restore to a point in time, then compaction of old versions.
Parse a model token stream into text, tool calls and errors; hidden tests split events at awkward boundaries.
Run a model call over thousands of documents with retry classification, per-item isolation and a resumable checkpoint.
Escape the maze: crawl an HTTP service to the exit URL with robust error handling, then collect auth headers while crawling.

modules.title: Take-homes and work samples
modules.brief: Scoping a take-home and its report, and the build-and-defend format with a plan, a timed build and a review.

lessons.title: Scoping a take-home and writing the report reviewers want
lessons.brief: A take-home is graded on what was cut and why as much as on what was built, and the README and eval report are where that judgement is visible. The lesson covers scoping a three-to-four-hour brief, the eval report a reviewer reads first, and Anthropic's account of redesigning its performance take-home as models improved. The reader can finish a take-home and defend each omission.

existing.note: Debugging multi-file code moves to codebase-rounds; build-and-defend work samples are new.

lessons.title: Playbook: build-and-defend work samples
lessons.brief: Sierra's April 2026 loop removed coding and algorithm rounds and runs Plan (define a product), Build (two hours alone with any AI tools) and Review (demo, code review of the data model and abstractions, path to production and how AI was used); candidates report day-long builds at Cursor and few-hour builds at Cognition. The playbook covers scoping in the Plan, spending the Build so the Review has something to inspect, and the review questions reported at Cursor. It ends with a self-review rubric.

lessons.title: Notebook data rounds
lessons.brief: Some loops include a data-analysis round in a notebook, such as the reported Ramp round reconciling receipts with transactions, where the signal is how you check a matcher rather than how fast you write pandas. The lesson covers defining a match, measuring precision and recall on a labelled sample, and reporting what remains unmatched and why. The reader practises in a Pyodide notebook lab.

problems.brief: The three-hour RAG take-home: what you build, what you cut and what the report says, without hints naming the deliverables.
Long chats start failing with a 400 after a context change.
Plan a product in 30 minutes, build it in two hours with any AI tools, then answer the review questions on data model, abstractions, path to production and AI use.
A take-home on model APIs (a retrieval feature, a small agent or an eval harness) with a recorded walkthrough.
problems.reported: OpenAI (one candidate account via a vendor)

problems.brief: Review a submitted take-home: its eval report, its README and what its tests do not cover.
A customer-service agent for an outdoors company: pick two of five features, then name the metrics and dashboards you would want in production.
problems.reported: Sierra (candidate report via aced.io, about two years old)

modules.title: Bug squash, PR review and code comprehension
modules.brief: Rounds set in an existing multi-file codebase: fix seeded bugs, review a diff whose tests pass, and read code you did not write.

lessons.title: Bug squash in an unfamiliar library
lessons.brief: Bug-squash rounds hand over a real-looking library with a failing behaviour and expect a reproduction, a minimal fix and a test, under time pressure. Candidates report this at Stripe on open-source Python libraries and in the first phase of Meta's AI-enabled round. The lesson practises navigation, bisection and reproduction on original code.

lessons.title: PR review: tests pass, production breaks
lessons.brief: A PR review round gives a diff whose tests pass and asks what breaks on production data: freshness, nulls, unbounded memory, retries and cross-cutting effects. Candidates report it at Netflix, and Sierra is piloting a round with a medium-sized codebase and a draft PR from a colleague. The reader reviews against a list of production failure classes rather than style.

lessons.title: Reading code you did not write
lessons.brief: Google is piloting a Gemini-assisted code comprehension round for junior and mid-level roles, and Meta's AI-enabled round opens with understanding a multi-file problem. The lesson covers reading strategies (entry points, data flow, tests as specification) and using an assistant to read without trusting it. The reader can explain an unfamiliar module in ten minutes.

problems.brief: Bug squash in a multi-file Python package with three seeded bugs (a missing visitor method, an existence check that should be a file check, a resent request whose body stream was already consumed).
problems.reported: Stripe (candidate report via PracHub; exercises written fresh)

problems.brief: Review a feature-pipeline PR whose tests pass: what breaks in production, and what test would have caught each issue?
In a multi-file codebase: fix the bug, implement the feature, then optimise for larger test tiers.
A colleague's draft PR adds a cross-cutting feature to a medium-sized codebase: review it and improve it with a coding agent.
Implement a hash tree inside an existing repository, following its conventions and tests.
problems.reported: Cursor (candidate report via aced.io, entry level)

problems.brief: A 200-line data pipeline with at least two bugs, one of which only shows on the second run.

modules.title: AI-assisted rounds
modules.brief: Verification discipline when an assistant writes code, the dated policy reference per company and round, and directing a coding agent in a round.

lessons.title: Verification discipline when an assistant writes the code
lessons.brief: AI-assisted rounds score problem solving, code quality, verification and communication, and Meta's materials as summarised by a vendor say prompting is not the focus. Canva's write-up names failure patterns such as showcasing the AI, chasing features and going hands-off. The lesson teaches differential testing, diff reading and small steps, with the reader writing the tests that catch an assistant's plausible bug.

existing.note: The policy table becomes the dated policy-reference lesson; this lesson is the review and differential-testing discipline (level audit 5.1).

lessons.title: AI-use policies by company and round, dated
lessons.brief: Policies differ by company and by round: Anthropic defaults to no AI in live interviews and take-homes unless told otherwise, Amazon's quoted guidance bans it unless permitted, Meta replaced one onsite coding round with an AI-enabled one, Google's comprehension pilot is junior and mid only, and Sierra, Cognition, Shopify and Synthesia allow or expect it. Every row carries its source, its provenance label and its date. The page is reviewed quarterly.

lessons.title: Directing a coding agent inside a round
lessons.brief: When a round allows an agent, the signal is how you direct it: a plan before code, a check it must pass, and an independent review of what it produced. The lesson draws on Claude Code's best practices, MIT's 2026 agentic-coding exercises and Anthropic's account of a take-home where judgement about tooling was assessed. The reader practises narrating decisions while the agent works.

problems.brief: An AI-written rate limiter with a seeded race and a clock bug: write boundary tests with an injectable clock, then defend atomic check-and-update across servers and a store outage.
The assistant's cache passes its own tests: find the behaviour the tests never exercise.
Build a small distributed cache with an assistant in 60 minutes: decomposition, verification plan and the review of its output.
Add a TTL eviction policy to an existing cache module with an assistant, with tests that would catch an off-by-one in expiry.
What would you refuse to delegate to the assistant in an interview, and why?
Critique a transcript of a candidate using an assistant in a 60-minute round.

modules.title: Customer discovery, product sense and decomposition
modules.brief: Discovery as requirements engineering, the AI product-sense round, and FDE decomposition with regulated and government constraints.

lessons.title: Customer discovery as requirements engineering
lessons.brief: Discovery rounds score whether you find the evaluation criteria, past failed deployments, compliance, latency and residency constraints before proposing anything. The lesson practises reflecting back instead of pitching, and turning "it feels dumb" into a hypothesis and an experiment. The reader can run a 30-minute discovery with a sceptical stakeholder.

existing.note: Product sense and FDE decomposition become their own lessons.

lessons.title: The AI product-sense round
lessons.brief: Product-sense prompts reported for 2025 and 2026 include productising a capability, growing a metric with three engineers, and "when should you not use an LLM", and Meta reportedly runs a round where candidates prototype with an AI tool. Because outputs are probabilistic, the structure adds the failure the user cannot detect, the success metric with guardrails, cost per outcome and the eval plan before launch. Every company attribution is secondhand and is labelled so on the page.

lessons.title: Playbook: FDE decomposition with deployment constraints
lessons.brief: A vague enterprise brief becomes scope, a success metric, a data-access plan, a hosting choice, compliance questions and a two-week plan. A reported Anthropic question asks how the design changes for a regulated-industry customer and then for a government contractor, and decomposition prompts such as "the dashboard is wrong but they cannot say which number" are reported for FDE loops. The playbook works both and ends with the measurable pilot.

problems.brief: "The bot feels dumb": turn the complaint into hypotheses, an experiment and a decision.
The sceptical CTO role-play: discovery with a stakeholder who has seen two failed AI pilots.
A regulated-industry customer wants to use the Claude API: design the implementation, then say what changes for a government contractor.
You have text-to-music capability: how would you productise it?
problems.reported: OpenAI (aggregated candidate reports via a vendor)

problems.brief: Double image creation with only three engineers: what you build, what you measure and what you refuse.
A customer says their dashboard is wrong and cannot tell you which number: what do you do in the first hour?
A hospital has patient records in six systems that do not talk to each other: give a nurse one view.

modules.title: Deep dives, presentations and quizzes
modules.brief: Project deep dives with their probe list, paper presentations at staff level, and rapid-fire research quizzes.

lessons.title: Playbook: the project deep dive and presentation
lessons.brief: Deep dives probe alternatives considered, your part versus the team's, the measured result and what you would undo, and formats range from a 30-minute presentation (reported at OpenAI) to a five-minute recorded walkthrough (Cognition) and a short technical talk (Sierra). Synthesia's published staff loop includes a delivery and impact deep dive. The playbook gives a structure and the probe list to rehearse against.

lessons.title: Presenting a paper at staff level
lessons.brief: A reported Cohere staff loop asks candidates to present a paper from a provided list, and the round tests whether you can state the problem, the mechanism, the evidence and its limits, and what changed in practice. The lesson gives a 20-minute structure and the questions that separate reading a paper from understanding it. The reader rehearses with one of the paper walkthroughs on this site.

lessons.title: Rapid-fire research-engineer quizzes
lessons.brief: Some research-engineer loops include rapid-fire maths, statistics, CS and ML questions with a follow-up asking for intuition, such as why L1 gradients produce sparsity; the DeepMind report is from 2021 and labelled as old. The lesson builds timed cards with a typed answer and an intuition follow-up. It uses the site's numbers-to-know cards for review.

problems.brief: Present a paper from a provided list in 20 minutes and defend it against the probe list.
problems.reported: Cohere (candidate report via aced.io, staff level)

problems.brief: A 30-minute project presentation, then the probes: alternatives, your part, the measured result, what you would undo.
problems.reported: OpenAI (aggregated candidate reports via Hello Interview)

problems.brief: A five-minute recorded walkthrough of a take-home that a reviewer watches before the call.
An ML screen where the interviewer adds a constraint after each answer, ending with the intuition behind L1 sparsity.
Why did you use machine learning on this problem, how did you know it was the right use case, and did people adopt it?
A five-to-ten-minute technical talk followed by questions on the trade-offs you skipped.
problems.reported: Sierra (candidate report via aced.io, about two years old)

modules.title: Staff behavioural stories and the loop atlas
modules.brief: Staff-level stories with influence and risk, the dated atlas of loops per role family, and values rounds at labs.

lessons.title: Staff behavioural stories
lessons.brief: Staff stories show ownership, alternatives considered, measured impact and influence across teams, and reported prompts include release criteria for a new model, an ethical concern raised under pressure and whether people adopted what you built. The lesson builds three versions of each story (two minutes, five minutes, deep dive) without explaining STAR. The reader prepares stories for the prompts below and rehearses the pushback.

existing.note: The four-company loop table becomes the loop-atlas playbook; stories become staff-level.

lessons.title: Playbook: the 2026 loop atlas
lessons.brief: One page per role family (applied AI and FDE, research engineer, ML infra, AI security, software engineer at AI companies) shows rounds, the AI policy per round and level signals, with every row labelled official, press, candidate or vendor and a last-checked date. Sources range from Sierra's and Anthropic's own pages to candidate reports, and synthesised question banks are never used for company tags. The playbook ends with how to choose which loops to practise for.

lessons.title: Values and mission rounds at AI labs
lessons.brief: Values rounds at labs ask how you think about safety trade-offs, ambiguity and disagreement, and expect specific examples rather than positions. The lesson uses the labs' own published material (careers pages, interview guides, scaling policies) to show what each says it values. The reader prepares answers that are specific, honest and defensible.

playbooks.title: Playbook: fine-tune the embedder, add a reranker, or change the chunks
playbooks.decision: When retrieval fails on a domain, three levers compete for the same budget and each fixes a different failure.

playbooks.title: Playbook: migrate to a new model version or hold
playbooks.decision: A new model version arrives with a retirement deadline for the old one (Anthropic gives at least 60 days of notice), so holding is also a decision with a date.

playbooks.title: Playbook: framework, agent SDK or plain code
playbooks.decision: The decision is which abstractions you are willing to debug at 2 a.m.

playbooks.title: Playbook: human, code check or judge
playbooks.decision: Each check type has a cost per item and an error profile, and the cheapest check that catches the failure wins.

playbooks.title: Playbook: workflow or agent
playbooks.decision: The decision is who owns control flow for each step: code, or the model.

playbooks.title: Playbook: cost and latency budgets per step
playbooks.decision: Per-run caps exist on most platforms; per-step budgets are what keep one slow or expensive step from eating the run.

playbooks.title: Playbook: low-code tools versus code
playbooks.decision: n8n, Dify, Flowise and Zapier Agents are chosen on durability, testing, versioning, review, tenancy and licence, not on taste.

playbooks.title: Playbook: OCR pipeline, VLM parsing or page-image retrieval
playbooks.decision: Documents can be parsed to text, parsed by a vision-language model, or retrieved as page images, and each route has different failure modes and costs.

playbooks.title: Playbook: filtered vector search
playbooks.decision: Pre-filtering, post-filtering, filter-aware traversal, iterative scans and per-tenant partitions fail at different selectivities.

playbooks.title: Playbook: bash-only or specialised tools
playbooks.decision: A coding agent can run on bash alone (mini-swe-agent), on bash plus a string-replace editor (the two tools in the Claude 4 SWE-bench scaffold), on a broad built-in set (Claude Code), or with code as the action space.

playbooks.title: Playbook: CLAUDE.md, skill, rule, hook, sub-agent or MCP server
playbooks.decision: The decision is where a piece of knowledge or policy lives, and the inputs are whether it applies to every task, whether it is a procedure, whether it must be enforced and what it costs in context every turn.

playbooks.title: Playbook: cost and runaway controls
playbooks.decision: Turn caps, dollar caps, auto-mode fallbacks after repeated denials, a cap on consecutive Stop-hook blocks and per-instance budgets each stop a different runaway.

playbooks.title: Playbook: shipping a harness change safely
playbooks.decision: Anthropic's April 2026 postmortem describes three harness changes (a lower default effort, a thinking-clearing bug that also caused cache misses, and a verbosity line that cost 3% on a broad eval) that each passed review, tests or dogfooding.

playbooks.title: Playbook: choose the defence pattern for the task
playbooks.decision: The decision is which pattern and which rate-lowering layers a given agent gets, and the inputs are the trifecta legs present, whether actions are reversible, and the residual rate the business accepts in writing.

playbooks.title: Playbook: from threat model to tests on one agent
playbooks.decision: An email and calendar assistant with a send tool and a fetch tool is taken through five artefacts: a data-flow diagram, a per-session capability table scored on the Rule of Two and the lethal trifecta, an architecture change that removes one leg per session, a control per boundary labelled as holding by construction or lowering a rate, and a test per control.

playbooks.title: Playbook: choosing an isolation boundary for agent code execution
playbooks.decision: seccomp filters system calls and the kernel docs say it is not a sandbox on its own; Landlock lets unprivileged processes restrict their own filesystem and network access; containers share the host kernel, as runc's CVE-2024-21626 escape shows; gVisor implements the Linux interface in user space at a compatibility and per-syscall cost; Firecracker microVMs boot to guest init within 125 ms under its stated test conditions and do no network filtering of their own.

playbooks.title: Playbook: incident response for AI features
playbooks.decision: The CoSAI framework aligns with NIST SP 800-61 Rev.

playbooks.title: Playbook: running a red-team programme
playbooks.decision: A programme defines scope, threat actors, adaptive attackers as the default, what counts as a finding, severity, regression capture and disclosure.

playbooks.title: Playbook: SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 42001 for an AI feature
playbooks.decision: As of the CSA note of 30 August 2026 there are no AI-specific SOC 2 trust services criteria, so auditors map AI controls onto existing criteria and requests vary by firm; ISO/IEC 42001 certifies a management system, not a model.

playbooks.title: Playbook: shrinking the KV cache
playbooks.decision: Four families fail differently: architectural (GQA, MQA, MLA, hybrid linear layers, fixed at training time), eviction (H2O, SnapKV), quantisation (KIVI at 2 bits with keys per channel and values per token) and top-k sparse attention (DeepSeek's DSA).

playbooks.title: Playbook: prompt registry and release mechanics
playbooks.decision: A prompt is a deployable artefact with a version, an owner, a test suite and a rollout, and in Langfuse's model every edit is an immutable version fetched by a label that rollback simply moves.

playbooks.title: Playbook: the release ladder with numbers
playbooks.decision: Offline gate, shadow, canary, A/B and full rollout each have an entry condition, a measurement, a cost and an exit rule, and only the A/B test measures outcome metrics causally.

playbooks.title: Playbook: feedback loops that do not train sycophancy
playbooks.decision: Explicit feedback (thumbs, regenerate) and implicit feedback (accept, edit, abandon, escalate) are filters for which traces to read, not metrics or rewards without controls.

playbooks.title: Playbook: should we fine-tune?
playbooks.decision: Fine-tuning fixes format, style, narrow skills and cost; it loses to retrieval for knowledge (Ovadia et al.), and fine-tuning on facts the model does not know raises hallucination as those examples are learned (Gekhman et al.).

playbooks.title: Playbook: build versus buy
playbooks.decision: Three decisions get blurred: buy an AI product or build the feature, call an API or self-host weights, and train or adapt.

playbooks.title: Playbook: model selection and licence clauses
playbooks.decision: Selection is evals plus constraints, and the constraints include licence clauses: Llama 4's licence requires a separate licence above 700 million monthly active users, attribution and Llama-prefixed names for derivatives, while Gemma's terms reserve the right to restrict use and Apache 2.0 or MIT models carry no such clauses.

playbooks.title: Playbook: AI strategy for a company
playbooks.decision: Staff questions are about portfolio, platform and risk rather than prompts: which use cases first, which primitives to share, who decides, and what leadership will measure.

playbooks.title: Playbook: size the run
playbooks.decision: The inputs are target quality, expected inference volume, GPU count and type, and the deadline; the options are compute-optimal dense, inference-optimal smaller and longer, or MoE at a chosen sparsity.

playbooks.title: Playbook: profiling a kernel like an experiment
playbooks.decision: Profiling is an experiment: baseline, controlled changes, variance reduction, stop criteria, attribution and a correctness gate.

playbooks.title: Playbook: composing 4D and 5D parallelism
playbooks.decision: The order of decisions is fit one replica, reach the global batch, then maximise throughput, with TP inside nodes and PP or ZeRO-3 across them, and PP and ZeRO-3 rarely together.

playbooks.title: Playbook: not enough high-quality tokens
playbooks.decision: After aggressive filtering the options are relaxing filters, repeating epochs, rephrasing, synthesising or distilling, each with a cost and a risk.

playbooks.title: Playbook: what an image, a page, a second of video and of audio cost
playbooks.decision: Claude counts one visual token per 28-pixel patch with caps by tier, OpenAI's patch models count 32-pixel patches with a multiplier and its tile models charge a base plus a cost per 512-pixel tile, and Gemini charges 258 tokens per small image or per 768-pixel tile, 32 tokens per second of audio and documents video at more than one rate.

playbooks.title: Playbook: cascaded pipeline or speech-to-speech
playbooks.decision: A cascaded ASR, LLM and TTS pipeline gives control, tool use and logging per stage, while speech-to-speech models give lower latency and prosody at the cost of observability and per-minute pricing.

playbooks.title: Playbook: build-and-defend work samples
playbooks.decision: Sierra's April 2026 loop removed coding and algorithm rounds and runs Plan (define a product), Build (two hours alone with any AI tools) and Review (demo, code review of the data model and abstractions, path to production and how AI was used); candidates report day-long builds at Cursor and few-hour builds at Cognition.

playbooks.title: Playbook: FDE decomposition with deployment constraints
playbooks.decision: A vague enterprise brief becomes scope, a success metric, a data-access plan, a hosting choice, compliance questions and a two-week plan.

playbooks.title: Playbook: the project deep dive and presentation
playbooks.decision: Deep dives probe alternatives considered, your part versus the team's, the measured result and what you would undo, and formats range from a 30-minute presentation (reported at OpenAI) to a five-minute recorded walkthrough (Cognition) and a short technical talk (Sierra).

playbooks.title: Playbook: the 2026 loop atlas
playbooks.decision: One page per role family (applied AI and FDE, research engineer, ML infra, AI security, software engineer at AI companies) shows rounds, the AI policy per round and level signals, with every row labelled official, press, candidate or vendor and a last-checked date.

papers.title: FlashAttention 1 to 3: exact attention bounded by memory traffic
papers.why: FlashAttention is exact and does more arithmetic than the naive kernel, and wins by tiling in on-chip memory and recomputing in the backward pass to cut HBM reads. FlashAttention-2 reports 50 to 73% of A100 peak and FlashAttention-3 adds Hopper warp specialisation and FP8 with block quantisation. What changed in practice is that attention cost discussions must be about IO, and the walkthrough ends with what to say when asked whether it is an approximation.

papers.title: Sagas and compensation for steps that cannot be undone
papers.why: Garcia-Molina and Salem split a long-lived transaction into steps with compensating actions so partial progress can be undone without holding locks. Model-driven workflows call external systems that share no transaction, and some actions (an email, a payout) can only be compensated or gated before they happen. The walkthrough covers forward and backward recovery, compensation order, and what to say when a step has no compensation: put the approval before it.

papers.title: Late interaction, walked through
papers.why: ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim, and the storage blow-up is what decides whether late interaction is affordable. ColBERTv2 cuts the footprint with residual compression, PLAID cuts search latency, and MUVERA reduces multi-vector search to single-vector MIPS. The walkthrough ends with the storage arithmetic for a stated corpus and what to say when asked whether late interaction is worth it.

papers.title: MAST: why multi-agent systems fail
papers.why: MAST classifies multi-agent failures into specification, inter-agent misalignment and verification failures from annotated traces. Most failures it records are design failures rather than model errors, which is why adding agents rarely fixes them. The walkthrough ends with coding a set of traces against the taxonomy.

papers.title: SWE-agent and the agent-computer interface
papers.why: SWE-agent treats the model as a new kind of user that needs purpose-built interfaces: search capped at 50 results, a 100-line file viewer, an edit command guarded by a linter, old observations collapsed, and a $4 per-instance budget. Its ablations on SWE-bench Lite with GPT-4 Turbo are the payload: 18.0% with the full interface, 15.0% without the linter, 10.3% with no edit command, and lower scores with a 30-line window or the whole file. What to say in an interview is which of these choices still matter with stronger models and how you would measure it.

papers.title: The minimal harness: mini-swe-agent, CodeAct and Agentless
papers.why: mini-swe-agent is about 100 lines for the agent class, uses only bash with linear history, and runs each action as an independent subprocess, which makes swapping in a container trivial. CodeAct argues for code as the action space and Agentless replaces the loop with a fixed localise, repair and validate pipeline. The interview point is how much harness a strong model needs and what you lose by deleting it, with the caveat that scores across these papers use different models.

papers.title: Context resets versus compaction
papers.why: Anthropic's 2026-03-24 harness-design post found Sonnet 4.5 wrapping up early as it neared its believed limit, which made full resets with a structured handoff necessary; with Opus 4.5 the resets were dropped and automatic compaction was enough. The general lesson is that harness components encode assumptions about one model and must be re-tested per model. The walkthrough ends with how you would detect such an assumption before it ships.

papers.title: Classifiers as approvers: Claude Code auto mode and its peers
papers.why: Anthropic's auto-mode post reports a two-stage classifier that sees user messages and tool calls with tool results stripped, a 0.4% false-positive rate on 10,000 real actions, and a 17% false-negative rate on 52 real overeager actions, and calls it not a drop-in replacement for careful review on high-stakes infrastructure. Cursor says its Auto-review is not a security boundary and Codex auto-review never widens the sandbox. The walkthrough ends with what you put around an approver that misses one dangerous action in six.

papers.title: Generator and evaluator agents
papers.why: Anthropic's 2026-03-24 harness post found self-evaluation lenient and Claude a poor QA agent out of the box, then built a separate evaluator with few-shot score breakdowns, Playwright against the running app and hard thresholds per criterion. Sprint contracts were negotiated in files, and the planner and evaluator survived after a newer model made sprints unnecessary. The walkthrough ends with how you would know your evaluator is stricter than your generator.

papers.title: Parallel attempts and test-time scaling
papers.why: Large Language Monkeys raised SWE-bench Lite coverage from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250, and found voting and reward models plateau without automatic verifiers. Claude 4's parallel test-time compute sampled attempts, discarded patches that failed visible tests and picked with a scoring model, lifting Opus 4 from 72.5% to 79.4%. The point is that selection needs a verifier and that high-compute numbers are a different quantity from pass@1.

papers.title: Parallel agents without an orchestrator
papers.why: The C compiler build ran 16 Claude instances in containers against a bare git upstream, claimed tasks with lock files resolved by git conflicts and used no orchestration agent, with specialised roles for dedupe, performance and docs. The walkthrough compares it with Claude Code worktrees and batch fan-out into separate PRs, and with Cognition's argument against splitting context. What to say in an interview is which coordination primitive you would trust and why.

papers.title: Six design patterns for securing agents
papers.why: The design-patterns paper gives action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute and context-minimisation, each trading a specific utility for a specific guarantee. The walkthrough builds a toy executor per pattern and shows which attack each one stops. What to say in an interview is the utility you gave up and why it was acceptable.

papers.title: Data poisoning and backdoors
papers.why: Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that 250 poisoned documents backdoored models from 600M to 13B parameters with a denial-of-service trigger, while 100 were not enough, and the authors caution that the backdoor was narrow and low-stakes. Sleeper Agents found backdoors persisting through SFT, RL and adversarial training. The walkthrough ends with what this means for training on scraped or user data and what to say when asked how much poisoned data is needed.

papers.title: GEPA: reflective prompt evolution
papers.why: GEPA reports beating GRPO by 6% on average and up to 20% with up to 35 times fewer rollouts across six tasks, and beating MIPROv2 by over 10%, all as the authors' own results. The mechanism is natural-language reflection on full trajectories plus a Pareto frontier of candidates that each win on some example. The walkthrough ends with the DSPy usage, where the metric must return feedback text, and with the conditions a reviewer should attach to the headline.

papers.title: LoRA learns less and forgets less
papers.why: Biderman et al. found LoRA substantially underperforms full fine-tuning on code and maths in standard low-rank settings while forgetting less, and that full fine-tuning learns perturbations of 10 to 100 times higher rank. Read with LoRA Without Regret, the conditions are clear: LoRA matches full fine-tuning on small and medium SFT and RL when applied to all layers with a higher learning rate. The walkthrough ends with how to answer "LoRA or full fine-tune?" with conditions instead of a slogan.

papers.title: Fine-tuning on new knowledge encourages hallucinations
papers.why: Gekhman et al. found that examples introducing knowledge the model lacks are learned more slowly and, once learned, increase hallucination roughly linearly. This is why "fine-tune it on our docs" is the wrong tool for facts that change, and why retrieval wins for knowledge. The walkthrough ends with how to explain this to a product manager in two minutes.

papers.title: Chinchilla, replicated
papers.why: Besiroglu et al. found Chinchilla's parametric fit does not fit the extracted data, its intervals are implausibly narrow, and a re-fit agrees with the paper's other two methods. The walkthrough covers what that means for the 20x rule and for anyone extrapolating from small runs. It ends with the interview answer to "how sure are you about 20 tokens per parameter".

papers.title: FP8 training as DeepSeek-V3 did it
papers.why: DeepSeek-V3 ran FP8 GEMMs for forward and both backward passes with 1x128 activation tiles, 128x128 weight blocks and promotion to FP32 every 128 elements, kept embeddings, the output head, gating, norms and attention in higher precision, and reported relative loss error under 0.25% against BF16. The walkthrough compares per-tensor scaling with E4M3 and E5M2 formats. It ends with what "we trained in FP8" should make an interviewer ask.

papers.title: Sparsity as a design knob
papers.why: Kimi K2 fit a sparsity scaling law and chose 384 experts with 8 active, reporting fewer FLOPs than lower sparsity at the same validation loss, and kept 64 attention heads because doubling them would add substantial inference FLOPs at long context. The walkthrough reads the paper as a set of trade-offs between training and serving cost. It ends with what you would ask before copying the configuration.

papers.title: The GRPO family: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO and GSPO
papers.why: GRPO uses group-relative advantages, so a group where every sample is correct contributes zero gradient; Dr. GRPO removes a length bias; DAPO adds clip-higher, dynamic sampling, token-level loss and overlong shaping and drops the KL term, reaching 50 on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B in half the steps of the R1-Zero baseline; GSPO moves to a sequence-level ratio for MoE stability. TRL's current defaults encode several of these choices (no KL term, a DAPO loss type). The walkthrough ends with which choice you would make for a stated task and why.

papers.title: YaRN, walked through
papers.why: Position Interpolation left high-frequency dimensions with too little local resolution, and YaRN answers with a per-frequency ramp and an attention temperature term. gpt-oss extends dense layers to 131,072 tokens with YaRN and Qwen3 documents a factor-4 YaRN block. The walkthrough ends with the answer to "why not just raise the base".

papers.title: Attention sinks and streaming
papers.why: StreamingLLM showed window attention collapses once the first tokens are evicted because heads park attention on them even when they are not semantically important, and keeping those few KV entries restores quality over very long streams. gpt-oss builds the idea into the model with a learned per-head bias in the softmax denominator. The engineering consequence is that any KV eviction policy must pin the sink tokens.

papers.title: Multi-head latent attention and the KV bytes table
papers.why: DeepSeek-V2 compresses keys and values into a shared latent, caches the latent and keeps a small decoupled RoPE key because rotation does not commute with the absorbed projection. It reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache against DeepSeek 67B, a dense multi-head model, which is why the baseline must be stated whenever the figure is used. The walkthrough computes bytes per token for MHA, GQA-8 and MLA from published configs.

papers.title: Diffusion transformers, walked through
papers.why: DiT replaces the U-Net in latent diffusion with a transformer over latent patches and reports FID 2.27 on ImageNet 256, with quality improving as compute per image grows. Stable Diffusion 3 extends the idea with separate weights per modality and rectified flow. The walkthrough ends with what the move to transformers changed for serving (batching, parallelism, the same kernels as language models) and what to say when asked to explain a recent generation paper.

formats.name: Progressive build lab with tests
formats.what: One program grown over 5 to 10 steps; each step adds a capability and its tests; the next unlocks when tests pass.
formats.why: Forces production rather than recognition and is spaced by construction; CodeCrafters and Exercism use tests as the definition of done.
formats.feasibility: Feasible now. Needs LabRunner, a deterministic mock LLM module loaded by the Pyodide worker, the Emscripten in-memory filesystem for multi-file labs, and persisted code per lab. Timeouts use worker terminate-and-restart because interrupts need cross-origin isolation, which breaks the sign-in popup. Tests must check behaviour, never internal names: OpenAI found at least 59.4% of an audited SWE-bench Verified subset rejected correct solutions.

formats.name: Teardown of a real system with an annotated trace
formats.what: One page per named system from public sources: what it is, a diagram, one request traced, context strategy, permissions, cost, failure modes, and what is not public.
formats.why: The SRE book's "reverse engineering a production service" class in reading form; design rounds probe how real systems made trade-offs.
formats.feasibility: Feasible. Needs Diagram and Trace components and one trace JSON format close to the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions so teardowns, replays and trace problems share data; the validator should require a "not public" section.

formats.name: Incident replay
formats.what: The reader steps through a recorded timeline and commits to a hypothesis at marked checkpoints before the next event appears; the reveal is the operator's published postmortem.
formats.why: Google SRE's Wheel of Misfortune re-enacts postmortems; it trains diagnosis under ambiguity, which debug rounds test.
formats.feasibility: Feasible as an extension of AgentTrace with a hypothesis pick per checkpoint (gradable) and free text (local only). Every event carries its source URL. The Replit database-deletion replay waits until both primary accounts are read.

formats.name: Design critique
formats.what: A flawed artefact (design, config, prompt, tool list, code) with planted flaws; the reader lists flaws in free text, then ticks a checklist.
formats.why: Review is how senior engineers spend their time; writing before seeing the checklist is short-answer retrieval with feedback.
formats.feasibility: Feasible now with the checklist component in SPEC; show the number of planted flaws up front; every checklist item cites a source.

formats.name: Workflow design with a checklist and an optional simulator
formats.what: A business process plus constraints; the reader designs steps, state, retries, idempotency, approvals, budgets and rollout, then checks against a checklist.
formats.why: This is the form in which "build an AI workflow" is asked in loops.
formats.feasibility: Checklist grading is feasible now. The optional simulator needs a JSON workflow schema and a TypeScript interpreter with fault injection (a tool 500, a timeout, a duplicate delivery), which turns part of the self-rating into a graded result.

formats.name: Timed mock loop
formats.what: A seeded, timed run of problems shaped like a real loop per role preset, ending in a self-graded summary.
formats.why: Time pressure and switching between round types are what full mocks add; the evidence on mocks is observational, so no pass-rate claims.
formats.feasibility: Feasible once the bank fills the presets: the ML-infra and research-engineer presets need the training track, the security preset needs the security track, and the behavioural slot needs at least 12 behavioural problems (this plan has more). Each preset in loops.ts cites its source and carries an AI-allowed flag per slot.

formats.name: Paper walkthrough with a runnable number
formats.what: Problem, mechanism in engineering terms, the key number, a Pyodide cell that reproduces a toy version of it, what changed in practice, and what to say in an interview.
formats.why: Reproducing the number is production; reading the abstract is not.
formats.feasibility: Feasible; state the paper's licence before reproducing any figure.

formats.name: Annotated code reading
formats.what: A permissively licensed file with margin notes; the reader answers "what happens if" questions about lines before notes reveal.
formats.why: Developers read more code than they write and are rarely taught to read it (Code Reading Club).
formats.feasibility: Feasible with a code viewer with line anchors; pin a commit hash and show licence and copyright beside every excerpt; no excerpts from unlicensed repositories.

formats.name: Numbers-to-know cards with FSRS
formats.what: One fact per card with a source, a date checked and an expiry; typed recall; the scheduler reviews cards, not lessons.
formats.why: Spaced, typed retrieval is the best-supported technique for retention; Anki and Execute Program review small items.
formats.feasibility: Needs a cards collection with source, checked and expires fields, FSRS state per item (ts-fsrs, MIT), a progress-shape change and a Firestore rules change, and a stale-card report in validate-content.

formats.name: Decision playbook
formats.what: The decision, the inputs that change it, options with the conditions under which each wins, a worked case and what to measure after.
formats.why: Staff rounds probe judgement under constraints; playbooks give the structure that critiques and workflow problems then test.
formats.feasibility: Feasible now with the playbook skeleton in SPEC; each playbook links to at least one critique and one workflow problem.

formats.name: Dated "what changed" pages
formats.what: One page per quarter listing changes with a date, a status (draft, current, deprecated, removed) and the lessons each change affects.
formats.why: Interviewers ask about current practice and the field moves faster than lessons; MDN Baseline is a working model of a dated status.
formats.feasibility: Needs a changes collection and a build check that flags lessons older than an affecting change.

formats.name: Predict, explain the gap, then reveal
formats.what: Keep Predict blocks, then ask for one sentence on why the guess was off before the explanation shows.
formats.why: Prediction with self-explanation improved recall (Kim et al.), and short answers with feedback beat recognition (Kang et al.).
formats.feasibility: Feasible: a text box in Predict stored locally and never sent anywhere. Predictions must be derivable from inputs on the page, not recall of a vendor figure.

formats.name: Problem-first module order
formats.what: Each module opens with one problem the reader attempts before the lessons, then teaches, then returns to it.
formats.why: Problem solving before instruction beat instruction first for adults in a meta-analysis of 53 studies (Hedges' g 0.36), and guidance that helps novices can stop helping experts.
formats.feasibility: Feasible as a module-page change: mark one problem per module as the opener.

formats.name: Short-answer recall before reveal
formats.what: Concept and design problems ask for a typed answer before the worked answer and checklist appear.
formats.why: A short-answer quiz with feedback beat MCQ and re-reading three days later; MCQ without feedback did not beat re-reading.
formats.feasibility: Feasible with a local text box; self-rated from the checklist; never counted as graded.

formats.what: One coding problem with three or four stages, each adding requirements and hidden tests, with a visible clock.
formats.why: This is the dominant 2026 coding format reported at Anthropic, OpenAI, Ramp and Perplexity.
formats.feasibility: Feasible in Pyodide with stage-gated hidden tests; counts as gradable per stage.

formats.name: Repository problems
formats.what: A multi-file package with seeded bugs or a diff to review.
formats.why: Bug squash, PR review and code comprehension rounds are reported at Stripe, Netflix, Meta, Sierra and Google.
formats.feasibility: Feasible with the Emscripten in-memory filesystem and a file tree view; fix problems are graded by hidden behaviour tests, review problems by checklist.

formats.name: Timed work samples
formats.what: A brief, a planning window, a timed build with any tools the reader chooses, then review questions.
formats.why: Sierra, Cursor and Cognition run build-and-defend loops; the review is where seniority shows.
formats.feasibility: Feasible as a timed page with a rubric checklist; the build happens in the reader's own environment; self-rated only.

formats.name: Presentations and deep dives
formats.what: A prepared talk or project walkthrough followed by a probe list the reader answers aloud or in writing.
formats.why: Project presentations, paper presentations and short recorded walkthroughs are reported at OpenAI, Cohere, Cognition and Sierra.
formats.feasibility: Feasible as a probe list with a timer; any recording stays on the reader's device; self-rated.

formats.name: Follow-up chains
formats.what: The interviewer adds a constraint after each answer; the reader answers each stage before the next constraint appears.
formats.why: DeepMind ML screens and OpenAI design rounds are reported to add constraints mid-conversation.
formats.feasibility: Feasible as a staged reveal inside existing design and concept problems; self-rated per stage.

formats.what: A scripted policy keyed on the last message, with fault modes (malformed tool call, refusal, loop), shipped as a Python module the worker loads.

formats.feasibility: Feasible; one module shared by all labs; outputs deterministic so tests are stable.

levelBar.rule: The reader is a senior or staff software engineer who has shipped production systems and called a model API in production at least once.

Never define or explain by analogy: queues, backpressure, idempotency keys, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, token buckets, caches and cache keys, consistent hashing, Little's law, percentiles, head-of-line blocking, at-least-once versus exactly-once delivery.

Never define: indexes and query plans, inverted indexes, ACLs and row-level security, transactions, tombstones, schema migration, HTTP status semantics, SSE and WebSockets, OAuth bearer tokens and audience, JSON Schema, pagination.

Never define: unit, integration, property-based, differential and replay tests, fixtures, canaries, shadow traffic, A/B assignment by stable hash, base rates, precision and recall, confidence intervals, paired versus unpaired comparisons, the binomial distribution, p-values.

Never define: floating-point non-associativity, memory bandwidth versus FLOPs, GiB versus GB, or ML vocabulary at the definitional level (token, embedding, cosine similarity, attention, softmax, temperature, fine-tuning, loss). Teach how these are implemented and what they cost.
Never explain interview mechanics (what a design round or take-home is, STAR, clarifying before drawing).
If a sentence would be removed from a design document written for a staff engineer on the team, remove it from the lesson.
Open on the decision or mechanism, not on a scenario about a junior engineer. At most one scenario per track, and only a real public incident with a source.
Name the systems analogy in a clause and move on to the difference; never explain the analogy's source.
Spend words on what the reader lacks: published numbers with their conditions, what changed in the last 18 months and why, failure modes seen in production, and the decision procedure.
Every Predict block asks for a number the reader can derive from inputs on the page (a KV size, a p-value, a break-even), never recall of a vendor percentage.
Carry one "In the room" question at staff level: a decision under at least two conflicting constraints with a deadline or budget, and a follow-up that pushes back.
Keep "When this is wrong"; it is the most senior section of a lesson.
No coaching sentences: nothing tells the reader what to say first, what interviewers hear, or what loses the question.
Modules open with a problem the reader attempts before the first lesson (problem-first order), because guidance that helps novices can stop helping experts.
Every hard or staff problem has a decision with at least two defensible answers, each with a stated cost; if only one answer is defensible the problem is medium at most.
At least one quantity is chosen and defended by the reader, not given; the answer states which choices are reasonable.
Include a constraint conflict: latency against correctness, cost against recall, autonomy against safety, a deadline against measured regressions, or labelling budget against coverage.
State a failure mode of the recommended answer inside the answer, not only as a follow-up.
Hints are questions to ask the interviewer or measurements to request, never the mechanism or the formula; delete any hint that lets a reader without the knowledge answer.
At most one easy problem per module; easy items are warm-ups or the first stage of a chain, never Core 100 by default.
The defect is not on a commented line, not the only changed line, and not named in the title or subtitle.
The evidence is incomplete; the strong answer says what it would collect and what it would do without it.
At least one red herring is a real but secondary defect, so the reader ranks rather than identifies.
Hidden property or invariant tests in addition to visible examples; visible tests never enumerate every rule.
Leave at least one interface or policy decision to the reader (eviction, preemption order, tie-break) and test invariants, not one canonical output.
Include a performance or memory constraint that a naive solution fails, within Pyodide's standard library.
End with a follow-up on what changes to run the code in a real engine or client.
The reader chooses at least one assumption and the accepted band admits reasonable choices; the answer says which choices are unreasonable and why.
The answer names the dominant term and the assumption that flips the conclusion.
Published inputs carry source and date; scenario inputs are labelled as scenario.
Include an operating constraint: team size, deadline, an existing system that cannot be rewritten, a regulator, a budget, or a stakeholder who disagrees.
The answer includes a "what you give up" statement and something written down: a risk note, a rollout plan with rollback triggers, or a decision memo.
No rubric paragraph; the rubric is a checklist the reader ticks.
The flawed artefact is realistic enough that a reviewer could have approved it; at least two flaws are ones a senior reviewer misses on first read.
The checklist has 6 to 12 items, including at least one judgement call where the right answer is "acceptable if".
Each hard or staff problem carries at least three staff follow-ups, at least one pushback on the answer and one reversal condition.
Pushback shape: "Your verification costs three times the feature; which half do you cut, and what risk do you accept in writing?"
Reversal shape: "What would you need to see in production to reverse this decision?" or "Two senior engineers disagree; how do you decide without deciding by rank?"
Operating shape: "You have sixty days before the model is retired and twelve of forty prompts regress; which ship degraded, and who signs off?"
Retire the generic template ("How would you verify it? How does it fail? What is the alternative?") unless each is made specific.
All options within 20 percent of the longest option's length; the correct option must not be reliably the longest or the conditional one.
Every wrong option is something a senior engineer has believed; no filler options.
At most one option describes a superseded version of a spec or product.
Debug problems with choices include at least two real defects; the stem asks which explains the observed symptom.
Never state in the stem the fact that makes the answer obvious.
Analogy preambles ("You already know", "You have used", "If you have written", "Think of a", "You have sat").
Scripted first sentences, "what interviewers hear", and grading commentary inside answers ("the strongest answers", "listening for", "separates senior answers", "the interviewer is checking").
Definition by appositive, rhetorical headings and hints, one-word follow-ups ("Ship? No."), the identical "Scenario, not a real company" opener, and trivia predictions.

Every number is measured, sourced with a URL and the date checked, or computed in front of the reader; vendor-measured numbers are labelled as the vendor's own; abstract figures are "the paper reports".

Company tags only from a public source naming the company and topic, labelled official, press, candidate report or vendor with a date; synthesised question banks never tag a company; reported exercises are taught with original material.
Version-sensitive facts (SDK defaults, spec revisions, product names) carry a version or date, and every lesson has an updated date checked against its sources.

Twelve LLM features across chat, search, extraction and agents, each calling models its own way: design the shared inference platform.
Days to train a stated dense model on a stated number of H100s at an MFU you choose and defend, using 6ND.

DPO versus PPO-based RLHF and why DPO skips the reward model; then specify a DPO dataset: fields, chosen and rejected sources, ties, noisy labels and filtering.
Engine and trainer log-probabilities disagree in an "on-policy" GRPO run: diagnose the mismatch and apply truncated importance sampling.

KV cache at 256K for a 1:7 attention-to-Mamba hybrid versus a dense MoE of similar size, from the published configurations.

Critique this design document for a multi-tenant chat backend with billing and moderation.
What a 1M-token context promise costs per request and per day at stated traffic, from list prices and a published model config.
Enterprise RAG with per-user permissions; the rubric becomes a checklist and the answer includes what you give up.
A multi-tenant chat backend with metered billing that counts cache reads and writes correctly.
A coding-agent platform: session log, lazily provisioned sandboxes, credential proxy, egress policy and cost per task.
A KV-cache decode step for a toy decoder whose output equals the full recompute, with grouped-query heads.

corrections.wrong: 800 ms voice-to-voice presented as a standard.
corrections.fix: Label 800 ms as one vendor's target; the Pipecat maintainers' June 2026 update sets 1,500 ms and measures a typical stack at about 1.3 s.

corrections.fix: Use RULER, NoLiMa and HELMET-style tasks; HELMET found needle results do not reliably predict downstream performance.

corrections.wrong: Image-token figures without the model family.
corrections.fix: Claude, OpenAI and Gemini count image tokens differently (28 px patches, 32 px patches or 512 px tiles, 258-token tiles); every figure names its family.

corrections.fix: OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning closed to new organisations on 7 May 2026 and ends new jobs for existing customers on 6 January 2027.

corrections.wrong: "Exactly once" claims for durable execution without naming the idempotency key.
corrections.fix: Durable execution is at-least-once per step; exactly-once outcomes need an idempotency key or a deduplicating provider, and approval does not guarantee exactly-once execution.
